docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Astrona is the CLI behind astrona.io's hands-on labs, and it works the same way whether a lab config comes from a local directory, a URL, or a git repository — so anyone can author and run their own labs without the platform.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• New to Astrona? Start with Installation, then run through the Quickstart.

  • Building a lab? Authoring a Lab walks through the full config.yaml shape with a worked example.

  • Looking up a flag or a YAML field? CLI Reference and Lab Config Schema are generated straight from the source.

  • Wiring astrona into CI? CI Integration covers astrona test and JUnit reporting.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Local kind clusters — auto-detects Docker or Podman on your PATH and creates/deletes the kind cluster accordingly, no manual provider flags needed.
  • QEMU VM labs — for labs that need a real OS (not just a container), runtime.type: qemu boots one or more VMs from a base image, with SSH wired up automatically.
  • Config from anywhere — point --config/-c at a local directory, a local file, an http(s):// URL, or a git repository via --git.
  • Bootstrap — run init scripts and apply Kubernetes manifests when a lab starts.
  • Testing stage — a CI-only stage that applies a reference solution, so a lab author can prove their own lab is actually solvable and passes grading before publishing it.
  • Proctor grading — a student never grades their own work: astrona submit hands the environment to the Proctor, which runs declarative checks and/or custom scripts and returns a PASS/FAIL verdict.
  • CI-friendly — astrona test runs the whole bootstrap → testing → submit → teardown pipeline in one command, with --junit-xml output for any CI system that understands JUnit.

docs.title: Project links
docs.text:
• Source: github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli
  • Platform: astrona.io
  • License: Apache License 2.0

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Go (version pinned in go.mod)
  • just
  • kind, kubectl, Docker or Podman — for actually running a lab
  • uv — for building/serving these docs (nothing else Python-related needed; uv run handles the rest)

docs.title: Justfile recipes
docs.text:
Recipe What it does just build Build the development binary at ./astrona; nothing is installed or moved just run <args> Build and run ./astrona, forwarding CLI arguments just clean Remove the built binary just fmt Fail if any file needs gofmt just fmt-fix Auto-fix formatting just vet go vet ./... just test go test ./... just check fmt + vet + test — run before committing just oat Build ./astrona and run the acceptance suite's smoke tier; --include full adds the full tier (see Acceptance suite) just docs-gen-cli Regenerate docs/reference/cli/ from the actual astrona command tree just docs Serve the docs site locally at http://127.0.0.1:8000 with live reload just build-docs Build the static docs site (mkdocs build --strict) — what CI runs

Run just with no arguments to list every recipe.

just build
./astrona --help
./astrona settings path
./astrona run ./examples/k8s-basics-01 --browser

Or build and run in one step:

just run --help
just run settings path
just run run ./examples/k8s-basics-01 --browser

./cmd/astrona is the Go source directory, not the executable. Running it directly can report permission denied; use ./astrona after just build, just run <args>, or go run ./cmd/astrona <args> instead.

Use ./astrona to run your local build. Plain astrona may run the installed release from your PATH. The former just install recipe has been removed.

Unversioned builds (including plain go build and go run) store their credentials, settings, acceptance receipts, lab state and caches under ~/.astrona-dev. Git clones are in ~/.astrona-dev/cache/repos. They use astrodev- cluster names (astrodev-test- for authoring tests), so release discovery and destroy '*' do not select development clusters, or vice versa. First use requires its own terms acceptance. Settings review and login are optional. Existing release data is neither copied nor migrated.

Tagged releases, built with -X main.Version=vX.Y.Z, keep ~/.astrona, the existing OS Git cache and astro- cluster names. Do not stamp a local test binary with a release version unless you intend to use release data. Development builds disable update checks, self-upgrade and installation of other release binaries; rebuild from source to update them. Background lab helpers run the same binary and keep the same profile.

This isolates Astrona-managed state, not the machine: container engines, images, host ports and your kubectl configuration are still shared. Port collisions remain possible. Lab scripts still run on your machine. Development builds default to http://localhost:3000; release builds default to https://astrona.io. astrona login --site, ASTRONA_URL, or a site remembered with a development sign-in can select another server. ASTRONA_URL overrides the remembered site; the login flag overrides it for sign-in. Logging in and submitting can affect the account on the selected server. On Windows, build and run inside WSL. An unversioned native launcher refuses to forward commands to the installed release.

docs.title: Working on the docs
docs.text:
This site is MkDocs + Material for MkDocs, versioned with mike. Source lives under docs/, config at the repo root mkdocs.yml.

just docs

opens a live-reloading local copy. The CLI reference under docs/reference/cli/ is generated (via astrona docgen, a hidden command wired into just docs/just build-docs) — don't hand-edit it, edit the command's Short/Long/flag descriptions in cmd/astrona/cmd_*.go instead.

Adding a command: put it in a help group in cmd/astrona/groups.go (astrona --help lists commands by group, in workflow order) and add its generated page(s) to the matching group of the CLI Reference in mkdocs.yml. Unit tests fail if either is missing.

docs.title: Theme and browser checks
docs.text:
The docs use the frontend's Mission Control palette and typography. The matching tokens live in docs/stylesheets/extra.css; their source is astrona-web/app/assets/css/_tokens.scss. docs/overrides/main.html adds the shared background and motion control. home.html contains the homepage hero; the guide links and feature descriptions stay in docs/index.md.

Material still owns search, code copying, mobile navigation and mike version selection. Keep overrides small and use the url template filter for internal links so release-specific paths work. Do not hand-edit generated command pages. Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono are requested from Google Fonts, as on the frontend; system fonts remain available when those requests are blocked.

Decorative SVGs are hidden from assistive technology. Content is visible without JavaScript. Motion must respect prefers-reduced-motion and the saved pause choice in docs/javascripts/motion.js; do not make animation part of navigation or hide content until an animation runs.

Build the site, then check it in Chromium:

just build-docs
uv run --with playwright playwright install chromium
uv run --with playwright python .github/scripts/check-docs-theme.py \
  --site-dir site --screenshots /tmp/astrona-docs-screenshots

Use --browser /path/to/chromium to reuse an installed browser. The check starts a temporary localhost server under /dev/ and checks desktop/375px layouts, navigation, search, copy controls, reduced motion and a no-JavaScript page. It does not run labs or contact Astrona's services. Screenshots stay outside the repository. Also check the deployed mike version selector after a release.

Versioning and deployment (on push to main and on release tags) are handled by .github/workflows/docs.yml — see that file for the exact mike deploy invocations.

docs.title: Security-sensitive areas
docs.text: If your change touches remote script execution, QEMU base image handling, remote config fetching, git config sources, or path resolution, read AGENTS.md and the relevant security reference first — these are explicit trust boundaries with existing conventions (HTTPS-only, size caps, path containment) that new code should follow.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
just check                                          # fmt + vet + unit tests
go build -o astrona ./cmd/astrona
./astrona test -c examples/k8s-basics-01 --junit-xml=report.xml   # e2e against a real kind cluster

The Ubuntu catalog integration test runs the first published lab without logging in:

bash .github/scripts/test-catalog-lab.sh ./astrona /tmp/astrona-catalog-diagnostics

For Podman, pass podman as the third argument and run with rootful Podman (for example, sudo env "PATH=$PATH" bash .github/scripts/test-catalog-lab.sh ./astrona /tmp/astrona-catalog-diagnostics podman). The script explicitly selects the requested engine using KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER.

It needs Linux, Docker or Podman, Kind and kubectl, plus network access to GitHub and Docker Hub. It isolates credentials and kubeconfig, uses --headless for headless setup without a new account session, verifies node readiness, repairs the first lab's intentional image typo with imagePullPolicy: Never to confirm the Alpine preload, then destroys the lab and checks that its cluster, containers, context and saved state are gone. Failures retain logs and diagnostics and trigger cleanup. CI runs it on Ubuntu 24.04 with Docker's classic and containerd image stores and with rootful Podman.

docs.title: Acceptance suite
docs.text:
acceptance/ holds a Robot Framework suite that drives the built ./astrona the way a learner and a lab author would. It has two tiers, chosen by tag:

  • smoke runs on every pull request (Acceptance (smoke) in CI, report in the oat-smoke-report artifact).
  • full adds the lab tools (shell, soft reset, doctor, diagnose, port forwards), a signed-out catalog lab, the two VM targets and a signed-in learner (the login suite). The Acceptance (full) workflow runs it on every release tag, RCs included, before anything is built, in three jobs: Acceptance full (kind) runs the smoke and full tiers without the vm and login tests, Acceptance full (vm) runs only the vm tests and Acceptance full (login) only the login tests. The release only builds when all three pass, and their reports are attached to the GitHub release as oat-report-<version>-kind.zip, oat-report-<version>-vm.zip and oat-report-<version>-login.zip. Run it by hand from the Actions tab.
just oat                    # build ./astrona, run the smoke tier, write oat-report/
just oat --include full     # smoke and full tiers
just oat --exclude kind     # only the checks that create no cluster
just oat --include vm       # smoke tier plus both VM targets
just oat --include vm --exclude kind    # VM targets only (and the smoke checks that need neither)
just oat --include vm --exclude desktop # VM with terminal only, e.g. on a Linux box without X
just oat --include login     # smoke tier plus the signed-in learner
just oat --test "Run Creates The Lab"

Other tags say what a test needs: kind creates a cluster, network reaches the internet (astrona.io, the lab catalog), vm boots a QEMU VM, desktop opens that VM's window, login starts its own Keycloak. The workspace UI is a terminal app that needs an interactive terminal, so it is covered by the PTY tests in go test, not here.

It needs kind, kubectl and Docker or Podman, plus uv (Robot Framework is pinned in acceptance/requirements.txt). Each suite gets a throwaway HOME, so your own labs and settings under ~/.astrona-dev are untouched; the container engine's config still comes from your real home. kind cluster names are shared by the whole engine, so a suite refuses to start while a cluster named after its example lab (k8s-basics-01) exists. Set OAT_ISOLATE_HOME=false to run against your real HOME.

docs.title: VM suites
docs.text:
60_vm_terminal.robot and 70_vm_desktop.robot cover astrona's two VM targets with the labs in acceptance/labs/: run, list, status, a failed and then a passing submit (the answer is typed into astrona ssh), stop refusing a VM lab, and destroy, after which no qemu process and no VM state may be left. The desktop suite also checks that the VM opens its window (display: true), the desktop astrona offers today: on macOS the window server must list a window owned by the qemu process; on Linux an X display must show a window titled after it. That window has no graphics or input devices configured yet, so the suite checks that it exists, not what it shows.

They need qemu with hardware acceleration: on macOS brew install qemu (HVF, Apple Silicon or Intel), on Linux qemu-system-x86 (or qemu-system-arm with qemu-efi-aarch64), qemu-utils, genisoimage and a usable /dev/kvm. The desktop suite on Linux also needs qemu-system-gui, x11-utils and a display: run it under xvfb-run on a machine without one. Without KVM astrona falls back to software emulation, which is too slow for the suite; CI fails the vm job when /dev/kvm is missing rather than skipping it. A suite refuses to start while a qemu process for its lab (oat-vm-terminal, oat-vm-desktop) is running.

The VM base image is a Debian 13 genericcloud qcow2 (about 330 MB, amd64 or arm64 to match the host) from a dated build at cloud.debian.org. Its URL and the SHA-512 sums from that build's SHA512SUMS are pinned in acceptance/resources/astrona.resource. It is downloaded once into ~/.cache/astrona-oat/images/ ($XDG_CACHE_HOME/astrona-oat, or OAT_CACHE_DIR when set), verified on every run and hard-linked into a copy of the lab (astrona refuses a symlinked base image). To move to a newer build, change the date in the URL and both sums together. Delete the cache folder to free the space.

docs.title: Login suite
docs.text:
80_login.robot is a signed-in learner: astrona login --headless, then a headless Chromium opens the link it prints and signs in, then whoami, a catalog lab run under a lab session, a submit graded as not passed, progress, destroy and logout. It needs no account and no secret. The suite starts its own sign-in stack and removes it afterwards:

  • Keycloak (quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8, the image the Astrona workspace runs) in a container on a free loopback port, with the realm in acceptance/keycloak/: a public astrona-cli client with the OAuth 2.0 device grant and a consent screen. Setup creates a test user whose random password exists only in the suite's process; it is never logged or written down.
  • A fake Astrona site (Python's http.server in a thread) that answers the CLI's /api/cli calls: it passes the device flow through to Keycloak, accepts a lab-session call only with a bearer token Keycloak's userinfo vouches for, and records what the CLI sent so the suite can check it (a session for the catalog lab created by the test user, the result posted on submit, the sign-in revoked on logout).

So it does not exercise the real astrona.io device page (astrona-web) or astrona-svc-labs, only the CLI's side of their contract.

It needs Podman or Docker (the suite uses whichever answers, Podman first; set OAT_CONTAINER_RUNTIME=docker to choose), kind for the catalog lab, and Playwright's Chromium, installed once:

uv run --with-requirements acceptance/requirements.txt playwright install chromium

The first run pulls the Keycloak image; Keycloak then needs up to a minute to start. --include full runs this suite too; add --exclude login to leave it out.

Path Contents acceptance/suites/ One .robot file per area; tag each test with its tier (smoke or full) and what it needs (kind, network, vm, desktop) acceptance/labs/ The VM labs the VM suites run; their base.qcow2 is linked in at run time, never committed acceptance/resources/astrona.resource Shared keywords: Run Astrona, Run Astrona Json, Run Kubectl On Lab acceptance/keycloak/ The Keycloak realm the login suite imports acceptance/libraries/SignInStack.py The login suite's Keycloak container, fake site and browser sign-in acceptance/libraries/AstronaLib.py Only what Robot cannot express cleanly: isolated HOME, JSON parsing, kind and qemu lookups, the VM image cache, the desktop window check

docs.title: Dependency updates
docs.text:
Renovate — Mend's hosted GitHub App, configured by .github/renovate.json5 — opens PRs for dependency updates; they get the full CI run like any other PR (jobs and logs: developer.mend.io). Renovate merges its PRs after checks pass, using its own merge process rather than GitHub's native auto-merge. New releases are only proposed after they're 3 days old. The Dependency Dashboard issue lists everything pending.

When a same-repository renovate[bot] PR from a renovate/ branch merges into main, Renovate patch release creates the next stable patch tag at that exact merge commit. For example, v0.4.6 becomes v0.4.7, then v0.4.8. Only the final number changes, regardless of whether the dependency update itself is major, minor, patch, or a digest. Pre-release tags do not affect this calculation. Ordinary PRs and closed, unmerged PRs do not trigger a release.

The workflow queues merges and runs the existing binary, Linux package, Homebrew, and versioned documentation pipelines. It calls these workflows explicitly because a tag created with GITHUB_TOKEN does not trigger another push workflow. No new token is needed; Homebrew publication still uses the existing HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN secret.

Retry a failed run from Actions: it reuses its existing patch tag. An older merge already included in a later stable tag is skipped to avoid releasing older source as a newer version. Tags are never moved or overwritten. The first stable tag must already exist. The allocation policy tests run with python3 -B -m unittest discover -s .github/scripts -p 'test_renovate_release.py'.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Pushing a tag vX.Y.Z runs .github/workflows/release.yml: it builds the four binaries with build provenance, publishes the GitHub release as latest, updates the Homebrew tap and then installs from the tap on macOS and Linux to check it.

A tag with a - — a release candidate like v0.4.0-rc1 — is published as a pre-release: it never becomes "latest", so astrona upgrade, the update notice and Homebrew keep offering the last stable release, and the tap isn't touched. Testers install an RC on purpose with astrona versions install 0.4.0-rc1.

docs.title: Grading (the Proctor)
docs.text:
A student never grades their own work — the same way a real exam is graded by a proctor, not by the person taking it. astrona submit hands the running environment to the Proctor, a single component (internal/proctor) that both the student-facing submit and the lab-developer-facing test command go through. No other command reads validation.checks/validation.script directly.

If you restart an existing lab through the UI's discard confirmation, the new run is local only. astrona submit still grades it and records the local result, but does not upload it to the Astrona API, even if you are signed in. This choice is saved with the run and also applies after reopening the CLI.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
validation:
  checks:
    - name: "lab-ns namespace exists"
      type: "resourceExists"
      resource: "namespace/lab-ns"
    - name: "pod is ready"
      type: "podReady"
      resource: "pod/my-pod -n lab-ns"
    - name: "custom command check"
      type: "command"
      command: "kubectl get deploy my-app -o jsonpath={.status.readyReplicas}"
      expect: "3"
  script:
    name: "verify-configmap-content"
    type: "file"
    source: "validate.sh"
  scripts:
    - name: "check-network"
      type: "file"
      source: "validate-network.sh"

docs.title: Declarative checks (validation.checks)
docs.text:
type Runs Passes when resourceExists kubectl --context <ctx> get <resource> exit code 0 podReady kubectl --context <ctx> wait --for=condition=Ready --timeout=60s <resource> (or the check's timeout) exit code 0 within 60s command the given shell words directly (not through a shell) exit code 0, and every matcher set holds on trimmed stdout jsonpath kubectl --context <ctx> get <resource> -o jsonpath=<jsonpath> every matcher set holds on the value count kubectl --context <ctx> get <resource> -o name the number of objects is within min / max http GET <url> (10s timeout) status is expectStatus (default 200), and every matcher set holds on the body

Time limits: every check runs for at most 1m (http: 10s; podReady: its 60s wait) unless it sets timeout (e.g. timeout: 2m). A check that runs past it is stopped, together with everything it started, and fails with timed out after … — it earns no points, and the rest of the lab is still graded. See Time limits.

Matchers (for command, jsonpath, http): expect (exact), contains, expectRegex — set any combination; all must hold.

validation:
  checks:
    - name: scaled to 3
      type: jsonpath
      resource: deploy/web -n shop
      jsonpath: "{.spec.replicas}"
      expect: "3"
    - name: image pinned
      type: jsonpath
      resource: deploy/web -n shop
      jsonpath: "{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}"
      expectRegex: "^nginx:1\\.27"
    - name: at least 3 web pods
      type: count
      resource: pods -l app=web -n shop
      min: 3
    - name: site answers through the gateway
      type: http
      url: http://web.localtest.me:8080/
      contains: Welcome to nginx

A failed check says what it found: {.spec.replicas} is "2" — want exactly "3", found 2, want at least 3, GET … → 404, want 200. http checks reach the lab through a port forward or the gateway addon. astrona validate checks each check has the fields its type needs.

resourceExists, podReady, jsonpath and count run kubectl on your machine, and only ever against the lab's own isolated kubeconfig and context (or a linked cluster's) — never your own ~/.kube/config. So they need a kind lab: astrona validate rejects them in a qemu lab, which has no cluster for kubectl (use a validation script, which runs inside the VM), and grading stops with an error (exit 1) if a running lab has no kubeconfig of its own (a kind lab started by an older astrona — astrona reset fixes it). resource may only carry the flags -n/--namespace, -l/--selector, --field-selector and -A/--all-namespaces; any other flag (--kubeconfig, --server, -o, …) or a value starting with - is rejected. Before the first of these checks, the Proctor makes sure the cluster answers: an unreachable cluster is a grading error (exit 1, nothing recorded or sent), not a failed check.

On a kind lab, command checks (and every script) run with KUBECONFIG set to the lab's own kubeconfig, so a plain kubectl ... grades the lab's cluster regardless of the student's current-context. They also get ASTRONA_KUBE_CONTEXT, ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER and ASTRONA_CONTAINER_ENGINE, so a check can reach the lab's node containers without hardcoding the lab name (see runtimes).

docs.title: Script checks (validation.script / validation.scripts)
docs.text:
Beyond existence checks — for verifying actual content, behavior, or anything a kubectl get can't express. script (singular) runs first if set, then every entry in scripts (plural), in order. Exit code 0 is a pass, non-zero is a fail — a failing lab is a normal graded outcome, not a tool error. A validation script may run for 5m unless it sets timeout; one that runs longer is killed, with every process it started, and fails with timed out after 5m.

For a qemu runtime, scripts run over SSH inside the VM instead of on the host. Exit code 255 is reserved there: it's what ssh exits with when it can't reach the VM, so it's treated as "grading couldn't run" (exit 1, nothing recorded or sent), not as a fail — a script must not exit 255 to mean "fail". For a multi-VM lab, the shared root validation block's scripts run once per VM (each result suffixed (vmName) in the report; root checks run once), and each VM's own nested runtime.qemu[].validation block (if set) is graded after that, scoped to just that VM: its checks, then its scripts, each result suffixed (vmName) too (and, in submit -o json, carrying "vm": "<vmName>"). A single-VM lab grades its one VM's nested block after the root one. A command check in a VM's own block runs inside that VM over SSH, like a script (its words quoted, never interpolated), while a root command check runs on this machine; an http check runs from this machine in either. Only the root validation.passPercent sets the pass mark: astrona validate (and run) reject a passPercent in a VM's own block.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
Output is pytest/robot-style — one line per check, then a summary:

  PASS  lab-ns namespace exists (0.18s)
  PASS  hello-config configmap exists (0.09s)
  FAIL  verify-configmap-content (0.31s)
        expected value "hello-world", got "unset"

2 passed, 1 failed in 0.58s

PROCTOR: FAIL

The command's exit code reflects the verdict — submit/test exit non-zero on a FAIL, so both are safe to gate a script or CI job on.

A lab with nothing to grade — no validation.checks and no validation scripts — never passes: submit and test stop with an error (exit 1) and record nothing. astrona validate warns about it; that's fine for an ungraded playground, which is only ever run.

docs.title: Hints, score and attempts
docs.text:
Each check and validation script can carry a hint — shown only when it fails — and points (default 1):

validation:
  passPercent: 75            # optional: pass at 75% instead of requiring every check
  checks:
    - name: namespace shop exists
      type: command
      command: kubectl get namespace shop -o name
      expect: namespace/shop
      points: 3
      hint: "Namespaces are cluster-scoped — kubectl create namespace <name>"

  FAIL  configmap app-config in shop (0.03s)
        hint: A ConfigMap lives in a namespace — did you pass -n shop?

1 passed, 1 failed in 0.15s
Score: 3/4 points (75%) — pass mark 75%

Attempt #2: 3/4 (+3 point(s) since #1)
  now passing: namespace shop exists

PROCTOR: PASS
  • Write hints as nudges toward the concept, not the answer — the guide doc has the full solution.
  • Pass rule: without passPercent, every check and script must pass (as before). With it, the submission passes once the weighted score reaches it — like a certification exam's pass mark.
  • astrona submit --no-hints grades without showing hints (exam conditions).
  • Every astrona submit is recorded in ~/.astrona/results/<lab>.jsonl; each submission shows the change since the previous one, and astrona submit --history lists all attempts with the best score. astrona test (CI) doesn't record attempts.
  • astrona submit with no lab named — no argument, nothing picked with astrona use, no lab config in the current directory — grades the only running lab (Submitting astro-my-lab (the only running lab).), found again through what astrona run remembered. With several running it lists them, each with the command that names it.
  • A catalog lab started while signed in also sends each result to its lab page. Sending never changes the exit code.
  • A submit is final. Every recorded result, PASS or FAIL, ends the attempt and stops its timer, and then submit deletes the lab, as astrona destroy does: once the result was sent (or queued because Astrona couldn't be reached — it goes out later under the same key, never twice), or, for a run without a lab session (local-only, a lab from your own files), once it is saved here. There is no option to keep the lab; teardown.keepCluster does not apply. Only a tracked result Astrona refuses, or one that can't be sent or queued, leaves the lab. Use astrona submit --watch to check your work without ending the attempt.

docs.title: Live grading while you work
docs.text:
astrona submit --watch            # re-grade every 5s (--interval to change, min 2s)

Redraws a compact board — ✓/✗ per check, hints, score, exam time — every few seconds until Ctrl-C, so you see a check flip to ✓ the moment your fix lands. Watch runs are not recorded as attempts and end nothing: this is how to check your work while the attempt stays open. Run a plain astrona submit only when you're done — it ends the attempt and deletes the lab. In watch mode validation scripts' output is hidden and podReady checks give up after 2s instead of waiting a minute. When the output isn't a terminal, a new board is printed only when a result changes. With exam.strict, once the time limit has passed the board shows "Over the time limit — a submit now would not count as a pass" instead of "Passing", the same rule a plain submit applies. Because nothing is recorded, --watch refuses -o json, --junit-xml and --history with an error rather than ignoring them.

docs.title: Exam mode
docs.text:
exam:
  timeLimit: 2h      # clock starts when `astrona run` has the lab ready
  hideHints: true    # no hints, like the real exam
  strict: true       # a submission after the limit can't pass
validation:
  passPercent: 66    # e.g. a CKA-style pass mark (see above)

Score: 9/12 points (75%) — pass mark 66%
Time: 1h12m of 2h0m used (48m left)
PROCTOR: PASS
  • The clock lives in ~/.astrona/exams/<lab>.json; astrona reset starts a fresh one, astrona destroy clears it. It keeps running while a lab is paused with astrona stop, like a real exam.
  • Without strict, an over-time submission is still graded normally — the time is just reported ("over time by 5m").
  • astrona submit --history adds a TIME USED column, marking over-time exam attempts. A learning lab's time counts from Start in the browser workspace, or from when the lab became ready; astrona submit prints it as Time spent.
  • astrona test (CI) ignores exam settings.

docs.title: JUnit XML for CI
docs.text:
Both astrona submit and astrona test accept --junit-xml=<path>:

astrona submit --junit-xml=report.xml

Writes a standard JUnit XML report alongside the terminal output — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, and most other CI systems render this natively as a test report. See CI Integration.

docs.title: Progress across labs
docs.text:
astrona progress

LAB            RESULT        BEST         ATTEMPTS   FASTEST PASS   LAST
k8s-web-01     passed (#2)   5/5 (100%)   3          18m0s          2h ago
net-policy-02  not yet       3/5 (60%)    4          -              1d ago

1 of 2 lab(s) passed.

Built from the attempt history every astrona submit records: whether and on which attempt you passed, your best score, how many attempts, the fastest passing time for exam labs, and when you last worked on it. -o json for export or scripts.

docs.title: submit vs test
docs.text: astrona submit astrona test Who runs it a student, on a lab they already run a lab author, in CI, proving their own lab Applies testing.* (reference solution) first No Yes Tears down afterwards No (you still own the environment) Always, even on failure Cluster name prefix astro- astro-test- (never collides with a real astrona run)

docs.title: Lab Lifecycle
docs.text:
A lab moves through four stages, each an optional block in config.yaml. Every command only runs the stages relevant to it — astrona run never touches testing or validation, astrona submit never touches bootstrap.

astrona run          astrona submit           astrona destroy
─────────────►  ┌──────────────┐  ────────►  ┌─────────────┐
 bootstrap       │  (your work)  │   Proctor    teardown
                 └──────────────┘   grading

astrona test  ──────────────────────────────────────────────►
 bootstrap  →  testing  →  submit (Proctor grading)  →  teardown (always)

docs.title: bootstrap
docs.text:
Runs on astrona run and at the start of astrona test. Three parts, all optional, run in this order:

bootstrap:
  init:
    - name: "setup"
      type: "file"      # "file" | "folder" | "url"
      source: "setup.sh"
  manifests:
    - name: "base"
      type: "folder"    # "file" | "folder" | "url"
      source: "manifests/"
  waitFor:
    - resource: deploy/web          # rollout complete
    - resource: pod
      selector: app=db              # every matching pod Ready
      timeout: 5m
  • init — scripts run in order (on kind, after the cluster's DNS is up), through whichever executor the runtime provides (host bash for kind, SSH into the VM for qemu). A folder source runs its regular *.sh files in filename order — number them (01-x.sh, 02-y.sh) to control ordering. Hidden files, other extensions (README.md, editor backups like setup.sh~), subfolders and symlinks are skipped.
  • manifests — applied with kubectl apply against the cluster's context. Requires a kind runtime (or a runtime with a kubectl-reachable cluster) — astrona run errors out immediately if bootstrap.manifests is set on a runtime with none.
  • waitFor — readiness gates, checked in order after manifests. kubectl apply returns as soon as the API server accepts the objects, while pods may still be pulling images; without a gate, "ready" only means "applied". Each gate waits (default 2 minutes) for a rollout to finish or a condition to be met, and retries while its target doesn't exist yet (an operator creating it, a CRD still registering). If a gate times out, astrona run fails and prints the target's current state plus the namespace's recent events. kind only. See WaitFor.

testing takes the same waitFor list: under astrona test it gates grading on the reference solution actually being up, so the Proctor never races pods that are still starting.

docs.title: testing
docs.text: Same shape as bootstrap (init + manifests), but only ever runs as part of astrona test, never astrona run. This is where a lab author puts the reference solution — the manifests/scripts that drive the cluster into the "lab completed" state, so astrona test has something real to grade. A student taking the lab never sees this stage; it exists so a lab author's CI can prove their own lab is solvable and passes the Proctor's checks before publishing it.

docs.title: validation
docs.text: Not a "run" stage — it's what the Proctor executes when you run astrona submit (or as the grading step inside astrona test). Declarative checks plus one or more custom pass/fail scripts.

docs.title: teardown
docs.text:
Runs on astrona destroy, and always (even on failure) at the end of astrona test.

An explicit config, Git source, catalog lab, or saved selection must resolve successfully before astrona destroy proceeds. If it cannot be loaded, nothing is destroyed. Discovery of the sole running lab is only a fallback when no source was selected. Discovery also rechecks the run under its mutation lock; a lab restarted during discovery is kept.

teardown:
  init:
    - name: "dump-logs"
      type: "file"
      source: "teardown/dump-logs.sh"
  keepCluster: false
  • init scripts run first — same file/folder/url shape as bootstrap.init, best-effort (a failing teardown script only warns, it never blocks the cluster from being deleted).
  • If a kind lab's environment is already gone, the scripts still run on the host for host-side cleanup — with KUBECONFIG=/dev/null, so a script's kubectl can never reach your own current context instead of the lab. A qemu lab's scripts only ever run inside its VMs: if the VMs are gone or unreachable, they're skipped with a warning.
  • A remote lab (--git, URL, catalog) must be approved before astrona destroy runs its teardown scripts, just like run. If it isn't (you decline, or there's no terminal and no --trust), the scripts are skipped with a warning and the lab is still destroyed.
  • Linked clusters (runtime.kind.clusters) can have their own teardown.init; they run after the lab's, in reverse start order, each with KUBECONFIG pointing at its cluster (skipped if that cluster is gone).
  • The lab's linked clusters are destroyed even if destroying the lab itself fails.
  • If the lab's astrona test copy is active, destroy leaves it running and prints a warning.
  • If astrona run pointed your kubectl at the lab, destroy switches it back to the context you had before (only while the lab's context is still current — see kubeconfig isolation), then forgets what was remembered about the lab (~/.astrona/labs/<lab>.json: its config source and lab session).
  • The exam clock and the lab's memory are removed only once the lab is deleted, or confirmed not to exist. If Docker or Podman is installed but doesn't answer, astrona can't tell whether a kind lab still exists: destroy stops before changing anything — no teardown scripts, nothing deleted, saved state, session and exam clock kept — and asks you to start Docker or Podman and run destroy again. run and reset stop the same way, and astrona list shows remembered labs as EngineUnreachable instead of dropping them. A qemu lab destroyed by name doesn't need the container engine.
  • The lab's port forwards are stopped whenever a lab is destroyed by name, whatever runtime it turns out to have.
  • keepCluster: true makes astrona destroy skip deleting the environment — useful while iterating on a lab from your own files, since astrona destroy re-run without it will still clean up. It never keeps a catalog lab or a run with a lab session, and astrona submit ignores it: every submit deletes the lab.

docs.title: Starting over: astrona reset
docs.text:
astrona reset -c ./labs/my-lab          # asks before throwing the lab away
astrona reset -c ./labs/my-lab --yes    # no prompt (required in scripts/CI)

reset runs the lab's teardown scripts, destroys it, and then does everything astrona run does — the lab ends up exactly as a fresh run leaves it (any changes made while working on it are gone). If the lab isn't running, it's simply created.

  • The config is validated before anything is destroyed — a broken config aborts with "nothing was reset" and leaves the existing lab as it was.
  • teardown.keepCluster is ignored: reset always recreates.
  • --soft keeps the cluster(s) and only puts the lab back: it deletes every namespace created after the platform (kube-system, addons, …) was set up, clears what isn't astrona's from default, re-runs the bootstrap and restarts port forwards — about 5 seconds instead of 40. Cluster-wide objects a student created (CRDs, ClusterRoles, …) aren't reverted; use a full reset for those. A lab started by astrona before v0.3 has no baseline yet and needs one full reset first.
  • --cluster <name> rebuilds just one linked cluster of a running lab, leaving the lab and its other clusters as they are.
  • In a terminal it asks for confirmation; without a terminal it refuses unless --yes is passed.
  • A full reset of a catalog lab asks for confirmation when running without a login, like run (--without-login explicitly accepts running without account progress tracking; --headless skips the reminder and new account sessions). When signed in, it starts a fresh lab session and opens the new lab page once the lab is rebuilt. --soft and --cluster keep the current session and need no sign-in.

astrona run on a lab that's already running asks the same question: destroy it and start over? — yes does what reset does, no keeps the lab as it is. astrona run --yes starts over without asking; without a terminal, run on a running lab stops and names --yes. If other labs are running, run also offers to destroy them first (handy when moving from one lab of a training to the next) — a multi-VM qemu lab counts as one lab, all its VMs destroyed and the lab forgotten together, as astrona destroy <lab> does — only when asked in a terminal; --yes never touches other labs.

To pause a lab instead of losing it, see astrona stop / astrona start.

submit, stop, and start refuse to run while another command changes the same lab. Submission keeps the run reserved through grading, recording, and result delivery, so a concurrent reset cannot attach its grade to a new attempt. Start and stop also reserve the lab's linked clusters before changing containers.

With no selected lab, these commands can choose the only matching running or stopped lab. An unreadable saved selection or a failed explicit config selection is an error; it never selects a different lab as a fallback.

docs.title: Source types, everywhere
docs.text:
Every script/manifest reference (bootstrap.init, bootstrap.manifests, testing.*, teardown.init, validation.script) shares the same ResourceItem shape:

- name: "human-readable label"
  description: "optional, printed before the step runs"
  type: "file"      # or "folder" or "url" (manifests: "file" | "folder" | "url")
  source: "path/or/URL"

url sources — scripts and manifests alike — are downloaded to a size-capped temp file before running or applying (a manifest URL is never handed to kubectl apply -f <url> directly). Every remote download (scripts, manifests, the lab config, QEMU base images, astrona release binaries) is https:// only, and that includes redirects: a redirect to a plain http:// URL is refused rather than followed. Every download also has an explicit byte cap so a misbehaving remote can't exhaust disk.

docs.title: Command output
docs.text:
astrona run, test, submit, and destroy render progress as a compact per-phase step view — one line per step (✓ done, ✗ failed, - skipped) with its elapsed time, grouped under section headers (Bootstrap, Machine: <name> for a multi-VM qemu lab, and so on). On an interactive terminal the in-progress step shows a spinner.

The raw output of every underlying command (kind, qemu, kubectl, each bootstrap script) is not shown by default. Instead:

  • It is always written in full to a per-run log file at ~/.astrona/logs/<command>-<lab>-<timestamp>.log. The path is printed at the end of a run. Browse past runs with astrona logs.
  • If a step fails, the tail of that step's output is printed inline right before the error, and the command exits non-zero.
  • Passing --verbose streams everything live as it happens and disables the spinner — the pre-step-view behaviour. The log file is still written.

Non-interactive output (piped, redirected, or CI) automatically drops the spinner and ANSI styling and prints one plain line per step.

On a terminal, problems stand out in color: Error: and what went wrong in red (hints on what to do next follow in the normal color), [WARN] in yellow, [INFO] in cyan, and grading results as green PASS / red FAIL with a yellow hint:. Set NO_COLOR=1 to turn colors off everywhere; piped and redirected output never has them.

When a step fails, its error and the tail of its output are printed with the path of the full log — astrona logs view opens it.

docs.title: Questions astrona asks
docs.text:
Question Answer it up front with Throw a lab away? (reset, logs clean, run on a running lab) --yes / -y Run a lab from a URL, git repo or bundle? (shows what it will do) --trust Download and install the astrona version a lab needs? --install-version (a newer release only — switching to an older one is always asked at a terminal)

The last two approve running someone else's code, so they have their own flags rather than a general -y. Without a terminal astrona never waits for an answer: it stops and names the flag.

For a qemu lab, a successful astrona run also prints a Connect: block with the ready-to-paste astrona ssh <name> command for each VM.

For a kind lab with runtime.portForwards, astrona run starts those forwards after bootstrap and prints a Port forwards: block with each forward's local URL and status (Ready/NotReady/…). astrona port-forward list shows the same status any time later.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Grading covers exactly what the Proctor checks and how astrona submit/astrona test report the result.

docs.title: Run Logs
docs.text:
Every lifecycle command — astrona run, test, submit, destroy — tees its full output to a per-run log file, no matter which display mode you used. The compact step view (or --verbose stream) is what you see live; the log file is the complete record, including every line of subprocess output the step view collapses.

For a cluster-level picture (pods, events, node and container logs) rather than astrona's own output, see diagnostics — collected automatically when astrona run fails after creation or astrona test fails, or on demand with astrona diagnose. If Kind creation itself fails, Astrona retains the failed nodes temporarily, exports their logs to a private directory under ~/.astrona/diagnostics/, then deletes only that new cluster. A pre-existing cluster with the same name is refused and left alone. Ctrl+C during astrona run or astrona reset works the same way: the step that is running stops, and only what that run created is removed (a second Ctrl+C quits at once). Diagnostics are best effort and commands have time limits; the original startup error still determines the exit status.

docs.title: Where they live
docs.text:
~/.astrona/logs/<command>-<lab>-<UTC timestamp>.log

e.g. run-astro-disk-lab-20260830T120000Z.log. The directory is created on first use, owner-only (0700, log files 0600) since logs hold full script output and the command line, and never pruned automatically — see astrona logs clean.

docs.title: File format
docs.text:
# astrona run  lab=astro-disk-lab  2026-08-30T12:00:00Z
# astrona run -c ./labs/disk --verbose

=== Lab: astro-disk-lab ===

--- create cluster ---
<raw docker / kind / qemu / kubectl / bash output>
--- ok: create cluster (42s) ---

--- apply manifests ---
--- skip: apply manifests (none) ---

# done: result=ok steps=2/0/0 duration=44s
  • Line 1 — command, lab name, and start time (RFC 3339, UTC). Authoritative; the filename is only a fallback.
  • Line 2 — the exact argv the run was invoked with.
  • === … === — a section header (a lifecycle phase, or a per-VM group).
  • --- … --- — a step starting; --- ok: / --- skip: / --- FAIL: — that step resolving, with elapsed time or a skip reason.
  • [WARN] … — a non-fatal warning.
  • Footer — # done: result=<ok|fail> steps=<ok>/<skipped>/<failed> duration=<elapsed>, written when the command finishes (including a clean interrupt). A log with no footer is from a run that was killed outright; astrona logs list shows its result as UNKNOWN, or FAIL if any step had already failed.

docs.title: Reading them back
docs.text:
astrona logs (alias log) is the read side:

Command Purpose astrona logs list Table of recorded runs, newest first — index, command, lab, start, duration, result, size. astrona logs view [ref] Show one run's log through your pager ($PAGER, else less); --tail, --grep, --no-pager. astrona logs path [ref] Print a log's absolute path — for cat, grep, editor, etc. astrona logs export [ref] Copy logs out of ~/.astrona to a file or directory. astrona logs clean Delete old logs (--keep, --older-than; requires --yes to actually delete).

docs.title: Referring to a run
docs.text:
Anywhere a [ref] is accepted:

  • omitted or latest — the most recent run (honouring --lab / --command).
  • an index from astrona logs list — 1 is always the newest.
  • the UTC stamp from the filename — 20260830T120000Z.
  • a filename or an absolute path to the log.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
logs list, logs view, and logs export take --format:

  • raw (view/export) / table (list) — the default human view.
  • json, yaml — machine-readable. For list it's the array of run metadata; for view / export it's the parsed log: {meta, lines: [{kind, text}, …]} where kind is header, section, step, ok, skip, fail, warn, done, or output.

docs.title: Runtimes: kind vs qemu
docs.text:
A lab's runtime.type picks which backend astrona spins up. Every command (run, submit, destroy, test) works the same way regardless of which one a lab uses — they all resolve to the same LabEnvironment shape internally.

runtime:
  type: kind   # default — omit the whole `runtime:` block for the same effect

docs.title: kind (default)
docs.text: A local Kubernetes cluster via kind, on whichever container engine (Docker or Podman) astrona finds first on your PATH. This is the default and needs no runtime: block at all — every pre-existing lab config with no runtime.type keeps working unchanged.

docs.title: Cluster shape (runtime.kind)
docs.text:
By default a lab gets kind's defaults: one control-plane node, the node image bundled with the installed kind, and the kindnet CNI. A lab that needs more declares runtime.kind:

runtime:
  kind:
    version: v1.31.2          # match the exam's Kubernetes version
    nodes:
      workers: 2              # scheduling, taints, drain, DaemonSets
    networking:
      disableDefaultCNI: true # bring your own CNI in bootstrap
      podSubnet: 192.168.0.0/16

astrona renders this into a kind cluster config file (a private temp file, removed afterwards) and runs kind create cluster --config <file> --image <node image>. The rendered config is printed in the run log (astrona logs view), and the step line shows the shape, e.g. Create kind cluster "astro-my-lab" (podman; kindest/node:v1.31.2, 1 control plane + 2 workers, no default CNI).

Things to know:

  • Version vs. kind release. version: v1.31.2 boots kindest/node:v1.31.2. Node images are built per kind release, so pick one listed in the release notes of the kind version your students use — or pin image: by digest from those notes for a fully reproducible lab. If creation fails, the error names the image to check.
  • disableDefaultCNI. Nodes stay NotReady and pods Pending until the lab's own bootstrap installs a CNI — that's expected, and it's exactly what a CNI lab wants the student (or bootstrap) to fix.
  • Resources. Every node is a container. Two workers roughly triples the memory of a single-node lab — keep an eye on Podman/Docker Desktop VM limits. Caps: 3 control planes, 6 workers.
  • Not exposed, on purpose. kind's own config can also bind-mount host directories into nodes (extraMounts), publish node ports on all interfaces (extraPortMappings), and patch kubeadm arbitrarily (kubeadmConfigPatches). A lab config can come from any URL or git repo, so astrona only accepts the typed fields above — a remote lab can shape its cluster, but can't use it to reach into the student's machine. (The only host port mapping astrona ever generates is the gateway addon's own, always on 127.0.0.1.)

docs.title: Addons (runtime.kind.addons)
docs.text:
Common cluster components a lab can switch on instead of installing them in its own bootstrap scripts:

runtime:
  kind:
    addons:
      cni: calico            # Calico v3.32.2 instead of kindnet — enforces NetworkPolicy
      certManager: true      # cert-manager v1.21.2
      metricsServer: true    # metrics-server v0.9.0 — kubectl top, HPA
      gatewayAPI: envoy      # Gateway API + Envoy Gateway v1.9.2, GatewayClass "eg"

They're installed right after the cluster is created and before bootstrap, in a fixed order (CNI first — nothing schedules without one — gateway last), each waited on until it's actually ready, so bootstrap scripts and manifests can rely on them. Adds roughly a minute per addon on a fresh machine, less once images are cached.

Supply chain. Each addon is pinned to one upstream release. The manifest's SHA-256 is compiled into astrona; it's downloaded over HTTPS once, verified, cached in ~/.astrona/cache/addons/<sha256>.yaml, and re-verified on every use — a mismatch is never applied. A lab config chooses which addons, never what gets applied or from where. New versions arrive with astrona releases.

Gateway API from the host browser. With gatewayAPI: envoy, every Gateway with gatewayClassName: eg shares one Envoy deployment. Listeners on port 80 and 443 are reachable from your machine at 127.0.0.1:8080 / 127.0.0.1:8443 (change with gatewayPorts). *.localtest.me resolves to 127.0.0.1, so an HTTPRoute with hostnames: [web.localtest.me] is at http://web.localtest.me:8080:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: { name: lab }
spec:
  gatewayClassName: eg
  listeners: [{ name: http, protocol: HTTP, port: 80 }]
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: lab }]
  hostnames: [web.localtest.me]
  rules: [{ backendRefs: [{ name: web, port: 80 }] }]

Under the hood astrona adds a NodePort Service (envoy-gateway-system/astrona-gateway, node ports 30080/30443) in front of the shared Envoy and has kind map those node ports to the host — on 127.0.0.1 only. Gateways report Programmed, so waitFor: [{resource: gateway/lab, condition: Programmed}] works. astrona test installs the same addons but skips the host port mapping, so it never clashes with a running astrona run of the same lab.

Classic Ingress isn't offered: ingress-nginx is retired upstream. Cilium isn't offered yet (it has no plain-manifest release).

  • After kind create cluster, astrona waits until the default ServiceAccount exists before anything else runs — kind returns slightly before the cluster accepts Pods, which used to make a lab's first kubectl apply fail intermittently (serviceaccount "default" not found).
  • bootstrap.manifests / testing.manifests apply against the cluster via kubectl --context kind-<cluster-name>.
  • validation.checks of type resourceExists/podReady run against the same context.
  • Scripts (bootstrap.init, teardown.init, validation.script) run on the host — there's no VM to SSH into — with KUBECONFIG set to the lab's own kubeconfig (see below), so a plain kubectl in a script always hits the lab.
  • Those scripts, and command checks, also get the lab's cluster by name, so they never need to hardcode it:
Variable Value ASTRONA_KUBE_CONTEXT The context in KUBECONFIG, kind-astro-<lab> ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER The kind cluster, astro-<lab>. Its node containers are $ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER-control-plane, $ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER-worker, $ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER-worker2, … ASTRONA_CONTAINER_ENGINE docker or podman, whichever runs the cluster: "$ASTRONA_CONTAINER_ENGINE" exec "$ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER-control-plane" …

A script that uses them works unchanged on any cluster that sets them, for example a cluster shared by several labs. Keep a fallback for an older astrona that does not set them: ${ASTRONA_KUBE_CONTEXT:-kind-astro-<lab>}.

In a full lab exam, several tasks share one exam cluster. Their scripts and checks get ASTRONA_KUBE_CONTEXT=exam-<n> and ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER=astro-exam-<attempt>-<n>, with a KUBECONFIG whose current context is exam-<n>. A script that checks the current context against ASTRONA_KUBE_CONTEXT passes there as it does in a normal run. - runtime.portForwards exposes in-cluster services on 127.0.0.1 — see Port forwards.

docs.title: DNS for the lab network (runtime.kind.dns)
docs.text:
runtime:
  kind:
    dns: [1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1]   # default: 8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4

With Podman, right after the cluster is created the CLI sets the upstream DNS servers of the kind network (podman network update --dns-add …). Node and container names still resolve on the network itself. Every other lookup goes to these servers instead of your computer's resolver. That covers the kubelet's image pulls and CoreDNS's upstream for pods. Without dns, the CLI uses Google Public DNS (8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4), so a slow or broken host resolver (a VPN, a hotel network) does not stall the lab. At most 3 IP addresses.

The kind network is shared by every kind cluster on the machine, so the last lab created sets it. Docker networks have no upstream-DNS setting, so with Docker the lab uses the host's DNS. If the update fails, the lab still starts, with a warning, and uses your computer's DNS. To undo it: podman network update --dns-drop 8.8.8.8 --dns-drop 8.8.4.4 kind.

docs.title: Preloaded images (runtime.kind.preloadImages)
docs.text:
runtime:
  kind:
    preloadImages:
      - nginx:1.27-alpine
      - busybox:1.36

Right after the cluster is created (before addons and bootstrap), each image is made available inside every node so pods start without pulling it:

  1. If your container engine (Docker/Podman) doesn't have it yet, it's pulled once on the host — after that, repeat astrona run/astrona test need no network for it.
  2. It's saved to a private temporary archive and loaded with kind load image-archive into every node.

Why: faster lab start (no per-node pulls), no Docker Hub rate limits in CI, and labs that work offline once the host has the images. Pod events show Container image "…" already present on machine.

Rules: every image needs an explicit tag or digest, never :latest or untagged — Kubernetes always re-pulls those (imagePullPolicy: Always by default), which would make preloading pointless. At most 30 images. Images are pulled for the host's architecture, which is the nodes' architecture too.

Astrona honors KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER=docker or podman for engine detection as well as Kind commands. An explicitly selected engine must be installed and running; astrona will not silently switch to the other engine. With no provider set, it prefers a running Docker daemon, then Podman.

docs.title: Image preloading on Linux and WSL
docs.text:
For Docker versions that support save --platform (daemon API 1.48+), astrona exports preloaded images for the Docker daemon's Linux architecture only. This avoids Kind's content digest ... not found import failure with Docker's containerd image store and multi-platform images such as nginx:1.27-alpine. Older Docker versions and Podman retain their existing archive export behavior.

The ATS000 first lab deliberately starts with a mistyped image tag. Its initial ImagePullBackOff is the exercise; the correct nginx:1.27-alpine image is preloaded. After repairing the Deployment, its two replicas should become ready without another registry pull.

For Podman, astrona expands Docker Hub shorthand (nginx:1.27-alpine → docker.io/library/nginx:1.27-alpine, team/app:1 → docker.io/team/app:1) before inspecting, pulling and saving images. Explicit registries remain as written. This works on Ubuntu without configuring Podman's unqualified search registries or answering a registry prompt.

docs.title: Pausing a lab (astrona stop / astrona start)
docs.text:
astrona stop my-lab     # stops the node containers, pauses port forwards
astrona start my-lab    # starts them again, waits for the API, restarts port forwards

Stopping frees the CPU and memory the lab's node containers use without losing anything — the cluster, its workloads and its port forward definitions all come back on start. astrona list shows a paused lab as Stopped; astrona destroy works on it as usual. With no lab name, stop picks the only running kind lab and start the only stopped one (or the lab from -c).

Limits:

  • Single control plane only. A lab with nodes.controlPlanes > 1 is refused: its node containers get new IP addresses on restart, and etcd's peer configuration is bound to the old ones, so the API never comes back. Use astrona destroy + astrona run for those.
  • kind labs only for now; qemu labs aren't supported yet.
  • Pods restart with their nodes, so anything not persisted (e.g. emptyDir, in-memory state) starts fresh.

docs.title: Kubeconfig isolation
docs.text:
Every kind lab gets its own kubeconfig, ~/.astrona/kind/<lab>/kubeconfig (mode 0600), containing only that cluster. astrona:

  • points your kubectl at the lab once it's ready, and back on destroy. When astrona run (or a full astrona reset) has the lab ready, the kind-<lab> context becomes the current-context of your own kubeconfig ($KUBECONFIG is respected, like kubectl does) and astrona prints which context you had before:

    kubectl now points at this lab (kind-astro-my-lab). Your previous context "prod" comes back with: astrona destroy astro-my-lab

    astrona destroy (or deleting the lab after a passing astrona submit) switches back to that context — but only if the lab's context is still current: if you've switched to another one meanwhile, that's left as it is and destroy says so. If the previous context no longer exists, nothing is switched and destroy says so; if you had none, it's unset again. The context to go back to is kept in ~/.astrona/labs/<lab>.json (mode 0600). Starting a lab over (run on a running lab, reset) keeps the context from before the lab first ran. Labs started on top of each other chain: run lab A (from prod), then lab B (from A's context), and destroying A first hands prod on to B, so destroying B still brings you back to prod. The context is put back before the lab is deleted — if the delete then fails, your context stays restored and a later astrona destroy just removes what's left. - --keep-context on run/reset leaves your current-context alone: reach the lab with astrona shell or kubectl --context kind-astro-<lab> …. Either way, the switch never happens mid-build — kind create cluster's own switch is undone straight away, and only the finished lab is made current. - still lets kind add the kind-<lab> context to your own kubeconfig, so kubectl --context kind-astro-<lab> … works from any terminal. - runs lab scripts and command validation checks with KUBECONFIG=<lab kubeconfig>, plus ASTRONA_KUBE_CONTEXT, ASTRONA_KIND_CLUSTER and ASTRONA_CONTAINER_ENGINE (see above). - deletes the file on astrona destroy.

To work in a lab:

astrona shell my-lab                      # isolated Bash terminal; `exit` to leave
astrona shell my-lab -- k9s               # or run one command
export KUBECONFIG=$(astrona kubeconfig my-lab)

Inside astrona shell, $ASTRONA_LAB holds the lab name (e.g. add it to your prompt). With no lab-name, both commands use the lab config from -c, or the only running kind lab. A lab created by an older astrona (no isolated kubeconfig yet) gets one generated on first use.

docs.title: Terminal workspaces
docs.text:
Kind terminals in the browser workspace and astrona shell run in a dedicated container. /workspace is both the starting directory and $HOME, backed by ~/.astrona/runtime/<lab>/work on your machine (~/.astrona-dev for development builds). New and reopened terminals share this directory. To bring in a file, copy it into that directory from your normal host terminal.

The first opening builds a tools image with Bash, kubectl, Helm, k9s, Git, Python, Vim and Nano. Later openings reuse it. This requires a running Docker or Podman engine and internet access for the first build. Host binaries and shell startup files are not available inside the terminal. Run Astrona commands, including astrona resource, from your normal host terminal.

The container receives only this lab's Kubernetes credentials, including its linked clusters. It has a read-only system filesystem, no added Linux capabilities, and no access to your home directory, SSH agent or container engine socket. cd / can explore the container's Linux filesystem; it cannot reach host paths. An isolation failure stops terminal startup; Astrona does not open a host shell as a fallback. Kubernetes commands still have administrative access to the lab's clusters. This protection covers student terminals, not author-supplied bootstrap, validation or resource scripts run by the host CLI.

QEMU terminals and astrona ssh work inside the VM, starting in ~/.astrona/runtime/<lab> in the remote user's home. No host directory is shared. SSH local-command escapes, user SSH configuration and agent forwarding are disabled. The CLI's own SSH connections that run lab scripts as the astrona account use the same isolation, plus key-only, non-interactive login with a connect timeout.

Closing a terminal or reopening the browser workspace preserves workspace files. Deleting the lab or playground and a full reset discard them. A soft reset keeps Kind workspace files. Copy anything you want to keep out before deleting a run.

docs.title: Port forwards
docs.text:
A kind lab can declare runtime.portForwards so a student reaches in-cluster services from their own browser or client, without running kubectl port-forward themselves:

runtime:
  portForwards:
    - name: web
      resource: svc/frontend
      hostPort: 8080
      targetPort: 80
      scheme: http

astrona run starts them last, after bootstrap scripts, manifests and waitFor gates, waits up to 30s for each to become ready, and prints how to reach them:

Port forwards (bound to 127.0.0.1 only):
    web   Ready      http://127.0.0.1:8080   ->  svc/frontend:80 (ns default)    Frontend UI
    db    NotReady   tcp://127.0.0.1:5432    ->  svc/postgres:5432 (ns data)

  Not ready yet (still retrying in the background):
    db: error: unable to forward port because pod is not running. Current status=Pending

How it works. Each forward gets its own detached supervisor process (a hidden astrona port-forward supervise), which runs kubectl --context kind-<lab> port-forward --address 127.0.0.1 … and restarts it with backoff (1s doubling up to 10s) whenever it exits — plain kubectl port-forward dies whenever the pod behind it restarts. State lives in ~/.astrona/portforward/<lab>/<name>/ (spec.json, status.json, supervisor.pid, supervisor.log — check the log when a forward won't come up).

Stopping a forward checks the saved process start time before signalling its process group. For older records without that timestamp, the process must identify itself as the supervisor for that exact lab and forward. An unrelated process that reused the PID is left alone.

Status (astrona port-forward list):

Status Meaning Ready kubectl reported Forwarding from … and the local port accepts a TCP connection right now NotReady Supervisor running, kubectl not forwarding yet/again — pod not running, no endpoints, restart backoff Error The same non-transient kubectl failure 3+ times in a row (e.g. services "x" not found) — still retrying, likely needs a fix. "Pod not running yet" and "lost connection to pod" stay NotReady however long they last Stopped Supervisor not running (stopped, killed, reboot, or the cluster was deleted) — astrona port-forward start -c <config>

Ready proves kubectl is listening on the host side, not that the application in the pod answers.

Security. Forwards always bind 127.0.0.1 — the address can't be set from the config, so a lab config fetched from a URL or git repo can never expose the cluster to your network. Host ports below 1024 are rejected, and resource/namespace are validated as Kubernetes names before they reach kubectl (passed as an argument list, never through a shell).

Lifecycle.

  • astrona run — starts them (replacing any already running for the lab). A forward that fails or isn't ready yet only warns; the lab is still up.
  • astrona port-forward list|start|stop — inspect, (re)start after a reboot, stop. See the CLI reference.
  • astrona destroy — stops them before deleting the cluster. With teardown.keepCluster: true they keep running too.
  • astrona test — never starts them (CI has no browser, and they'd clash on host ports with a real run).

docs.title: qemu
docs.text:
Boots one or more full virtual machines from a base image instead of a container-backed cluster — for labs that need a real OS: kernel modules, systemd, package managers, multi-host networking, anything a container can't give you.

runtime:
  type: qemu
  qemu:
    - image:
        type: url          # "file" | "url" | "oci"
        source: "https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/.../noble-server-cloudimg-amd64.img"
        checksum: "sha256:..."   # optional but strongly recommended
      arch: amd64
      cpus: 2
      memoryMB: 2048
      diskSizeGB: 20

Key differences from kind:

  • There's no KubeContext — bootstrap.manifests/testing.manifests are rejected with an error if set, since there's no kubectl-reachable cluster.
  • Every script (bootstrap.init, teardown.init, validation.script) runs inside the VM over SSH, as a dedicated astrona superuser account (passwordless sudo, key-auth only) that astrona provisions on every VM — separate from the human-facing student account. Each account gets its own ephemeral ed25519 keypair, generated and removed on teardown. Script content is piped over stdin to bash -s — never interpolated into a shell string. They never fall back to the host: if the VMs are already gone when astrona destroy runs, teardown.init is skipped with a warning.
  • astrona ssh <lab-name> opens an interactive session into a running VM (name as shown by astrona list, with or without the astro- prefix) as student by default — override with --user. It logs in with the lab's ephemeral key; for a lab that sets sshPasswordAuth, --ask-password logs in with the password instead — ssh itself prompts for it (no echo), so it never appears in the process list, your shell history or astrona's environment. The older --password <pw> still works but is deprecated and warns on every use: the password sits in argv (visible in ps) and shell history, and astrona hands it to ssh through an environment variable that ssh's local helper processes inherit. Root SSH login is disabled on the VM. After astrona run finishes, a Connect: block prints the ready-to-paste astrona ssh <name> command for each VM.
  • student can be locked down (sudo removed, password auth disabled) without affecting bootstrap/testing/teardown, since those always run as the independent astrona account.
  • Base images are cached under ~/.astrona/cache/images — inspect with astrona images list. Checksum verification is strongly recommended (image.checksum/image.checksums) but not required; an unverified image falls back to an online freshness check plus the existing cache.
  • A base image must be self-contained: astrona refuses a qcow2 that declares its own backing file or an external data file (data_file), since either is a path stored in the image that could point at any file on your machine. The one exception is an oci artifact that ships a delta together with its base (e.g. image.qcow2 backed by base.qcow2): astrona flattens the two into one image, but only after checking that every file in the backing chain resolves — symlinks included — to a file inside the pulled artifact, is qcow2, and declares its backing format explicitly.
  • astrona destroy only signals the saved qemu PID if that process is still this VM's qemu-system process (started with -name astrona-<lab>). If the PID now belongs to something else — e.g. after a host reboot — it warns, leaves that process alone, and just removes the lab's state.
  • A new VM has 6 minutes in total to accept SSH and finish cloud-init. Every SSH connection the CLI makes itself (readiness, scripts, checks, resource upload) gives up connecting after a few seconds and drops a connection the VM stops answering for about 30 s; an SSH failure (exit 255) is reported as an unreachable VM, never as a failed check. astrona ssh sessions have no time limit.
  • A VM that fails to start — the image, disks, seed or launch fails, or it never becomes SSH-ready — leaves nothing behind: astrona stops the qemu process it started (with the same check) and removes the VM's state under ~/.astrona/qemu/<vm>/ (disks, keys, seed, pidfile, console log). The last lines of the VM's console are kept in the run log. Base images and the image cache are never touched.
  • A VM state dir without handle.json under ~/.astrona/qemu/ — left by an older astrona version, or by a run killed before it saved its handle — is removed with its disks by astrona destroy <lab> (that lab's own dir) and by local data cleanup. It is kept, with an error or a preview note, while a qemu-system process with -name astrona-<vm> is still running, and symlinks there are never followed.

docs.title: Image sources
docs.text:
image.type is one of:

Type source is Notes file a local path (relative to the lab config's base directory) no download, no freshness check url an http(s):// URL to a .qcow2/cloud image downloaded and cached; checksum/checksums recommended oci an OCI registry reference (e.g. ghcr.io/...) pulled via oras

docs.title: Single VM vs multi-VM
docs.text:
runtime.qemu is always a list. A single-VM lab is a one-element list whose entry has no name — the original shape every qemu lab used. Its entry may still carry its own bootstrap/validation block: it runs in the one VM right after the root one. Add a second entry (each one now named) to make it a multi-VM lab:

runtime:
  type: qemu
  networks:
    - name: internal
      cidr: 10.10.0.0/24
  qemu:
    - name: jumphost
      image: { type: url, source: "...", checksum: "sha256:..." }
      networks:
        - { name: internal, ipv4: 10.10.0.10 }
      sshAccess: [backend]     # passwordless SSH from jumphost into backend
    - name: backend
      image: { type: url, source: "...", checksum: "sha256:..." }
      networks:
        - { name: internal, ipv4: 10.10.0.11 }

In a multi-VM lab:

  • Each VM's saved handle identifies its parent lab. Creation and config-based teardown reserve the VM names and refuse names belonging to another lab, even when the names match the config. A child without readable ownership is kept; inspect it and use astrona destroy <exact-vm-name> if you intend to remove it. Destroying a parent by name rechecks each discovered child's ownership before removing it.

  • Every VM gets an implicit host-only management NIC (astrona's own control channel) in addition to any declared networks.

  • sshAccess wires up passwordless SSH from one named VM into another — both must already share a runtime.networks segment; it doesn't create connectivity on its own, only trust over a path that already exists.
  • The lab's shared root bootstrap/validation run once per VM, in runtime.qemu's order; a VM's own nested bootstrap/validation block (if set) runs after that, scoped to just that VM. A nested validation block's command checks run inside that VM, and its results are suffixed (vmName) — see Grading.

docs.title: Choosing one
docs.text: Default to kind unless a lab specifically needs a full OS, kernel-level behavior, or multi-host networking that a Kubernetes cluster can't model — it's faster to boot and has no VM image to manage.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Choose the installation method for your machine. Each page contains its own commands and package-specific notes.

Platform or method Instructions macOS or Linux with Homebrew Homebrew Debian or Ubuntu APT / DEB package Fedora or a Red Hat compatible distribution DNF / RPM package Ubuntu with Snap Snap package Windows Windows and WSL 2 (preview) macOS or Linux, download script Quick install Download a binary yourself Manual install

docs.title: After installing
docs.text:
1. Set up dependencies and verify your installation.
  2. Optionally enable shell completion.
  3. Follow the Quickstart to run your first lab.

The CLI presents its usage terms before the first operational command. Kind labs need a running Docker or Podman engine; astrona setup helps prepare it.

docs.title: Manage your installation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Astrona
  • CLI preferences and settings review
  • Local data and cache cleanup

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
For a Kind lab, astrona run offers to open the browser workspace: the task and terminals into the lab in a local web page. astrona ui <lab> opens it again.

This walks through the full loop — bring a lab up, work on it, get graded, tear it down — using the examples/k8s-basics-01 lab shipped in the repo. Clone the repo first, or point --git at it directly (see Remote Config Sources).

docs.title: 1. Check your toolchain
docs.text:
astrona check

Fix anything reported as ✗ before continuing (and if something breaks later, astrona doctor checks the machine, the lab and the running lab in one go) — kind, Docker/Podman, and kubectl are required for this example.

docs.title: 2. Pick the lab and bring it up
docs.text:
(Looking for the published trainings instead? astrona labs lists them and every lab is runnable by name — sign in first with astrona login (it opens astrona.io in your browser, where you click Authorize), since catalog labs are tied to your Astrona account; see the Lab Catalog.)

astrona use examples/k8s-basics-01   # every command below now works on this lab
astrona run

astrona use remembers the lab (like kubectl's current context), so you don't repeat -c on every command; astrona use alone shows which lab, --clear forgets it. Lost track? Run astrona on its own: it shows the lab, whether it's running, the exam clock, your last result and the command to run next, followed by every command (the same list as astrona --help). astrona list marks the current lab too. Inside a lab directory that lab is used instead, and -c/--git — or the lab as an argument, astrona run ./other-lab — always win.

This:

  1. Reads examples/k8s-basics-01/config.yaml.
  2. Creates a kind cluster named astro-k8s-basics-01 (astrona prefixes every cluster it creates with astro-).
  3. Runs the lab's bootstrap.init scripts (here, hello.sh).
  4. Applies any bootstrap.manifests.

At this point the cluster is up and the trainee's actual work begins — this particular lab expects a lab-ns namespace with a hello-config ConfigMap holding specific content, which isn't created for you (that's the exercise).

Progress prints as a compact step view; each step's full output goes to a log file under ~/.astrona/logs/ (path shown at the end) and is printed inline only if a step fails. Add --verbose to stream everything live instead. Revisit any past run's log with astrona logs — astrona logs view opens the latest in your pager.

Read the task:

astrona docs question

(astrona docs lists the lab's other docs — case study, prerequisites, and the step-by-step guide with the solution.)

docs.title: 3. Inspect it
docs.text:
astrona status

One screen for where you are with the lab: cluster health, how to connect, port forwards, the exam clock (timed labs), your last submission and score, and a suggested next step:

Lab astro-k8s-basics-01 (kind)

  Cluster      Ready (1/1) · Kubernetes v1.37.0 · up 28s
  Connect      astrona shell astro-k8s-basics-01
  Last submit  1/2 points (50%) FAIL · 3m0s ago · attempt #1

Next: astrona submit to grade your work

For every lab on the machine:

astrona list

Shows every astrona-managed lab (kind clusters and qemu VMs), with runtime, status, and uptime — a kubectl get-style table. For kind labs, STATUS is live cluster health:

STATUS Meaning Ready (n/n) every node is Ready NotReady (r/n) only r of n nodes Ready — e.g. a CNI that isn't installed yet Unreachable node containers are up but the API doesn't answer (3s timeout) Degraded (r/n containers running) some node containers stopped Stopped all node containers stopped EngineUnreachable Docker or Podman is installed but doesn't answer, so this remembered lab can't be checked — start the engine; nothing is forgotten

astrona list -o wide adds the Kubernetes version and port-forward status (1/1 Ready); -o json prints the same for scripts.

Once the lab is ready, your kubectl points at it:

kubectl get ns

astrona destroy switches kubectl back to the context you had before (run prints which one). Prefer to leave your current-context alone? astrona run --keep-context, then work from a lab shell — your $SHELL with kubectl pointed at the lab (type exit to leave) — or name the context:

astrona shell k8s-basics-01
kubectl --context kind-astro-k8s-basics-01 get ns

See kubeconfig isolation.

docs.title: 4. Submit for grading
docs.text:
astrona submit

Hands the running cluster to the Proctor, which runs this lab's validation.checks (does lab-ns exist? does hello-config exist?) and its validation.script (does the ConfigMap actually hold the right content?). Output is pytest-style — a PASS/FAIL line per check, then a summary — and the command's exit code reflects the verdict, so it's safe to gate a script on.

docs.title: 5. Tear it down
docs.text:
astrona destroy

Runs teardown.init scripts, then deletes the cluster (unless the config sets teardown.keepCluster: true).

docs.title: The lab-author loop
docs.text:
