If you're authoring a lab rather than taking one, astrona test runs the whole thing non-interactively against a reference solution, to prove the lab is actually solvable before you publish it:

astrona test examples/k8s-basics-01 --junit-xml=report.xml

This bootstraps, applies testing.manifests (the reference solution — here, examples/k8s-basics-01/solution/), submits to the Proctor, and always tears down afterwards, even on failure. It runs against a test--prefixed cluster name so it never collides with a lab you already have up via astrona run. See CI Integration for wiring this into a pipeline.

docs.text:

docs.title: APT (Debian & Ubuntu)
docs.text:
Download the latest stable .deb, verify its SHA-256 checksum, and install it. This detects amd64 (Intel/AMD) or arm64 (ARM) automatically. You need curl, sha256sum, and permission to use sudo.

(
  set -eu
  case "$(uname -m)" in
    x86_64) arch=amd64 ;;
    aarch64|arm64) arch=arm64 ;;
    *) echo "Unsupported CPU architecture" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
  release_url="$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/latest)"
  tag="${release_url##*/}"
  package="astrona-${tag#v}-linux-$arch.deb"
  base="https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/download/$tag"
  download_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
  cd "$download_dir"
  curl -fSL "$base/$package" -o "$package"
  curl -fsSL "$base/SHA256SUMS" -o SHA256SUMS
  awk -v file="$package" '$2 == file { print }' SHA256SUMS | sha256sum -c -
  sudo apt-get install "./$package"
  astrona --version
)

The commands below for DNF and Snap use the same download and verification process. Each resolves a single release tag so the package and its checksums come from the same release. These packages become available after the first release containing the Linux packaging feature; a missing asset stops the commands before installation. Downloaded files remain in the temporary directory; the subshell keeps your current directory unchanged.

APT installs Git and CA certificates automatically. The package includes pinned, checksum-verified Kind, kubectl and ORAS, installed privately under /usr/lib/astrona/tools. Astrona and its lab scripts use those tools without replacing tools you already have on your shell's PATH. astrona shell uses the tools in its isolated terminal container.

Install and start Docker or Podman separately. For optional VM labs on Debian/Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install qemu-system-x86 qemu-system-arm qemu-utils genisoimage openssh-client

This is a local release package. A hosted APT repository has not been configured, so apt-get install astrona without the downloaded file will not find Astrona. Repeat the download-and-install commands to upgrade. Remove with sudo apt-get remove astrona; this preserves ~/.astrona. Destroy running labs before uninstalling.

docs.text: Set up and verify Astrona, then run your first lab.

docs.title: DNF (Fedora & Red Hat compatible distributions)
docs.text:
Download, verify and install the latest stable .rpm for your CPU:

(
  set -eu
  case "$(uname -m)" in
    x86_64) arch=amd64 ;;
    aarch64|arm64) arch=arm64 ;;
    *) echo "Unsupported CPU architecture" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
  release_url="$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/latest)"
  tag="${release_url##*/}"
  package="astrona-${tag#v}-linux-$arch.rpm"
  base="https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/download/$tag"
  download_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
  cd "$download_dir"
  curl -fSL "$base/$package" -o "$package"
  curl -fsSL "$base/SHA256SUMS" -o SHA256SUMS
  awk -v file="$package" '$2 == file { print }' SHA256SUMS | sha256sum -c -
  sudo dnf install "./$package"
  astrona --version
)

DNF resolves Git and CA certificate dependencies. The RPM includes private Kind, kubectl and ORAS tools. Install and start Docker or Podman separately. QEMU, SSH and an ISO builder are optional VM dependencies; their package names and availability depend on your distribution and enabled repositories. CI checks installation on Fedora and AlmaLinux 9; a Red Hat subscription and enabled repositories may be needed on RHEL.

This is a local release package. A hosted DNF repository has not been configured, so dnf install astrona without the downloaded file will not find Astrona. Run the download-and-install block again to install the latest stable release, or install a newer release file manually. Remove with sudo dnf remove astrona.

Removing the package preserves ~/.astrona. Destroy running labs before uninstalling.

docs.text: Set up and verify Astrona, then run your first lab.

docs.title: Homebrew (macOS & Linux)
docs.text:
brew install astrona-io/tap/astrona

The tap is updated by every release, pinned to the same binaries and SHA-256 values as the GitHub release. CI installs the formula with real Homebrew on macOS and Linux for every change that could affect it, and again from the tap right after each release. Upgrade with brew upgrade astrona, or astrona upgrade — on a Homebrew install it runs brew upgrade astrona for you instead of downloading the binary itself.

What the Homebrew install gives you on top of the binary:

  • Lab tools are installed automatically: kind, kubectl (kubernetes-cli), git for catalog/repository labs, oras for OCI VM images, qemu for VM labs, and cdrtools (mkisofs) for cloud-init seed images. Homebrew resolves and installs their dependencies too. Docker or Podman you install and start yourself — e.g. brew install podman && podman machine init && podman machine start, or Docker Desktop.
  • Shell completion for bash, zsh and fish is set up — no astrona completion step (see Shell completion).
  • Man pages: man astrona, man astrona-run, … one per command.
  • No Gatekeeper prompt on macOS: a binary downloaded in a browser gets the quarantine flag and macOS may refuse to run it; one installed by Homebrew doesn't.

Two things to know:

  • An older astrona earlier on your PATH (e.g. ~/.local/bin/astrona from the quick install) hides the Homebrew one — which -a astrona shows the order; remove the old one.
  • brew uninstall astrona removes the program, not ~/.astrona (lab state, results, approvals, installed versions). Destroy running labs first (astrona destroy <lab>); delete ~/.astrona yourself if you want it gone.

docs.text: Set up and verify Astrona, then run your first lab.

docs.title: Manual install
docs.text:
1. Go to GitHub Releases.
  2. Download the binary for your platform: astrona-darwin-arm64, astrona-darwin-amd64, astrona-linux-arm64, or astrona-linux-amd64.
  3. Make it executable and move it onto your PATH:
chmod +x astrona-<os>-<arch>
mv astrona-<os>-<arch> ~/.local/bin/astrona

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Set up and verify Astrona, then run your first lab.

docs.title: Quick install (macOS & Linux)
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && \
OS=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]') && \
ARCH=$(uname -m) && \
[ "$ARCH" = "x86_64" ] && ARCH="amd64" || true && \
[ "$ARCH" = "aarch64" ] || [ "$ARCH" = "arm64" ] && ARCH="arm64" || true && \
curl -L -o ~/.local/bin/astrona "https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/latest/download/astrona-${OS}-${ARCH}" && \
chmod +x ~/.local/bin/astrona

Make sure ~/.local/bin is on your shell's PATH.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Astrona shells out to a few external tools — astrona check (below) verifies all of these for you:

Tool Required Needed for kind Yes creates and deletes the local Kubernetes cluster Docker or Podman Yes container runtime kind runs on (either works) kubectl Yes applies manifests and runs the Proctor's declarative checks git Optional only for --git (cloning/pulling a lab config from a repo) qemu-system-x86_64 / qemu-system-aarch64, qemu-img, ssh, ssh-keygen Optional only for runtime.type: qemu labs oras Optional only for a qemu lab pulling its base image from an OCI registry (image.type: oci) mkisofs / genisoimage / xorriso / hdiutil (any one) Optional only for runtime.type: qemu (builds the cloud-init seed image)

docs.title: The short way: astrona setup
docs.text:
After installing Astrona, one command gets the rest of the machine ready:

astrona setup             # shows each step and asks before doing it
astrona setup --dry-run   # only show the plan
astrona setup --yes --accept-terms  # explicitly approve steps and CLI terms

It looks at what astrona check would report and fixes what it can:

On What setup does macOS brew install whatever is missing of kind, kubectl and Podman, then podman machine init --cpus 4 --memory 8192 and podman machine start (or starts Docker Desktop if that is what you have), and waits until the engine answers macOS without Homebrew tells you to install Homebrew first, then run setup again Linux with Homebrew brew install kind and kubectl Linux without Homebrew downloads the kind (GitHub release) and kubectl (dl.k8s.io) versions pinned in this astrona release into ~/.local/bin, verified against SHA-256 checksums pinned in astrona (amd64 and arm64) before anything is moved into place; a mismatch installs nothing. On other architectures it tells you to install them yourself Linux, no container engine prints the command to install Docker for your distribution — a container engine needs sudo and distribution-specific setup, so setup never runs that for you

It ends by running astrona check. Without a terminal to ask on, setup refuses to change anything unless you pass --yes.

docs.title: Podman is installed but a lab will not start on macOS
docs.text:
Kind labs, including playgrounds, need a reachable container engine. A failed podman info check can mean the Podman machine is stopped, but it can also mean the connection is misconfigured. Run these commands to see which:

podman machine list
podman info

If your machine is stopped, start it with podman machine start (add its name if you use a non-default machine). If no machine exists, run astrona setup to review and approve the initialization steps. Setup retries failed health checks while waiting for the engine to start.

If the machine is already running, inspect the error from podman info and your connections with podman system connection list. Do not delete or recreate the machine to troubleshoot: it may contain other containers and volumes.

Once podman info succeeds, run astrona check and retry your lab command. The signed-out warning is separate: guest runs still need a working engine, and signing in does not repair a container connection.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
astrona check

This prints a ✓/⚠/✗ per item and exits non-zero only on a ✗. It checks three things:

Dependencies. A missing required tool is a ✗; optional ones (qemu toolchain, git) only warn, since they're only needed for specific runtimes or flags. Each missing tool says how to install it — with Homebrew installed that's the brew install command, and the end of the list gives one line for everything missing:

Install what's required: brew install kind podman kubernetes-cli
Optional tools, all at once: brew install git qemu oras cdrtools

astrona doctor prints the same line for missing required tools.

Container engine. Whether Docker/Podman is actually running (a stopped podman machine or Docker daemon is the most common cause of confusing kind errors), and whether it has enough resources — for Docker Desktop and podman machine that's the VM's memory/CPUs, not your Mac's:

Check ✗ ⚠ Engine reachable (docker info / podman info) not running — Memory under 2 GiB under 4 GiB CPUs — 1 CPU Rootless engine on cgroup v1 (kind needs v2) — Linux only: fs.inotify.max_user_watches / max_user_instances — under 524288 / 512 (multi-node kind fails with "too many open files")

Each ⚠/✗ prints the command that fixes it, e.g. podman machine stop && podman machine set --memory 8192 --cpus 4 && podman machine start.

Your lab — when a lab config is found (-c/--git, the lab picked with astrona use, else ./config.yaml). No config in the current directory just means no lab section; a config that is there but can't be loaded (malformed YAML, a lab picked with astrona use that has moved) is a ✗ under Lab, with the error:

astrona check -c ./labs/my-lab

Lab astro-my-lab:
  ✓  lab memory estimate                    ~6.9 GiB for this lab of 9.7 GiB
  ✓  host port 8080                         gateway http, free
  ✗  host port 18290                        port forward 'web', in use
        fix: find the user with `lsof -nP -iTCP:18290 -sTCP:LISTEN`, or change the port in the lab config
  • Memory estimate — a rough figure from the lab's nodes and addons, plus astrona kind labs already running; ⚠ when it's over 75% of the engine's memory.
  • Host ports — every portForwards host port and the gateway addon's ports must be free (skipped while the lab itself is running).
  • The lab config is validated too (runtime.kind, runtime.portForwards).

docs.title: When something isn't working: astrona doctor
docs.text:
astrona doctor runs all of the above and looks at the running lab, then says what's wrong and how to fix it:

Running lab astro-linked-labs-01:
  ✓  nodes                                  Ready (1/1)
  ✓  linked cluster idp                     Ready (1/1) · idp.astrona.internal
  ✗  port forward idp                       Stopped · http://127.0.0.1:30080
        fix: astrona port-forward start
  ⚠  pods in astro-linked-labs-01-idp       1 unhealthy: auth/broken: ErrImagePull (…)
        fix: astrona diagnose collects their logs and events

Error: 1 problem(s) found — the ✗ lines above say how to fix each

It checks this machine (tools, container engine, inotify), the lab (its config, whether this astrona may run it, memory and free ports when it isn't running) and the running lab (nodes, linked clusters, port forwards, unhealthy pods, exam clock). It only reads — nothing is started or changed — and exits non-zero on any ✗ — including a lab you named (argument, -c, --file, --git, astrona use — astrona doctor . counts) that isn't there or whose config doesn't parse; only when no lab is named and the current directory has none does it check the machine alone. --bundle also writes the full diagnostics bundle. Unhealthy pods are ⚠, not ✗: in a lab they may be the exercise.

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text:
Installed with Homebrew? Completion for bash, zsh and fish is already set up — skip the steps below (Homebrew's shell setup must be loaded, see brew info astrona).

astrona completion <shell> prints a completion script for bash, zsh, fish or PowerShell. Besides commands and flags, it completes lab names from what's actually on your machine — astrona destroy <TAB>, stop, start, shell, kubeconfig, diagnose, ssh, port-forward list|stop — filtered to what makes sense (start offers stopped labs, ssh qemu VMs), each with its runtime and status. Type part of the name without astro- and the short form is completed.

It also completes:

  • --cluster <TAB> (shell, kubeconfig, net, reset) — the lab's linked clusters
  • astrona versions install <TAB> — published releases you don't have yet; versions remove <TAB> — the installed ones
  • a lab directory or config file wherever a command takes one (astrona use ./<TAB>, astrona run ./<TAB>)
zshbashfish 
astrona completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_astrona"   # then start a new shell

astrona completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/astrona

astrona completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/astrona.fish

docs.title: Snap (Ubuntu)
docs.text:
Download, verify and install the latest stable .snap for your CPU. Snap must already be installed on your system:

(
  set -eu
  case "$(uname -m)" in
    x86_64) arch=amd64 ;;
    aarch64|arm64) arch=arm64 ;;
    *) echo "Unsupported CPU architecture" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
  release_url="$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/latest)"
  tag="${release_url##*/}"
  package="astrona-${tag#v}-linux-$arch.snap"
  base="https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/download/$tag"
  download_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
  cd "$download_dir"
  curl -fSL "$base/$package" -o "$package"
  curl -fsSL "$base/SHA256SUMS" -o SHA256SUMS
  awk -v file="$package" '$2 == file { print }' SHA256SUMS | sha256sum -c -
  sudo snap install --dangerous --classic "./$package"
  /snap/bin/astrona --version
)

The Snap bundles Kind, kubectl, ORAS, Git and CA certificates. Classic confinement lets lab scripts use your host files, kubeconfig and Docker/Podman sockets. Install and start a host container engine separately; optional VM tools also come from the host.

--dangerous is Snap's option for installing a local file without a Store assertion. Check the downloaded package against the release's SHA256SUMS first. This builds a local-installable Snap; publishing snap install astrona --classic requires registration of the Store name and approval for classic confinement. Locally installed Snaps do not update automatically. Installing a newer local file with the command above updates it. Remove with sudo snap remove astrona.

DEB, RPM and Snap packages preserve ~/.astrona on removal. Destroy running labs before uninstalling. CI builds packages for both architectures, installs and reinstalls them with real package managers, checks bundled tool discovery and upgrade protection, then verifies removal preserves user data.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Set up and verify Astrona, then run your first lab.

docs.title: Staying up to date
docs.text:
astrona upgrade

astrona upgrade checks GitHub for the latest release, downloads the binary for your OS/architecture, verifies it against the SHA-256 digest GitHub records for it (and its build provenance when the GitHub CLI is installed), and atomically replaces the currently running executable — only when the release is newer than yours. On a Homebrew install it runs brew upgrade astrona instead (brew reinstall astrona with --force), so Homebrew keeps track of the install.

On DEB, RPM and Snap installs, astrona upgrade prints the package installation command and exits without modifying package-owned files, including with --force. Download and install the newer package using the APT, DNF or Snap instructions.

astrona tells you when a newer release exists — [INFO] astrona v0.2.3 is available (you have v0.2.2) — astrona upgrade · what's new: <release notes> — at most once a day. It asks GitHub at most once a day too (cached in ~/.astrona/update-check.json), so commands don't wait on the network. It never checks in CI (CI/GITHUB_ACTIONS/… set) or when stderr isn't a terminal; ASTRONA_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 turns it off everywhere.

Older releases can be installed next to the latest — see Astrona Versions.

docs.title: Windows (preview)
docs.text:
Labs need Linux, so on Windows astrona runs inside WSL 2 (Linux inside Windows). astrona.exe is a small launcher that sets that up and then forwards every command into it — you keep typing astrona … in PowerShell.

Requirements: Windows 10 22H2 or Windows 11, virtualization turned on in your BIOS/UEFI, and Docker Desktop.

In PowerShell:

irm https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/latest/download/astrona-windows-amd64.exe -OutFile $env:LOCALAPPDATA\astrona.exe
& $env:LOCALAPPDATA\astrona.exe setup

(astrona-windows-arm64.exe on ARM PCs.) astrona setup on Windows, one step at a time — run it again after a restart or a manual step, and finished steps are skipped:

  1. WSL 2 — wsl --install --no-distribution if WSL is missing (Windows asks for admin; restart afterwards).
  2. Ubuntu — wsl --install -d Ubuntu; a window asks you to choose a Linux username and password. Set ASTRONA_WSL_DISTRO to use another distribution.
  3. Docker — checks docker info works inside Ubuntu. If not, install Docker Desktop, start it, and turn on Settings → Resources → WSL integration for Ubuntu (guide).
  4. astrona inside Ubuntu — the Linux astrona, into ~/.local/bin (same release as the launcher; a development build of astrona.exe says so and installs the latest release). The download is checked against that release's SHA256SUMS before it is made executable; if the checksum is missing or does not match, nothing is installed.
  5. kind and kubectl — runs astrona setup inside Ubuntu.
  6. PATH — copies astrona.exe to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\astrona and adds that folder to your user PATH (no admin).

After that, any command — astrona labs, astrona run …, astrona submit … — runs inside Ubuntu, with the same output and exit codes (astrona submit still exits 2 for "graded, didn't pass"). Your arguments are passed through as they are, never re-parsed by a shell (the launcher uses wsl --exec, which skips the distribution's default shell). astrona --launcher-version prints the launcher's own version.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Set up and verify Astrona, then run your first lab.

docs.title: Astrona Versions
docs.text: A lab is written against an astrona release. When a later astrona changes behavior the lab relies on, the lab can say which releases may run it — and astrona runs it with one of those, installed side by side.

docs.title: Declaring it: astronaVersion
docs.text:
apiVersion: astrona.io/v1
astronaVersion: "<=0.2.1"          # or ">=0.2.0, <0.3.0", "0.2.1", "!=0.2.2"
metadata:
  name: my-lab

Comparisons are =, !=, >, >=, <, <=, separated by commas (all must hold); a bare version means exactly that one. Versions are major.minor.patch (a leading v is fine; 0.3.0-rc1 sorts before 0.3.0). Omit the field and any astrona runs the lab.

(apiVersion is a different thing: the format of the config file. astronaVersion is which releases may run the lab.)

docs.title: Older versions side by side
docs.text:
astrona versions available          # published releases
astrona versions install 0.2.1      # → ~/.astrona/bin/astrona-0.2.1
astrona versions list               # this astrona + the installed ones
astrona versions remove 0.2.1

The newest astrona stays astrona; older ones are astrona-<version>. Downloads are verified against the SHA-256 digest GitHub records for each release binary — a mismatch is refused, and nothing unverified is ever made executable.

docs.title: Build provenance
docs.text:
Releases after v0.2.2 also carry a signed build provenance attestation: proof that the binary was built by astrona-cli's own release workflow from this repository. When the GitHub CLI (gh, logged in) is installed, astrona versions install and astrona upgrade check it too:

Result What happens Verified installed — "build provenance verified" Release ≤ v0.2.2 (built before attestations) installed — "this release predates build provenance attestations" Newer release without its attestation, or one that doesn't verify refused — the binary may have been replaced No gh, or not logged in installed on the SHA-256 check alone, with a hint

To check a download yourself: gh attestation verify astrona-darwin-arm64 --repo astrona-io/astrona-cli, or sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS with the checksum file attached to each release. Add ~/.astrona/bin to your PATH to run e.g. astrona-0.2.1 yourself.

docs.title: What happens when a lab needs another version
docs.text:
Commands that run, test, grade or validate a lab (run, test, submit, reset, validate, status, …) check its astronaVersion. If this astrona isn't allowed, it hands the whole command over to the newest installed astrona-<version> that is — you just keep typing astrona (when that version is older than the one you run, it asks first; see below):

$ astrona test ./labs/new-lab
[INFO] this lab needs astrona >=0.6.0 — running it with astrona 0.6.0 (~/.astrona/bin/astrona-0.6.0)
…
PROCTOR: PASS
  • The lab is passed on once, as the -c/-f/--git/--git-ref this astrona resolved — your own lab argument and lab flags are replaced, since an older version may not know astrona use or a lab given as an argument, and what you typed may not be what was resolved (a catalog lab ignores --git-ref, for example). Your other flags are passed on unchanged.
  • Flags the other version doesn't have stop it first. Before handing over, astrona asks that version which flags the command takes (its --help); one it doesn't know — newer than it, like run --keep-context or --yes — ends the command here, naming the flag: this lab needs astrona <0.3.0, so it runs with astrona 0.2.4 — which has no --keep-context for `astrona run`; run it again without --keep-context. If that version can't be asked, it is handed the command and its own flag parsing decides.
  • None installed? astrona never downloads anything just because a lab config says so — a config may come from someone else's repository. Instead:
    • At a terminal it asks first: 
      This lab needs astrona >=0.6.0 (this is 0.5.2). Download and install astrona 0.6.0,
verified against GitHub's SHA-256 digest? [y/N]
      Yes installs the newest release that fits and continues the same command with it; no (the default) stops, and tells you the astrona versions install … command for later.
    • Without a terminal (CI, scripts) it stops with that command — or pass --install-version to install it without asking.
  • An older release is always asked about. When the version a lab needs is older than the astrona you're running — installed or not — astrona asks at the terminal every time, whatever flags you pass (--install-version included): 
    This lab needs astrona <=0.5.1, which is older than this one (0.5.2). Run it with astrona 0.5.1? [y/N]
    Without a terminal (CI, --headless) it refuses and prints how to run that version yourself: astrona versions install 0.5.1, then astrona-0.5.1 <command> ….
  • A remote lab is approved first. For a lab from --git or a URL, the trust prompt happens in this astrona, before anything is installed or handed over — for every command that hands over, not only run/submit/test/reset. The approval is stored in ~/.astrona/trust.json, so the version it's handed to doesn't ask again. If this astrona can't even parse the lab's config (it was written for another version), it can't show what the lab does, so there's no prompt: the lab must already be approved at this exact version, or you pass --trust after reviewing it.
  • Never older than 0.4.15. astrona never hands a lab over to — or installs for one — a release older than 0.4.15, the newest release with security fixes: a lab asking for an older one would otherwise run without them. The floor moves up with every release that fixes a security issue. A lab that only fits an older release stops with an explanation; if you trust it, install that version yourself and run it as astrona-<version>.
  • Only astrona-* binaries in ~/.astrona/bin (where astrona versions install puts them) are used — ones elsewhere on your PATH are ignored, so a stray binary never runs a lab.
  • astrona docs and astrona destroy don't check: reading a lab's docs doesn't depend on the version, and cleaning up must always work.
  • A developer build (no release number) runs every lab and doesn't hand over.

astrona 0.2.1 and older don't know astronaVersion

They warn about an unknown field and otherwise run the lab normally — but their astrona validate reports it as an error. Validate such a lab with a current astrona.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Terms acceptance is specific to the notice shipped with each binary. --accept-terms is not forwarded during an automatic version handover: older CLIs do not recognize it, and another release can have different terms. A target with the same notice can reuse the local receipt outside CI. If a target needs acceptance in CI, invoke that installed binary directly with --accept-terms after reviewing its terms output. Releases predating this feature have no terms prompt; upgrading the main executable cannot change those older binaries.

astrona upgrade installs the latest release over astrona, verified against the same GitHub digest, and only when it's actually newer than the one you have. Installed with Homebrew? Then astrona upgrade runs brew upgrade astrona (brew reinstall astrona with --force) instead of downloading the binary itself, so Homebrew keeps track of the install. astrona versions install works the same either way (it installs into ~/.astrona/bin, not Homebrew's directory).

docs.title: Authoring a Lab
docs.text: A lab is a directory with a config.yaml (or whatever --file points at) plus whatever scripts/manifests/docs it references. This walks through building one from scratch, using examples/k8s-basics-01 as the worked reference.

docs.title: Scaffolding New Content (For Teachers & Authors)
docs.text:
To make content creation fast, consistent, and collaborative, Astrona provides a built-in blueprint scaffolding command. By default, it dynamically pulls the template blueprint from a remote git repository based on the required <type> argument and replaces placeholders in filenames and contents with your customized arguments.

astrona content init <type> [path] [flags]
  • <type> (Required): Must be either ats (Astrona Training Series - hands-on sandbox lab) or atp (Astrona Training Path - course path/section).
  • [path] (Optional): The target directory to initialize. If omitted, this defaults to the value of the --slug flag (creating a directory named after your slug).

docs.title: Dynamic Blueprint Defaults
docs.text: Depending on the content type specified, the tool clones a dedicated template repository if no custom --repo is defined: - atp: Clones git@github.com:astrona-io/training-path-blueprint.git - ats: Clones git@github.com:astrona-io/training-sandbox-blueprint.git

docs.title: Custom Scaffolding Arguments
docs.text:
You can supply the following customization arguments via command-line flags to template the newly initialized content:

Flag Variable Default Description -i, --path-id path_id ATPxxx Unique identifier of the training path/lab (e.g., ATP010) -s, --slug slug path-slug URL-safe and directory-friendly slug name of the path (becomes default folder name) -t, --title title Path Title Human-readable title of the path -d, --description description (engaging summary) A short summary of what the learner will achieve -v, --version version 0.1.0 Initial version of the training content -g, --language language en Learning language (e.g., en, fr, de) -a, --author-name author_name Author Name Name of the author/teacher creating the content -l, --license license Apache-2.0 Content license (default is Apache 2.0 license) -r, --repo repo "" Custom template repository to clone from (overrides default blueprints)

docs.title: Example Scaffolding Commands
docs.text:
1. Initialize an ATP (Training Path) into a custom directory: 

    astrona content init atp labs/my-custom-path \
  --path-id "ATP040" \
  --slug "linux-networking-basics" \
  --title "Linux Networking Basics" \
  --author-name "Alice Smith"

  2. Initialize an ATS (Lab Sandbox) defaulting to a folder named after your slug: 

    astrona content init ats \
  --path-id "ATS012" \
  --slug "virtio-disk-discovery" \
  --title "Virtio Disk Discovery Lab" \
  --author-name "Bob Jones"
    This will automatically clone the sandbox template and create a new directory ./virtio-disk-discovery/.

docs.title: Validating Content (For Teachers & Authors)
docs.text:
Once a Training Path (atp) has been scaffolded and filled in, validate its path.yaml before publishing:

astrona content validate <type> <source> [flags]
  • <type> (Required): ats (a training repository, its astrona.yaml) or atp (a training path, its path.yaml).
  • <source> (Required): Either a local folder path (the raw content files, containing path.yaml) or a git repository URL (https://, git@host:, ssh://, or a .git suffix). Use --git-ref to pin a git source to a branch or tag.

Validation:

  1. Confirms path.yaml exists at <source> and parses as YAML.
  2. Checks apiVersion is content.astrona.io/v1alpha1 and kind is TrainingPath.
  3. Walks every spec.stages[].content[] entry and resolves its repository at version (a git branch or tag) via the same git cache used by --git elsewhere in this CLI — this both verifies you have access to the referenced content repo and warms the local cache for later steps.
astrona content validate atp ./paths/my-custom-path
astrona content validate atp https://github.com/astrona-io/kubernetes-networking-atp.git --git-ref v1.2.0

docs.title: Validating a training repository (ATS)
docs.text:
astrona content validate ats ./ATS014
astrona content validate ats https://github.com/astrona-io/ATS014.git --git-ref main

Checks astrona.yaml the way astrona.io's content sync reads it, and prints the totals (ATS014: 146 readings, 56 labs, 0 playgrounds, 20 quizzes (174 questions)). It fails (✗) on what would keep the training or an item off the site, and warns (!) about what is worth a look:

  • training.id is set; every item has a title, a known type — reading, lab, playground or quiz — and a path inside the repository that exists: a Markdown file for a reading, a directory with a config.yaml for a lab or playground, a YAML question bank for a quiz.
  • A quiz (knowledge check) bank has kind: question_bank and schema_version: 1, and each question an unique id, a prompt, 2–6 options with unique ids and a text, a correct_option that is one of them, and type: single_choice (or none). Its source_readings must exist; one that is not a reading in astrona.yaml gets no "read it again" link (warning). The site uses at most 30 questions. Fields, an example and the JSON Schema: Writing a Question Bank.
  • The quiz item's pass_score is a percentage above 0 and at most 100 (the site's default is 70); a question_count that differs from the bank is a warning — the site counts the bank.
  • A bank with status: draft, an option or question without an explanation, and a quiz.yaml the manifest does not list are warnings.

A knowledge check looks like this in astrona.yaml, right after the module's summary:

      - type: quiz
        title: "Knowledge Check: How A Request Moves Through The Mesh"
        path: sections/section-000/module-01/quiz.yaml
        pass_score: 70

docs.title: path.yaml shape (ATP)
docs.text:
apiVersion: content.astrona.io/v1alpha1
kind: TrainingPath
metadata:
  id: ATP001
  slug: linux-foundation-certified-sysadmin-lfcs
  title: "Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator (LFCS)"
  version: "1.0.0"
  authors:
    - name: "Alice Smith"
      email: "alice@example.com"
spec:
  stages:
    - id: "ATP001-STG001"
      title: "Operations Deployment"
      weight: 25
      content:
        - ref: ATS002
          repository: "git@github.com:astrona-io/ATS002.git"
          path: "."
          version: "1.0.0"

Each stages[].content[] entry references an external content repository (typically an ATS lab): repository is the git URL, version the branch/tag to check out, and path the subdirectory within it.

Because a built bundle lays content out as <output>/<stage-id>/<ref>, and path.yaml often comes from a cloned repo, validate and build reject, before fetching anything:

  • a stage id or content ref that isn't a single name of letters, digits, ., _ and - (no /, no .., not empty);
  • an absolute path, or one that escapes the content repository (../…).

A repository or version starting with - is also rejected before git runs.

docs.title: Building Content (For Teachers & Authors)
docs.text:
Once a Training Path validates cleanly, materialize it into a self-contained bundle — every referenced ATS repo resolved and copied locally, ready to ship or serve:

astrona content build <type> <source> [flags]
  • <type> (Required): Currently only atp is implemented, same as validate.
  • <source> (Required): Same as validate — a local folder path or a git repository URL, optionally pinned with --git-ref.
  • -o, --output: Output directory for the bundle (default ./dist).
  • --clean: Remove the output directory first if it already exists and is not empty. Without it, build refuses to write into a non-empty output directory.

Build:

  1. Runs the same path.yaml checks as validate.
  2. Resolves every spec.stages[].content[] entry's repository at version via the git cache (cloning/pulling as needed).
  3. Copies the resolved content (or its path subdirectory, if set) into <output>/<stage-id>/<ref>, skipping .git.
  4. Copies path.yaml itself to the bundle root.
astrona content build atp ./paths/my-custom-path --output ./dist
astrona content build atp https://github.com/astrona-io/kubernetes-networking-atp.git --git-ref v1.2.0 --output ./dist --clean

docs.title: Starting from a working lab
docs.text:
astrona init lab ./k8s-web-01

Creates a complete kind lab you can run immediately and reshape into yours: config.yaml (editor schema, preloaded image, readiness gates, jsonpath / count / resourceExists checks with hints and points, commented addon and exam options), the four student docs, a bootstrap manifest, a reference solution in solution/ for astrona test, and .github/workflows/lab.yml running astrona validate + astrona test on every pull request. As generated it passes validate and test, and its step-by-step guide solves it. The sections below explain each part.

docs.title: 1. Metadata
docs.text:
metadata:
  name: "k8s-basics-01"
  docs:
    prerequisites: "docs/prerequisites.md"    # knowledge/tooling needed before attempting
    question: "docs/exam-question.md"     # formal, self-contained task statement
    caseStudy: "docs/case-study.md"           # softer, hint-driven version of the same task
    solution: "docs/step-by-step-guide.md"       # full walkthrough with the answer

metadata.name becomes the cluster/VM name (prefixed astro- by astrona). metadata.docs are Markdown files, relative to config.yaml, that students read with astrona docs. The block is optional: a doc it doesn't list is found by its usual file name next to config.yaml — question.md, solution.md, prerequisites.md, case-study.md — so this is enough:

labs/lab-01/
  config.yaml      # metadata: { name: "ats-015-lab-010-01" } — no docs block needed
  question.md
  solution.md

astrona docs                 # lists what the lab provides
astrona docs question        # docs.question (question.md) — the task
astrona docs case-study      # docs.caseStudy (case-study.md)
astrona docs prerequisites   # docs.prerequisites (prerequisites.md)
astrona docs solution        # docs.solution (solution.md) — shown with a "full solution" warning

They're rendered for the terminal (headings, code blocks, lists, inline code, bold, links) and paged; astrona run ends with "Your task: astrona docs question" when the lab has a question. Write them as plain Markdown — tables and HTML are shown as-is. A YAML front-matter block at the very top of a doc (a --- line, YAML such as estimated_duration: 20m, a --- line) is hidden; if it has a title, that's shown as the doc's heading. A --- further down is still a horizontal rule. Doc paths can't point outside the lab directory, and control characters (terminal escape sequences) are stripped before anything is printed. Name the cluster context as kind-astro-<metadata.name> in your docs — or point students at astrona shell <lab>.

Set an expected working time in the question document's front matter to show the UI's lab progress bar:

---
title: Configure a deployment
estimated_duration: 20m
---

Create a deployment with three replicas.

Use a positive duration with units, such as 45m or 1h30m. The UI compares this estimate with active time spent and pauses it during idle periods. Exceeding it does not stop the lab or change its grade. Missing or invalid estimates show as unavailable. This display applies to labs, not playgrounds; exam deadlines and playground expiry remain separate.

docs.title: 2. Pick a runtime
docs.text: Omit runtime: entirely for a kind cluster (the default), or see Runtimes for a qemu VM-backed lab.

docs.title: 3. Bootstrap — what the student starts with
docs.text:
bootstrap:
  init:
    - name: "echo"
      type: "file"
      source: "hello.sh"
  manifests: []

Keep this to whatever scaffolding the exercise needs before the student's own work — the actual task (creating the namespace, deploying the app, whatever it is) should not be pre-built here.

docs.title: 4. Testing — your reference solution
docs.text:
testing:
  manifests:
    - name: "solution"
      type: "folder"
      source: "solution"

This only runs under astrona test, never for a student. Put the finished, correct solution here — the thing a student would produce if they solved the lab perfectly — so astrona test can prove your validation block actually passes against it.

docs.title: 5. Validation — how it's graded
docs.text:
validation:
  checks:
    - name: "lab-ns namespace exists"
      type: "resourceExists"
      resource: "namespace/lab-ns"
    - name: "hello-config configmap exists"
      type: "resourceExists"
      resource: "configmap/hello-config -n lab-ns"
  script:
    name: "verify-configmap-content"
    description: "Custom script check: confirms the configmap's actual content, not just that it exists"
    type: "file"
    source: "validate.sh"

Start with resourceExists/podReady checks for "does the thing exist," and reach for a script when you need to verify actual content or behavior (see Grading for the full check-type reference). A validation script exits 0 for pass, non-zero for fail — write it the same way you'd write a test assertion.

Scripts and checks have time limits — 30m for a bootstrap, testing or teardown script, 5m for a validation script, 1m for a check — so a command that hangs can't hang the student's run or submit. A script or check that runs longer is killed with everything it started and reported as timed out after … (a failed check when grading). Set timeout on the entry when it legitimately needs longer (timeout: 45m on a slow install) or should give up sooner (timeout: 20s on a check); see Time limits.

docs.title: 6. Teardown
docs.text:
teardown:
  init:
    - name: "dump-logs"
      type: "file"
      source: "teardown/dump-logs.sh"
  keepCluster: false

Usually just keepCluster: false (or omitted — that's the default). Add init scripts only if you need to capture state before the cluster disappears.

docs.title: Files the student needs: resources/
docs.text:
Instead of asking students to paste a script or a YAML file from question.md, put it in a resources/ folder next to config.yaml. When the lab starts, astrona copies it to ~/.astrona/resources/<lab>/ and lists what's there — nothing runs until the student asks for it:

sections/section-010/module-01/labs/lab-01/
  config.yaml  question.md  solution.md
  bootstrap/  solution/  validation/
  resources/
    setup-db.sh               # runs with bash
    broken-deployment.yaml    # applied to the lab with kubectl

No config is needed; a resources: list adds descriptions and run commands — see resources.

docs.title: 7. Prove it works
docs.text:
astrona validate -c path/to/your-lab     # seconds: typos, rules, missing files
astrona test -c path/to/your-lab --junit-xml=report.xml

astrona validate catches config mistakes — a misspelled field, a missing script — without creating anything; see editor support and validation for autocompletion in your editor.

Before publishing, check the lab isn't flaky:

astrona test -c path/to/your-lab --repeat 5

Repeat summary — 5 runs:

  ✓  Deployment web runs 2 replicas  5/5
  ⚠  2 web pods exist                3/5  flaky

--repeat N (up to 20) runs the whole lifecycle N times on fresh environments. A check that passes only sometimes almost always means grading raced the cluster — add a waitFor (in testing for the reference solution) for whatever the check depends on. Any failed or flaky run fails the command; with --junit-xml, each check is reported once with "passed k/N runs".

This is the whole point of the testing stage: it bootstraps your lab, applies your reference solution, submits it to the Proctor, and tears down — proving a student who does everything right will actually pass. Run this locally before publishing, and wire it into CI (see CI Integration) so a later edit to validation can't silently break the lab's own solution.

docs.title: Full schema reference
docs.text: See Lab Config Schema for every field, type, and default.

docs.title: Browser Workspace
docs.text: The browser workspace is a local web page for working on a lab, Kind or QEMU: the task on one side, a terminal on the lab on the other, in your own browser. astrona serves the page itself, on 127.0.0.1 only; nothing leaves your machine. It replaces the earlier terminal UI: astrona ui now opens this page.

docs.title: Open a lab in the browser
docs.text:
An interactive astrona run opens your browser as soon as it starts: it starts the local workspace server (or reuses a running one), prints a link and opens it in your default browser. You can follow everything from that tab:

  1. Terms. When the CLI terms are not accepted yet, or have changed, the tab shows them in a dialog. Accept and continue goes on; Decline and stop stops the command before anything is downloaded or started. Nothing else happens, and no time counts, until you answer.
  2. Setup. The tab shows each step in a terminal-style window, as the terminal does: what it is doing, ✓ / – / ✗ with how long each step took, and what a long step is waiting on. If setup fails, the tab shows the error and where the log is.
  3. The lab. Once the lab is ready the tab says so and waits for you: Begin this session opens the intro page. Nothing counts yet; an exam's clock still starts only when you click Start there.

While the lab is set up, a card shows whether this run is saved to your Astrona account. astrona run decides that when it starts the lab:

  • Signed in (a catalog lab, signed in): Signed in as on . The time you spend and your submitted result, pass or fail, are saved to your account. Submitting ends the attempt and removes the lab. For a playground, the card only says that the time you spend in it is saved.
  • Not signed in (a catalog lab, signed out): the run is not saved to an account; the time and your result stay on this computer. The card links to Create a free Astrona account on the site astrona signs in to (opened in a new tab) and tells you to run astrona login and start the lab again. Signing in while this run is open does not link it: a run is linked to an account only when astrona run starts.
  • Local only (--local-only): nothing from the run is sent.
  • A lab from your own files or --git has no account, and shows no card.

    • The intro page repeats this as one line, with the sign-up link when you are not signed in.

    Some questions are still asked in the terminal: whether to start a running lab over, whether to log in, and whether to trust a lab's repository. The tab says so while it waits. If you stop the command (Ctrl+C), the tab says that astrona stopped. A QEMU lab opens the same way, with a terminal on each VM (see QEMU labs).

    The browser setting changes this:

    • always (the default) opens the browser first, as above.
    • never keeps the command-line flow.
    • ask sets the lab up in the terminal and then asks:
    Open this lab in your browser? (yes/no/always/never):

    yes and no decide this run; always and never decide it and save the answer as the setting.

    Decide one run with a flag:

    astrona run ./labs/my-lab --browser      # open it, whatever the setting
astrona run ./labs/my-lab --no-browser   # keep the command-line flow

    Without a terminal on stdin and stdout, the workspace is not opened unless you pass --browser. On a machine without a browser (no display) the default and ask keep the command-line flow; --browser or a saved always prints the link and opens nothing. --headless never opens the browser.

    The link is printed every time the workspace opens, so you can open it yourself:

    Continue in your browser: http://127.0.0.1:47300/#code=…&launch=…
Browser workspace: http://127.0.0.1:47300/#code=…&lab=my-lab

    The first form is the browser-first run; the second is printed by astrona ui and by the ask flow.

    The #code= part is a single-use launch code that expires after two minutes. It stays in the fragment, so it never reaches the server log or a referrer, and the page removes it from the address bar after loading. If the tab you opened first is closed by the time the lab is ready, astrona opens a new one. A link that was already used, or is older than two minutes, shows Link expired: run astrona ui <lab> (or astrona ui status) for a fresh one.

docs.title: Reopen a running lab
docs.text:
astrona ui <lab> opens a running lab again, for a link that expired or a tab you closed:

astrona ui my-lab
astrona ui            # the only running lab; with none or several, every lab on this computer

It starts the workspace server if needed, prints a new link with a fresh code and opens it (or prints it when there is no browser). It never restarts the lab or its timer: an exam whose clock already runs keeps it, even when the lab was started without the browser. It reads the saved local config and cached repository; it does not check GitHub, update the checkout or rerun setup.

A lab named status, stop or serve is opened by its full name, since the short name is a subcommand: astrona ui astro-status (astrodev-status for development builds). astrona list shows the full names.

docs.title: Labs on this computer
docs.text:
A lab keeps running in the background after astrona run returns, until you end it; a playground also ends when its time is up. Each one uses CPU and memory, so it is easy to leave several running without noticing.

Labs on this computer lists every lab and playground running here, whether or not it was opened in the browser: its title, Kind or QEMU, whether it is running, how long it has been up and, for a playground, when it is deleted. For a lab the workspace knows, Open opens it and End playground or Remove removes it after the same confirmation as in the workspace. Other labs show the command that opens or removes them. Labs that are stopped but not removed are listed on one line below.

To get there:

  • astrona ui with no lab name, when no lab or several labs are running;
  • All labs at the bottom of the workspace's task panel;
  • See all labs on this computer after a playground ended or a lab was removed.

The page refreshes every five seconds. When the container engine does not answer, it says so, since Kind labs cannot be listed without it.

docs.title: QEMU labs
docs.text:
A QEMU (VM) lab opens in the browser like a Kind lab: the intro, Start, the timer, Submit and All labs work the same way. Its terminals are SSH logins into the VMs, as the lab's student user, starting in the lab's workspace directory in the VM (~/.astrona/runtime/<lab>), the same login astrona ssh gives you. There is no kubectl and no host shell.

  • A single-VM lab has one Terminal tab on its VM.
  • A multi-VM lab has one tab per VM, named after the VM. The first VM in the lab's config is the focus tab.

The VM tabs are fixed: a QEMU lab cannot declare tabs. When a shell ends (exit), Open a new shell logs in to the same VM again. The workspace connects with the lab's own key and known-hosts file only; it never uses your SSH config, agent or keys. If the VM does not answer within 10 seconds, ssh gives up and the tab shows that the shell ended; nothing else is started in its place.

astrona run still prints the astrona ssh command for each VM, and astrona status <lab> shows them again, for a terminal outside the browser.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
The first page shows the lab's prerequisites, its time limit and number of questions, and the rules for an exam. Environment ready means the lab finished setting up.

An exam's timer starts when you click Start, not when the lab is ready. From then on it keeps running if you close the page or lose the connection; the top bar counts down to the deadline. A lab in learning mode has no time limit, so after Start the top bar counts up instead and shows how long you have spent on it.

When the run is linked to your Astrona account, Start also starts the lab session's time on astrona.io, with the moment you clicked, so you don't need to open the lab page on the website. Offline, the start is saved on this computer and sent once Astrona can be reached; it never holds up Start. A local-only run sends nothing.

docs.title: The workspace
docs.text:
• Task (left): the question text, rendered from the lab's docs. Its top-level heading (such as # Exam Question: <lab>) is left out, since the panel already shows the task; the lab's name is in the browser tab's title. All labs and About Astrona sit at the bottom of the panel.
  • Terminal (right): a shell on the lab with kubectl pointed at its cluster (on a QEMU lab, an SSH login into its VM; see QEMU labs). Keyboard focus moves into the terminal after Start and when the page opens. Press F6 to leave the terminal; Shift+F6 works too. The skip links at the top move focus between task and terminal.
  • Divider: drag it, or focus it and use the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps, Home / End for the limits). The task panel starts at 25% of the width and can take 15% to 70%; it never gets narrower than 280 pixels. The browser remembers the width you chose.
  • Hide task: the button next to Task collapses the task panel to a thin rail, so the terminal gets the whole width. Click Show task on the rail (or use Skip to task) to show the task again; All labs (⌂) and About (ⓘ) stay at the bottom of the rail. The browser remembers this choice too.

When you are done, use Submit in the top bar (see Submit or end from the browser); astrona submit in a terminal does the same.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
The right panel shows the lab's tabs. The first, Terminal, is the shell on the lab's own cluster. A lab can add more with tabs: a terminal on a linked cluster, a page the lab serves through one of its port forwards, or documentation. You switch between them with the mouse or with the arrow keys and Enter; you cannot add or close a tab. Tabs keep running while another one is shown, so a terminal keeps its shell and its scrollback. When a shell ends, Open a new shell starts another in the same tab. Without tabs in the lab, the panel shows only the Terminal tab.

A page or documentation tab shows the page inside the workspace. Back to start returns to the page the lab configured, wherever you navigated, and Open in new window shows it in a separate window. Some documentation sites refuse to be shown inside another page: if a tab stays blank, use Open in new window.

docs.title: The terminal
docs.text:
The shell runs on your machine, held by the workspace server, not by the page:

  • Reload or close the page: the shell keeps running. Opening the page again reattaches to it and replays its recent output.
  • Another tab: opening the workspace in a second tab moves the terminal there. The first tab shows "This terminal was opened in another tab." with Use it here to take it back.
  • exit: ends the shell. Open a new shell starts another one; files in the lab are kept.
  • Connection lost: see below.

Output longer than the screen scrolls back like a local terminal: use the mouse wheel or trackpad, drag the scrollbar on the right (shown once there is history), or press Shift+Page Up / Shift+Page Down. The terminal keeps the last 5000 lines. The prompt line always sits above the hint bar at the bottom, and the shell's size (stty size) follows the visible area when you resize the window, hide the task or drag the divider.

The terminal draws with WebGL, so programs that use 24-bit ("truecolor") colours show them. Where WebGL is not available, it falls back to a renderer that shows those colours as the terminal's default colours; 16 and 256-colour output looks the same either way.

docs.title: Connection lost
docs.text:
When the page cannot reach the workspace server for more than a second or two (the server stopped or hangs, or the computer slept), a dialog covers the workspace and the page behind it is blurred, so nothing typed goes into a terminal that cannot receive it. It covers every tab, whichever terminal lost its connection:

The page keeps reconnecting and shows the attempt number. The dialog cannot be closed; it goes away by itself once the server answers, and you continue in the same shells, with their output and the task as they were, and the keyboard focus back where it was. Shorter drops do not show it.

If it does not come back, check with astrona ui status that the server is running. If it is not, astrona ui <lab> starts it again and prints a new link; the lab environment and its files are still there. A page from the earlier server then shows Session ended.

With reduced motion or reduced transparency set in the system, the workspace is dimmed rather than blurred.

docs.title: Submit or end from the browser
docs.text:
Browser submissions and removal use the same trust checks as CLI commands. An official catalog lab needs no separate approval when its clean checkout matches the commit published by Astrona. If that verification fails, the page cannot approve code: submit from a terminal to review it. Removal skips unapproved teardown scripts.

The top bar has one button to finish the session. Its label fits the run:

Run Button What it does Lab Submit lab Grades it, as astrona submit does. Exam Submit exam The same; the exam time is recorded at that moment. Playground End playground Deletes it now. Nothing is graded.

The button is disabled, with the reason next to it, when it cannot be used: before Start, while a submission is being graded, or once the lab is no longer running.

It always opens a dialog first that says what is about to happen for this run:

  • The checks run and the result, pass or fail, is saved on this machine as a new attempt, with the time you spent.
  • Where the result goes. A run linked to your Astrona account is sent to your lab page when astrona is signed in to the same site (or saved to send once Astrona can be reached). A local-only run is never sent. A run without a lab session keeps the result on this machine.
  • That submitting is final. Every submit ends the attempt, pass or fail: there is no fixing the lab and submitting again. Check your work first with astrona submit --watch in a terminal, which grades without ending anything.
  • That the environment is removed afterwards. Once the result is sent (or saved to send), or saved here for a run without a lab session, the cluster (or the VMs) and its terminals are removed. There is no option to keep them; teardown.keepCluster does not apply to a submit. Only a result Astrona refuses, or one that cannot be sent or saved, leaves the environment running.
  • If the checks cannot run (for example, the container engine or a VM stopped), nothing is recorded or sent and the lab keeps running.

Cancel has the focus and Esc closes the dialog. While grading runs, the dialog stays open. Keep the page open; if the connection drops, the page asks the server for the result again, and the same submission is never graded twice.

While the checks run, the dialog lists each one: waiting, running with the time so far, or passed or failed with how long it took. A check that retries for minutes shows as running rather than leaving the page looking stuck.

The results page shows pass or fail, the score, the pass mark, the attempt number and every check with its points. A failed check shows its hint only when the lab shows hints. Check commands, expected values and the solution are never shown. Below that it says whether the result was saved and sent and whether the environment was removed.

From there you can:

  • go back to the workspace while the environment still runs;
  • remove the environment (with a confirmation);
  • start over with astrona run <lab> in a terminal.

When the time is up, a banner says so and offers Submit. Nothing is submitted automatically. In a strict exam a submission after the deadline cannot pass, and the terminal stops taking input at the deadline. Closing or reloading the tab during a session or while grading asks for confirmation first.

docs.title: The workspace server
docs.text:
The workspace server listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Its terminals are the same isolated containers as astrona shell: they may only write the lab's own workspace, and never see your home directory, container engine socket or SSH agent. See terminal workspaces for file access and the protection boundary. The server stops by itself after 15 minutes without a page, terminal or running lab.

astrona ui status            # running?, a fresh link, pages and terminals
astrona ui status -o json
astrona ui stop              # stop the server and its terminals; labs keep running

After you update astrona, a browser-first astrona run replaces a server from the earlier build when nothing uses it, since the older page cannot show setup progress. If that server still has terminals or pages open, it is left alone, setup is shown in the terminal only, and the run says so: astrona ui stop ends it (labs keep running), and the next run starts the new one.

astrona ui status prints a new link with a fresh code each time. astrona ui stop ends every browser terminal but leaves the labs running; an open workspace then shows the connection-lost dialog. astrona run or astrona ui <lab> starts the server again.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text: The page follows your system's light or dark appearance. The terminal stays dark in both: the tools a lab runs colour their output for a dark terminal.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The server only answers on 127.0.0.1, refuses other Host and Origin headers, and sends a Content Security Policy that allows no inline scripts or styles. The page talks to it with a session token it gets in exchange for the single-use launch code. See the workspace API reference for the details.

docs.title: Guest login reminder
docs.text:
When you are not logged in, each lab run asks before starting the lab:

Log in now? (yes = log in, no = continue as guest, never = continue as guest and stop asking):

yes opens the browser sign-in flow and continues startup when it completes. never saves login-reminder=no. Catalog labs can track account progress after login; local labs stay local. Restore reminders with astrona settings set login-reminder yes. Noninteractive catalog runs still require --without-login when signed out.

For automation, use headless mode: astrona run <lab> --headless skips the browser question and login reminder and returns after setup.

docs.title: History
docs.text: Submission history uses the local results. Completed runs are recorded under ~/.astrona/results/runs (~/.astrona-dev/results/runs for development builds). These records contain names, catalog identifiers and timestamps, without credentials or session IDs, and survive destruction and cache cleanup. astrona progress summarizes graded attempts.

docs.title: CI Integration
docs.text: astrona test is built for CI: bootstrap → apply the reference solution → submit to the Proctor → always tear down, in one command, one exit code. This is what astrona-cli's own ci.yml e2e job runs against examples/k8s-basics-01 on every PR.

docs.title: Headless setup for external checks
docs.text:
Use --headless when your own script needs to check a running lab. This works with Kind and QEMU and never opens the browser workspace.

Settings confirmation is not required, including on a fresh runner:

astrona run ./examples/k8s-basics-01 --headless --accept-terms
# Run your checks against the running lab.
astrona destroy --headless -c ./examples/k8s-basics-01

For a catalog lab, also approve its remote code:

astrona run ATS000/section-010/module-01/lab-01 --headless --accept-terms --trust

For run and full reset, headless mode skips the browser question, login reminder and new account sessions, even when run in a terminal. The command returns after setup with the lab still running. It uses the normal lab name and does real provisioning; it does not apply the reference solution, grade the lab or clean up automatically. Arrange cleanup after failed checks as well as successful ones.

Missing terms acceptance or remote-code trust causes an error instead of a CLI prompt. An existing lab requires explicit --yes to replace it, deleting its work. Other running labs are left alone. Use a dedicated CI environment to avoid replacing a lab you are working on. External lab scripts must also be written to run without interactive input. --headless cannot be combined with --browser.

For the complete setup, reference solution, grading and cleanup workflow, keep using astrona test. That command is always headless.

docs.title: Headless commands
docs.text:
--headless is a global flag: place it before the command or alongside its other flags. Use it instead of run --test-mode; the old name remains a hidden, deprecated alias for existing scripts and prints a migration notice.

Commands Headless behavior run, reset Set up Kind or QEMU without UI prompts or new account sessions. Replacing a run still requires --yes; soft and linked-cluster resets also require it. run --local-only also marks the run local only, so a later submit records its result on this machine and sends nothing. test, validate, check, doctor, diagnose Run with explicit approvals and static progress output. test retains automatic grading and cleanup. submit Grade and send results for an existing tracked session. Every recorded result, PASS or FAIL, ends the attempt; once it is server-confirmed (or queued) the lab is deleted, and there is no option to keep it. A run with nothing to send (--local-only, a UI restart, a lab from your own files) is finished the same way once its result is saved locally. A result Astrona cannot be reached for is queued and sent later under the same key. Use submit --watch to grade without ending the attempt. start, stop, destroy, list, status, progress Use the normal command-line behavior and applicable approval rules. Lifecycle progress does not animate. bundle Require saved trust or --trust before loading unapproved content. res run Run a resource for external checks. QEMU uses SSH batch mode without allocating a terminal. setup Require --yes to install, or --dry-run to inspect the plan. settings review Require the exact --accept <review-id> if a review is pending. login Print an authorization link without opening a browser; still wait for approval on that site.

Read-only commands also accept the flag. Explicit watch commands continue until cancelled; submission and port-forward watches append output instead of clearing the screen. External scripts must supply their own noninteractive options.

ui, shell and ssh open interactive sessions, so they reject --headless. For scripted work in a QEMU VM, use a lab resource through astrona res run <name> --headless.

Headless mode does not approve downloads or destructive actions, and does not mean offline. It suppresses automatic release checks. Explicit account commands, submissions for an existing tracked session, and cleanup of that session retain their normal API behavior.

astrona reset ./examples/k8s-basics-01 --headless --yes --accept-terms
astrona submit ./examples/k8s-basics-01 --headless --accept-terms -o json   # ends the run and deletes the lab
astrona test ./examples/k8s-basics-01 --headless --accept-terms --junit-xml=report.xml

docs.title: Minimal GitHub Actions job
docs.text:
name: Test lab

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test-lab:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install kubectl
        run: |
          version="$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)"
          curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/${version}/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
          chmod +x kubectl
          sudo mv kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl

      - name: Install kind
        run: go install sigs.k8s.io/kind@v0.32.0

      - name: Install astrona
        run: |
          curl -L -o astrona "https://github.com/astrona-io/astrona-cli/releases/latest/download/astrona-linux-amd64"
          chmod +x astrona

      - name: astrona check
        run: ./astrona check --headless --accept-terms

      - name: astrona validate
        run: ./astrona validate --headless --accept-terms -c .

      - name: astrona test
        run: ./astrona test --headless --accept-terms -c . --junit-xml=junit-report.xml --diagnostics-dir=astrona-diagnostics

      - name: Upload JUnit report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: junit-report
          path: junit-report.xml

      - name: Upload diagnostics
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: astrona-diagnostics
          path: astrona-diagnostics/

Notes:

  • Settings review is optional. Configure preferences with astrona settings set if needed; fresh runners do not need a review receipt or ASTRONA_SETTINGS_REVIEW_ID. See settings review.
  • Review astrona terms and pass --accept-terms on every operational CI command. A cached receipt, CI=true, --yes, or --trust does not replace explicit acceptance. See CLI usage terms.
  • if: always() on the upload step — a failing astrona test still writes the JUnit report, and you want that artifact whether the check passed or not.
  • Testing a lab from another repo or a URL (--git … / -c https://…) needs --trust in CI — remote labs must be approved before they run (see Approving remote labs). Testing the repo's own checkout (-c .) doesn't.
  • Docker is already available on GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runners, which is all the kind runtime needs. A qemu runtime lab needs /dev/kvm for real hardware acceleration — GitHub-hosted runners don't have it, so a qemu-backed astrona test there would fall back to slow software emulation. Run qemu labs' CI on a self-hosted runner with KVM, or a GitHub-hosted runner that provides it.
  • Labs hitting Docker Hub rate limits in CI can list their images in runtime.kind.preloadImages: each image is then pulled once per job on the runner instead of once per node (and per restarted pod).
  • astrona test --repeat 3 catches flaky checks before students do — each run uses a fresh environment, so it's slower; a nightly job is a good place for it.
  • --diagnostics-dir puts the diagnostics bundle inside the workspace so the if: failure() step can upload it.
  • astrona test always tears down its own environment on exit (even on failure or a cancelled step, best-effort), so a CI job doesn't need its own cleanup step.
  • A cancelled job is handled too: on Ctrl-C or SIGTERM (what most CI runners send when a job is cancelled or times out) astrona test stops after the current step, collects diagnostics (per --diagnostics) and tears down, then exits 1. Further signals while it's tearing down are ignored, so a runner that sends SIGINT and then SIGTERM doesn't cut the teardown short; only SIGKILL skips it (the next astrona test of the lab still starts by removing any leftover). A step astrona is waiting on (e.g. a long waitFor) isn't cut short by SIGTERM, so give the job a cancel grace period long enough for it plus teardown.

docs.title: Diagnostics on failure
docs.text:
A failed CI run used to leave nothing behind but "FAIL" — astrona test tears the cluster down on exit. Now, when it fails, it first collects a diagnostics bundle (before teardown) and prints the unhealthy pods straight into the job log:

Diagnostics bundle: astrona-diagnostics
  Unhealthy pods (2):
    default/crasher: app: Error (exit 3); app restarted 2×; app: not ready
    default/web-7c76977dcb-nxbfw: web: ErrImagePull (failed to pull and unpack image "docker.io/library/does-not-exist:1": … repository does not exist …)
  12 warning event(s) — see summary.md.

The bundle (typically ~1 MB):

Path Contents summary.md Unhealthy pods with their reason, newest warning events cluster/ kubectl get nodes / pods / workloads / events (+ Gateway API resources if installed), describe nodes pods/ describe and logs (plus --previous logs after a restart) for every unhealthy pod kind-logs/ kind export logs: node journal, kubelet, containerd, every pod's log files vms/ qemu labs: each VM's serial console log clusters/<cluster>/ Labs with linked clusters: the same bundle (summary.md, cluster/, pods/, kind-logs/) for each linked cluster — often where a failing lab's real problem is versions.txt, errors.txt Tool versions; anything that couldn't be collected

Secrets, ConfigMaps and kubeconfigs are never collected. Pod describe output does include environment variables set inline in a pod spec — keep lab credentials in Secrets, and keep CI artifacts private.

Flag Default --diagnostics on-failure always to collect on success too, never to skip --diagnostics-dir ~/.astrona/diagnostics/<lab>-<timestamp> Where to write the bundle

The same bundle can be collected from a running lab with astrona diagnose.

docs.title: Machine-readable output: -o json
docs.text:
Every command whose output is data takes -o json and then prints exactly one JSON document on stdout — progress (including cloning/updating a --git lab or a catalog source, and fetching a config URL), warnings and script output go to stderr — so it can be piped straight into jq, a script or a UI:

Command JSON astrona submit -o json {lab, pass, earned, max, percent, attempt, checks: [{name, pass, points, message, hint, durationMs, vm}]} (vm only for a multi-VM qemu lab's per-VM results) (hints left out under exam conditions; still recorded as an attempt; exit codes as above) astrona submit --history -o json the recorded attempts astrona status -o json health, context, port forwards, linked clusters, exam clock, last attempt, suggested next step astrona validate / check / doctor -o json {ok, problems, results: [{section, name, status: ok\|warn\|fail, detail, fix}]} — exit code still non-zero on any fail (a lab config that can't be found or loaded is a fail result in this report too, not an empty stdout) astrona list / port-forward list / progress / logs list / images list / versions list -o json the listed items astrona resource list -o json (or astrona res -o json) {lab, dir, resources: [{name, file, description, how, run, vm, dir}]} — dir is the folder holding the lab's copy; resources is [] when it has none astrona whoami -o json {signedIn, username, site, keyId} — keyId is the device key's fingerprint, empty until the sign-in has one; signed out it is {signedIn: false, site} and still exits 1 astrona labs -o json the catalog: {fetchedAt, trainings: [{id, title, description, repo, labs: [{id, title, path}]}], errors} (trainings is [], never null, when nothing was found); labs <TRAINING> -o json that one training; labs --search <words> -o json [{training, lab: {id, title, path}}] astrona use -o json the current lab, or null — also after picking one (use <lab> -o json) or forgetting it (use --clear -o json, always null) 
astrona submit -o json | jq -r '.checks[] | select(.pass | not) | .name'   # what failed
astrona doctor -o json | jq '.results[] | select(.status == "fail")'

--watch modes redraw a live view and don't combine with -o json. Interactive questions (trust, reset, installing another astrona version) are asked on stderr too — in CI pass --trust / --yes / --install-version instead. A lab that needs a release older than the running astrona is refused in CI; run that astrona-<version> directly.

docs.title: Other CI systems
docs.text: The same commands (astrona check, astrona validate -c <path>, astrona test -c <path> --junit-xml=<path> --diagnostics-dir=<path>, upload the XML and — on failure — the diagnostics directory) work anywhere that can run a Linux binary and understands JUnit XML — GitLab CI (artifacts: reports: junit:), Jenkins (junit post-build step), etc.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
astrona test and astrona submit exit 0 only on a Proctor PASS — anything else fails CI, no extra flag needed. The code tells you which kind of failure it was:

Exit code Meaning 0 Graded, and the lab passed 1 astrona, the lab's setup or the environment failed — a missing tool, a failed bootstrap step, a broken config, a lab that isn't running. Nothing was graded (or a --repeat run broke before grading) 2 Graded, and the lab didn't pass — the checks ran and the solution is wrong (for --repeat: every failed run was graded, none broke)

So a pipeline can treat them differently, e.g. retry a 1 (infrastructure) but not a 2:

astrona test --accept-terms -c . ; code=$?
[ $code -eq 2 ] && echo "::error::the reference solution doesn't pass its own checks"
exit $code

docs.title: CLI usage terms
docs.text:
The first operational command, including plain astrona, displays the CLI usage terms and data-loss risk notice on stderr. Answer y or yes to continue. Blank input, no, or EOF cancels the command before lab downloads, sign-in or setup. An interactive astrona run that opens the browser (the default; see browser workspace) shows the notice in the browser tab instead: Accept and continue or Decline and stop. Declining, Ctrl+C in the terminal, or no answer within 30 minutes stops the command before anything starts. Read the notice without accepting it:

astrona terms

To accept explicitly, including in automation:

astrona terms --accept-terms
astrona test --accept-terms -c ./labs/my-lab

Acceptance is saved in ~/.astrona/terms.json with the notice revision, SHA-256, UTC timestamp, CLI version and acceptance method (browser when accepted in the browser tab). This is local state, not a server-side audit or account record. A newer CLI asks again if its bundled notice changes, even if its revision was not bumped. Updating only the website does not change an installed CLI's notice. CLI updates with unchanged terms do not ask again.

Without a terminal, missing or outdated acceptance fails with instructions; piping yes is not sufficient. Detected CI requires --accept-terms on every operational command, even with a saved receipt. The flag accepts the terms in the binary being run, so review them when upgrading a pipeline's pinned CLI. --yes, --trust, and saved settings never imply terms acceptance.

The notice also says what astrona sends while a signed-in lab runs (its CPU and memory use, see Resource usage) and how to turn that off. Revision 2026-11-10 added that paragraph, so a receipt for an earlier revision asks again.

Help, version output, completions and astrona terms remain available without acceptance. So do settings, data, logout, stop, destroy, and port-forward stop, so declining cannot prevent cleanup or preference repair. Their other safety checks still apply. Internal documentation generators and the background helpers an operational command starts (port-forward supervisors, the playground watchdog, the usage reporter and the offline-signal sender) do not prompt; the command that starts them has already passed the terms check.

Cache cleanup and data reset preserve the receipt. To forget it, remove only ~/.astrona/terms.json; the next operational command will ask again. A malformed receipt also needs fresh acceptance. A symlink or directory at that path is refused rather than replaced. Failure to save acceptance stops the command.

On Windows, native setup records acceptance in the Windows user's .astrona directory before changing WSL. Labs keep a separate receipt inside the chosen WSL distribution. Read the launcher's notice with astrona setup --terms, even before WSL is installed; astrona terms shows the Linux CLI's notice in WSL. astrona setup --yes --accept-terms supplies both approvals; without the flag, first-time setup can ask once on each side.
