The CLI remains Apache-2.0 licensed. This notice describes risks and points to the existing license; it does not guarantee immunity from liability. Maintainers should obtain legal review before relying on the wording as a legal agreement.

docs.title: Lab Catalog
docs.text:
You don't need a path or URL to start a lab: astrona knows the published trainings and every lab in them, by name.

astrona labs                                   # trainings
astrona labs ATS014                            # a training's labs
astrona labs --search "fault injection"        # search lab titles
astrona run astrona.io/ATS014/section-050/module-01/lab-01

A lab's catalog name may start with the organization — astrona.io/ATS014/…, the form astrona.io shows and the course material uses — or with the GitHub owner, astrona-io/ATS014/…, or leave it out: ATS014/…. All three are the same lab; a name with another owner (someone-else/ATS014/…) is refused, so the name always says where the code comes from. A module's playground isn't listed in the training's manifest but is found by its folder: astrona.io/ATS014/section-000/module-01/playground → sections/section-000/module-01/playground.

A catalog name works wherever a command takes a lab: astrona use astrona.io/ATS014/… picks it for every command, astrona run, submit, reset, test, validate and doctor ATS014/…, and also the commands that otherwise take a running lab's name — astrona status, shell, kubeconfig, destroy ATS014/… and astrona docs question ATS014/…. That way the one name a student copies from astrona.io works for every step. Running-lab names (my-lab, astro-my-lab) and globs work as before: catalog names always contain a /, lab names never do.

docs.title: Your Astrona account
docs.text:
Catalog labs run locally without a login, including astrona run ATS000/section-010/module-01/lab-01 and full resets. When signed out, astrona asks whether you want to continue without tracking progress and results on your Astrona account. The default answer is no; run astrona login to enable tracking. Pass --without-login to explicitly accept running without tracking, including in automation (a command without a terminal requires this flag). For automation, --headless skips the reminder and starts no new account session, even if you are signed in. See headless commands. When running without tracking, no account session is created and no lab page is opened. Sign in optionally to track your time and results on astrona.io:

astrona login      # opens astrona.io in your browser; click Authorize there
astrona whoami     # who is signed in, and on which site (-o json: {signedIn, username, site, keyId})
astrona logout     # revoke the sign-in and forget it

astrona login signs in through the Astrona website, the same way you sign in on astrona.io — you never see any other sign-in page. It opens a page on astrona.io in your browser and shows a short code in the terminal:

Opening your browser to sign in… If it doesn't open, go to https://astrona.io/cli/authorize?code=…
Confirm the code ABCD-EFGH matches the one in your browser.
Waiting for you to authorize this computer… (Ctrl+C cancels)

If you're already signed in on astrona.io, check that the code matches and click Authorize; if not, sign in on astrona.io first and you're brought straight back to that page. The terminal waits and finishes by itself. No password is ever typed into the terminal, and it works from a machine without a browser (open the printed link on any device). The computer shows up on your account under its hostname. Declining in the browser, or letting the code expire, leaves you signed out — run astrona login again.

The sign-in is kept in ~/.astrona/credentials.json (mode 0600; astrona refuses to use it if other users can read it) and renewed automatically; astrona logout revokes it on astrona.io and deletes the file. Login and logout wait for any in-flight token renewal before replacing or deleting the saved sign-in, so a background reporter cannot restore the previous account. A revocation notice from an older website connection only removes the sign-in that connection used; it preserves a newer login. A credentials file from an older astrona (before website sign-in) no longer works: astrona treats you as signed out and asks you to run astrona login again.

Each login also makes a new device key for this computer and keeps its private half in ~/.astrona/device-key.json (mode 0600, refused like the credentials file if other users can read it). Only the public half is sent to astrona.io. astrona signs every call to Astrona and every astrona connect with it, so a copied credentials.json is of no use on another machine. astrona whoami and astrona check show the key's fingerprint, the same one Account → Devices shows on astrona.io. astrona logout deletes the key with the sign-in. A sign-in from an astrona without device keys gets one the next time its token is renewed. If Astrona answers that a call's proof is missing or wrong, or astrona connect stops with "This computer's key does not match its sign-in", run astrona login again. A proof refused for its time means this computer's clock is off; astrona corrects for a small difference itself.

Updating the CLI keeps this login. Development builds made with just build use a separate login in ~/.astrona-dev/credentials.json; rebuilding also keeps it. Switching between a development build and an installed release switches profiles, so each needs its own login. The UI header shows the active profile and site. ASTRONA_URL selects a different site without moving your saved login.

Then astrona run ATS014/…:

  1. checks for an active sign-in before anything is fetched or built — signed out (or the sign-in expired), it runs locally without a session;
  2. when signed in, asks Astrona for a lab session (too many open sessions or an unknown lab stop it here, with nothing built);
  3. builds the lab;
  4. when signed in, prints the lab page URL. A matching course page connects to the ready Lab without redirecting the browser, and the clock starts there, so setup time never counts. Open the printed URL when you are not already in the course. If the build fails, Astrona records that outcome. When Astrona sets a time limit for the attempt, run says so: You have 60 minutes once the lab page opens.

A module's playground has no lab page: its clock starts with the session, its timer (which removes it at the time limit) starts once it's ready, and if the build fails its clock is stopped again. The time limit is what astrona asked for (metadata.timeLimit): a deadline from the site outside it, or less than 5 minutes away, is moved into range.

A full astrona reset ATS014/… does the same: a fresh session and a new lab page (for a playground: a fresh clock and timer) once the lab is rebuilt. Starting over — reset, or run on a lab that's already running — first stops the old playground's clock and timer, so the old timer never removes the new lab. reset --soft and reset --cluster keep the current session and need no sign-in. astrona run renew skips (and forgets) a playground whose cluster no longer exists.

Only labs of the published trainings (repositories owned by the astrona-io GitHub organization) work this way. A lab from a source you added yourself (astrona labs add, or an organization set with ASTRONA_CATALOG_ORG) runs like a --git lab: no sign-in, no lab session, no results sent — astrona says so when it resolves the name — so another repository can never start a session in your account.

The session is remembered with the lab in ~/.astrona/labs/<lab>.json (mode 0600: the site, the session id, the lab and its page — never a token). Then astrona submit:

  1. reads the saved run's local files without checking GitHub or downloading the repository again, reuses approval for that source revision, and grades the lab;
  2. sends the result — the same object astrona submit -o json prints — to the lab page, and prints Sent to your lab page (attempt N): <url>. Only a result graded from the lab the session was started for is sent (another config with the same metadata.name never reaches the page), and each check's message and hint are sent without control characters and cut at 2 KB;
  3. ends the attempt, PASS or FAIL: the result carries the time you spent (elapsedSeconds), the attempt is marked passed or failed, and its timer stops. A submit is final — there is no fixing the lab and submitting again on the same attempt. A failed grade returns exit code 2, even when submission succeeds;
  4. once the server confirms the result — or it is queued, below — automatically deletes the lab through the normal astrona destroy flow, including teardown scripts and kubectl context restoration. This also applies with --headless, -o json, and redirected input. There is no option to keep the lab: teardown.keepCluster does not apply to a submit. A local-only run (--local-only) is never tracked, so its result saved on this machine finishes it and deletes the lab too. If cleanup fails, submit exits 1, names the retry command, and preserves the recorded result. A run restarted during upload is never deleted.

Start a new attempt with astrona run <lab>. To check your work without ending the attempt, use astrona submit --watch: it grades locally without recording or sending results, finishing the attempt, stopping its timer or deleting the lab. Missing cached files must be restored before submission; submit does not download replacements for a saved run.

Each submit carries its own random key (idempotency_key). When Astrona can't be reached, answers with a server error, or needs a new sign-in, submit says the result is queued: it waits in the outbox (below) and goes out in the background with the same key, so a retry never records it twice — Astrona answers a key it already has with the stored result. A queued result still finishes the attempt and deletes the lab: the outbox sends the result before the lab's stop. A result for a session that already has signals waiting in the outbox goes behind them.

When Astrona refuses the result, the grade still stands and nothing is retried: an expired session (or one that isn't yours) says to run the lab again for a new attempt; an attempt that has already ended (a result was already submitted for it, pass or fail) says the attempt has ended and to start a new one with astrona reset <lab>; an attempt holding as many results as Astrona keeps shows Astrona's message plus astrona reset <lab> for a new tracked attempt; a session whose time ran out shows Astrona's message plus how to start a new attempt (astrona reset <lab>, or astrona destroy <lab> then astrona run <lab>). None of these deletes the lab, so astrona reset <lab> can rebuild it as a new attempt. If the run has a tracked session but you are signed out, the result waits in the outbox until you sign in again. An expired access token that cannot be renewed while offline also leaves the result queued. A run that never had a tracked session still needs a new run after login. Under -o json these lines go to stderr, so stdout stays exactly one JSON document.

astrona destroy of a lab that hasn't been submitted tells Astrona too: the attempt ends as destroyed — it stops showing as running on your labs page and never counts. Deletion sends only the session-closure reason, with no grading result or final usage summary. Unsubmitted work is discarded; a submitted attempt keeps its result, pass or fail. (astrona reset and a fresh astrona run close the old attempt the same way.)

Labs from your own files or repositories (-c ./my-lab, --git <url>) are not tied to an account: they run without signing in, and no page is opened.

Release builds default to https://astrona.io. Development builds (just build or unversioned go run) default to http://localhost:3000. You can explicitly select another site:

astrona login --site http://localhost:3000    # e.g. local development (plain http only to localhost)

The site is remembered with the sign-in: whoami, logout and catalog labs use it without repeating it. ASTRONA_URL overrides it for a single command (ASTRONA_URL=https://staging.astrona.io astrona whoami). The sign-in is only ever sent back to the site it came from: with ASTRONA_URL pointing elsewhere, you're signed out until you astrona login on that site. A site without astrona sign-in (/api/cli/config not found) makes login say so and suggest --site.

Signed in to any site other than astrona.io — a local or self-hosted Astrona — every command that sends it something says so first, so nothing goes to an unexpected place unnoticed:

[WARN] Not astrona.io — sending your lab results to http://localhost:3000

It is shown for the sign-in, a new lab session, astrona submit, astrona run renew, stopping a playground's clock and astrona logout; for astrona.io itself nothing extra is printed.

docs.title: Playgrounds
docs.text:
A module's playground (astrona run ATS014/section-000/module-01/playground) is a clean environment to try things in — nothing to submit, no lab page. Instead it is timed, and that time is recorded on your account as playground time:

  1. Like a lab, run checks the sign-in and asks Astrona for a session before anything is built, and says how long you have: Playground time started for <you> on <site> — 120 minutes until it stops and is removed. The clock starts here.
  2. The time limit is the playground's metadata.timeLimit in its config.yaml (90m, 2h, 1h30m; between 5 minutes and 24 hours — see the lab config reference), else the site's default of 2 hours.
  3. Once the playground is built, run starts a watchdog — a detached astrona process in its own session, so closing the terminal doesn't stop it — and prints when it ends: Playground ready. It stops and is removed at 16:40 (in 2h0m0s). The watchdog compares against the wall clock every minute (a laptop that slept still stops on time); at the deadline it stops the clock on the site as "time limit" and removes the cluster exactly like astrona destroy. Its output goes to ~/.astrona/labs/<lab>.watchdog.log. If it can't be started, run warns and the playground stays until you astrona destroy it — the site still stops the clock at the deadline.
  4. astrona destroy ends it sooner: it stops the watchdog and the clock (as "destroyed") and removes the playground. It prints nothing extra when that works; if the site can't be reached it warns — the clock then stops by itself at the time limit.

Still working when the limit is near? astrona run renew starts the timer again with the full time limit, without touching the playground. Its session goes on, and all of its time counts as playground time when it ends:

astrona run renew                                              # every running playground
astrona run renew astrona.io/ATS014/section-000/module-01/playground

Renewed astro-…: it now stops and is removed at 18:35 (in 2h0m0s).

A playground that already stopped can't be renewed — run it again. astrona reset of a playground does what run does: a fresh playground session with a new clock and watchdog once it is rebuilt. If a playground fails to build, its session is stopped, so no time is counted for it.

Before removing a playground, the watchdog locks it and rechecks the run, session, and deadline. A watchdog left over from before a renew, or from a replaced run, cannot stop the playground or remove the lab.

docs.title: Resource usage
docs.text:
While a signed-in lab or playground runs, astrona run also starts a usage reporter — another detached astrona process — that measures what the lab uses on your computer and sends it to the lab session every 15 seconds: CPU in cores and memory in bytes, for the kind cluster and its linked clusters (docker stats / podman stats) or the lab's QEMU VMs (ps). Nothing else is sent: no command output, no file contents, no process names. Astrona uses it to show what labs really cost to run, and what practising locally saves against the cloud.

The reporter ends on its own when the lab is destroyed or run again, when its session is gone or expired, or when the site stops taking samples (a lab that passed). It follows astrona run renew. Its output goes to ~/.astrona/labs/<lab>.usage.log. astrona submit and playground deletion also send a short summary (average and peak CPU and memory), which the site uses when no sample reached it. A run that is not signed in sends nothing.

To send none of this, choose one of two ways:

  • astrona settings set usage-samples no (or usage-samples in Preferences) turns it off for every run: no reporter starts, a running reporter stops at its next sample (within 15 seconds), samples still waiting in the outbox are dropped instead of sent, and astrona submit and playground deletion send no usage summary. Results already waiting in the outbox also omit their saved usage summary when delivered after you turn this setting off. Progress, results and the lab's clock are still sent. astrona settings set usage-samples yes turns it back on for the next astrona run.
  • astrona run --local-only <lab> keeps one whole run on this machine: astrona does not read your sign-in, starts no lab session, and sends no progress, results, clock signals or usage. astrona submit grades it and records the result locally only, then deletes the lab like any finished run. Starting a running lab over with --local-only detaches its old session without closing it on Astrona.

astrona logout stops the usage reporters of running labs, since they post with your sign-in. The labs keep running; samples measured before the sign-out that were not sent yet wait in the outbox until you sign in again (or are dropped if usage samples are off). A playground's watchdog keeps running, so the playground is still removed at its time limit. Signing in again does not restart a reporter for a lab that is already running.

docs.title: Paused time and working offline
docs.text:
The browser workspace does not pause your time. Once you click Start, the lab's clock keeps running when you close the page or lose the connection, and a playground is still removed at its time limit.

Everything astrona tells Astrona about a running lab — the start from the browser workspace, pauses and resumes, resource samples, destroy and the time-limit stop — is saved on your computer first (~/.astrona/outbox) and then sent. If the connection drops, it waits there and goes out in order, with the time each thing happened, once Astrona is reachable again: from the usage reporter, or a background astrona that the next command starts. While you are signed out, signals wait for astrona login. Each lab session's signals go out in order; one Astrona can't accept yet holds back only that session's later signals, not other sessions'. A signal still waiting after 7 days is dropped, and a damaged outbox file is set aside (renamed *.json.corrupt-*, removed after 7 days) instead of blocking its session. A graded result (astrona submit) that could not be sent waits here too, with its key, so it is recorded once however often it is retried.

docs.title: Where the catalog comes from
docs.text:
• Published trainings — repositories in the astrona-io organization with the astrona-training topic. astrona finds them with a GitHub search and reads every page of its results, up to the 1,000 GitHub returns for one search.
  • Your own — astrona labs add <git url> adds any git repository with an astrona.yaml (GitHub repos are read directly, others are cloned). astrona labs remove <git url> takes it out again, and astrona labs sources shows everything the catalog reads.

The catalog is cached for an hour in ~/.astrona/catalog.json; --refresh reads it again. When it can't be refreshed (offline), the last copy is used, with a warning. ASTRONA_CATALOG_ORG points it at another organization (empty: only your own sources).

docs.title: Lab names
docs.text:
A training's astrona.yaml lists its labs (content entries of type: lab, in modules, or in sections with their modules and capstone). A lab's name is the training id and the lab's path, without sections/ and labs/:

sections/section-050/module-01/labs/lab-01   →   ATS014/section-050/module-01/lab-01

The training id (training.id, else the repository name) must be a plain name — letters, digits, - and _ — and can't be an owner name (astrona-io, astrona.io): a name like astrona.io/ATS014/… always means the astrona-io repositories, never a training called astrona.io. A training with such an id is skipped, and listed among the catalog's errors.

Training ids are unique (in any case). When two sources declare the same id, the one from the astrona-io organization wins (else the first by repository URL); the other is skipped, and the catalog's errors name both repositories — so a source you add can't take over the name of a published training.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: A lab from the catalog is a remote lab: astrona fetches the training's repository with git and asks for your trust before running it, showing what it will do — like any --git lab (--trust approves it up front, e.g. in CI). An official training's lab (astrona-io) skips the prompt only when the fetched commit is the one astrona.io publishes for that training and the checkout is unchanged; any mismatch asks as usual (see Official labs). Everything a manifest says is treated as data: a lab path that would leave the repository is rejected. A path that exists on your disk always wins over a catalog name.

docs.title: Publishing a training
docs.text:
Give the repository an astrona.yaml:

training:
  id: ATS014
  title: "ICA: Traffic Management"
  description: …
modules:
  - id: module-010
    content:
      - type: lab
        title: "Route Requests By Header Lab"
        path: sections/section-010/module-01/labs/lab-01   # a lab directory with config.yaml

…and the astrona-training topic (in the astrona-io organization) — or tell people to astrona labs add its URL.

docs.title: Full Lab Exams
docs.text:
A full lab exam, such as the CKS practice exam, is a set of tasks from the lab catalog that you work through against the clock, on several Kubernetes clusters that run on this computer. astrona exam builds the clusters, shows the tasks, handles breaks, and grades everything at the end. You see your score on the exam page, not in the terminal.

You need to be signed in (astrona login), and your container engine needs enough memory for every cluster at once.

docs.title: Start an exam
docs.text:
astrona exam start cks

Before anything is created, astrona checks the exam's clusters against your container engine's memory. The clusters, plus any kind clusters already running, must fit in 75% of it. If they don't, astrona prints how much the exam needs and stops. Nothing is counted.

If they fit, the tasks are drawn and astrona:

  1. builds every cluster in parallel (--parallel sets how many at once);
  2. applies each task's setup to the cluster it is assigned to, with the lab's own CA first when the lab has one (sharedCA). The setup scripts and later the grading run with that cluster's exam-<n> context (see runtimes);
  3. adds a kubectl context for each cluster: exam-1, exam-2, and so on;
  4. opens the exam page (--no-browser prints its address instead).

The exam page follows these steps. If one fails, or you press Ctrl+C, every exam cluster is deleted and the attempt doesn't count. Run astrona exam start again for a new draw.

The clock does not run while the clusters are prepared. It starts when you press Begin exam on the exam page.

docs.title: Work on the tasks
docs.text:
astrona exam task 1

prints a task with its weight and the context it uses:

Task 7 (6.67%)   Use context: kubectl config use-context exam-3

astrona does not switch the context for you. Run the use-context command yourself before you start a task, as in the real exam.

astrona exam next and astrona exam prev move one task forward or back. Take the tasks in any order. When you move away from a task, astrona grades it quietly and keeps that result, so a crash later doesn't lose your work. You don't see these results.

astrona exam status shows the time left, the breaks used, and every task with its weight and context.

docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
astrona exam break

stops the clock and pauses every exam cluster, so kubectl against an exam-<n> context waits until the break ends. The exam page lists how many breaks you have and how long each may last (for CKS, 3 breaks of at most 15 minutes). A break ends when you run astrona exam resume, or by itself at its limit.

docs.title: Submit
docs.text:
astrona exam submit

asks for confirmation, then grades every task on its cluster, sends the results, deletes the exam clusters and the exam-<n> contexts, and switches kubectl back to the context you had before the exam. When the time runs out, the same happens without you: a background watchdog started by astrona exam start grades and cleans up at the deadline.

If results can't be sent (for example, you're offline), astrona keeps them and sends them with the next astrona exam command.

docs.title: Abandon
docs.text:
astrona exam abandon

ends the exam at once and deletes its clusters, without grading the tasks again. After Begin exam, the attempt is scored from the results already sent (the ones kept when you moved between tasks). Before Begin exam, it is cancelled and doesn't count.

docs.title: After a crash or a reboot
docs.text:
astrona exam resume

checks the exam's clusters, rebuilds any that are gone with their tasks' setups, and restarts the watchdog. The clock keeps running while it rebuilds, and work on a rebuilt cluster is lost.

To continue on another computer an exam you started elsewhere, name it: astrona exam resume cks. Every cluster is prepared again there.

docs.title: What runs on this computer
docs.text:
• One kind cluster per exam cluster, named astro-exam-<attempt>-<n>. Don't delete them during the exam.
  • The exam-<n> kubectl contexts in your kubeconfig. If you already have a context with one of those names that doesn't belong to an exam, start refuses until you rename it.
  • The exam's record in ~/.astrona/exams/current.json, and a watchdog process (astrona exam-watchdog) that logs to ~/.astrona/labs/.

docs.title: Lab Resources
docs.text: Labs and playgrounds ship scripts, manifests and other files in resources/ next to config.yaml. Astrona snapshots them when the lab starts. Nothing runs until the student asks.

docs.title: Inside the lab terminal
docs.text:
Open a lab tab, astrona shell <lab>, or astrona ssh <vm>. Astrona provides an editable ~/resources folder and a resource-only astrona helper:

astrona res
ls ~/resources
astrona res show count-versions.sh
astrona res run count-versions.sh -- "${SCOUT}/0"
bash ~/resources/count-versions.sh "${SCOUT}/0"

The full relative filename and the existing short name both work: count-versions.sh and count-versions. Nested entries such as tools/check.sh retain their folder structure. In Kind Bash terminals, Tab completes resource filenames after astrona res run, show, path, or copy.

SCOUT must be defined in the terminal where you run the command. Shell variables are expanded there; Astrona passes the resulting arguments literally, including spaces, quotes and arguments beginning with -. Use -- before script arguments.

All terminal tabs for a Kind run share the same editable files. QEMU tabs for the same VM share that VM's files. Opening another tab, reconnecting, or running a resource again preserves edits. A full reset restores the shipped originals. Different labs, and different VMs, have separate workspaces. A VM folder that already exists without an Astrona receipt is preserved; move it aside before initializing resources.

The helper supports res / resource / resources with list, show, path, copy, and run. It runs entirely inside the terminal or VM. Lifecycle and account commands still belong in your host terminal. The helper needs no host socket or credentials. copy refuses an existing destination.

docs.title: From your host terminal
docs.text:
astrona res --lab <lab>
astrona res run count-versions.sh --lab <lab> -- "${SCOUT}/0"
astrona res copy broken-deployment.yaml
astrona res path broken-deployment.yaml

By default, res run enters the lab environment: an isolated tools container for Kind, or the student account in the selected QEMU VM. It uses the same editable resources as interactive terminal tabs, never silently falling back to host execution. The command prints the lab, execution location and working directory.

For a Kind script that deliberately requires host tools, opt in explicitly:

astrona res run local-tool.sh --host --lab <lab> -- --example

--host can access your host files and uses your host tools. It is unavailable inside the resource-only helper and for QEMU resources. The existing host execution rules are retained for this explicit compatibility option.

Host res path, show and copy use the editable Kind workspace when it has been initialized; otherwise they use the original snapshot. For QEMU, use those commands inside the VM to inspect edits; the host has the shipped snapshot.

Host res copy --force replaces an existing destination only when it is separate from the source. Copying onto the source, into its own subdirectories, or over a directory containing it is refused before any files are changed. This also applies when the destination reaches those paths through a directory symlink.

docs.title: Execution rules
docs.text:
Resource Runs as Working directory in the lab Has run: The command split into arguments, without shell evaluation Resource folder, or containing folder for a file *.sh bash <file> Containing folder Kind *.yaml / *.yml kubectl apply -f <file> Containing folder Executable with #! The file itself Containing folder Other file or folder without run: Use show, copy or path —

Sibling files are available without additional copying. $ASTRONA_RESOURCE_DIR points at all the lab's resources. $ASTRONA_LAB identifies the selected lab. Kind commands use the lab's kubeconfigs and linked clusters, without mounting host homes, SSH agents or container engine sockets. Scripts requiring tools not included in the terminal image must supply those tools or explicitly use --host.

For QEMU, select a VM with --vm <name>, the resource's vm: field, or the lab's only VM. A multi-VM lab without a selection reports which VM to choose. YAML is a plain file in QEMU. Resources are installed through the student SSH identity, without sudo, on first access. Subsequent access checks the workspace receipt without re-uploading files. Custom SSH users/password sessions do not provision another user's resources automatically.

docs.title: Selecting a lab
docs.text:
From the host, Astrona picks resources in this order:

  1. --lab <lab> (running name or catalog name).
  2. $ASTRONA_LAB.
  3. The lab selected by -c / --git or astrona use.
  4. The only lab with resource snapshots.

Several possible labs cause an error listing the choices. Inside a lab terminal, the helper always works on that terminal's workspace.

docs.title: Authoring and sharing
docs.text:
Keep resources in the same repository and pinned revision as the task:

playground/
  config.yaml
  resources/
    count-versions.sh
    examples.json
    tools/
      check.sh

Everything directly in resources/ is included automatically, including folder contents. The optional resources: list adds descriptions and custom commands, or exposes a nested file as its own named resource. No separate student download or copy step is needed. See the resource configuration reference.

Resource short names must be unique. Remote code approval covers the exact lab revision and its resources. Copies reject symlinks and escaping paths and retain the existing file-count and size limits. Nothing executes while copying or opening a terminal. Host snapshots live under ~/.astrona/resources/<lab>; development builds use ~/.astrona-dev. Kind edits live under runtime/<lab>/work/resources. Destroy removes the workspace; --keep-resources retains the original snapshot.

docs.title: Linked Labs
docs.text:
Some things can only be practised with two systems: an app logging in against an external identity provider, a client calling a service in another cluster, network policy between "sites". A lab can run extra kind clusters side by side with its own — declared under runtime.kind.clusters in the same config.yaml — and knows how to reach them.

The worked reference is examples/linked-labs-01: an idp cluster serving a token endpoint, and a task to log in against it from the lab's own cluster. astrona init lab <dir> --linked scaffolds a lab like it.

docs.title: Declaring linked clusters
docs.text:
metadata:
  name: auth-lab

runtime:
  type: kind
  kind:
    preloadImages: [curlimages/curl:8.11.1]     # the lab's own cluster
    clusters:
      - name: idp                                # kind cluster astro-auth-lab-idp
        preloadImages: [nginx:1.27-alpine]
        nodes: {workers: 0}
        addons: {certManager: true}
        bootstrap:
          manifests:
            - {name: idp, type: file, source: clusters/idp/bootstrap/idp.yaml}
          waitFor:
            - {resource: deploy/idp, namespace: auth}
        testing:                                 # its part of the reference solution
          init:
            - {name: seed users, type: file, source: clusters/idp/testing/seed.sh}

Each entry takes the same cluster fields as runtime.kind (version, nodes, networking, addons, preloadImages, …) plus its own bootstrap and testing. Up to 5 per lab; names are lowercase letters, digits and - (max 20 characters). See runtime.kind.clusters.

Linked names must not collide with another lab. For example, auth-lab with linked cluster idp cannot replace a standalone lab named auth-lab-idp. Astrona checks every linked name before changing any cluster and only replaces existing clusters recorded as belonging to this lab. The same ownership check protects teardown scripts, linked resets and deletion. If an older installation has lost its saved ownership, inspect astrona list and explicitly destroy the leftover cluster by its full name before retrying; editing a config cannot claim an existing cluster.

DNS refresh also checks ownership and locks every linked cluster it updates. Busy or replaced linked clusters are skipped with a warning and excluded from the refreshed DNS routes; the lab remains accessible.

docs.title: Dependencies and start order
docs.text:
By default clusters are created one at a time: every linked cluster first, then the lab's own. Each one is only created once the previous is fully ready — its bootstrap done and its waitFor gates passed. Use dependsOn when one linked cluster needs another:

    clusters:
      - name: db
        bootstrap: {manifests: [{name: db, type: file, source: clusters/db/bootstrap/db.yaml}],
                    waitFor: [{resource: statefulset/db, namespace: data}]}
      - name: idp
        dependsOn: [db]          # created only once db is ready
        bootstrap:
          init:
            - {name: configure, type: file, source: clusters/idp/bootstrap/configure.sh}   # gets $ASTRONA_CLUSTER_DB_HOST
  • Dependencies are created first; otherwise clusters start in the order listed.
  • A cluster's scripts get the ASTRONA_CLUSTER_* addresses of the clusters it depends on (the lab's own scripts get all of them).
  • If a cluster fails, the run stops there: nothing that depends on it — and not the lab itself — is started, and the error says what was skipped. astrona destroy cleans up what was created.
  • Unknown names, a cluster depending on itself, and cycles are rejected by astrona validate.
  • astrona test applies the clusters' testing blocks in the same order; astrona start restarts them in it.

docs.title: Creating clusters in parallel
docs.text:
--parallel N (on run, reset and test, max 5) creates up to N linked clusters at once — faster on a machine with memory to spare:

astrona run -c ./my-lab --parallel 3
  • dependsOn still holds: a cluster starts as soon as everything it depends on is ready, so independent clusters come up together.
  • The kind create cluster step itself runs one at a time, so your kubectl current-context is still restored correctly and ~/.kube/config is never written by two creates at once; everything after it (addons, bootstrap, readiness) runs in parallel.
  • After the first failure nothing new starts; clusters already being created finish, and the error lists what was never started. astrona destroy cleans up what exists.
  • Each cluster logs to its own run log (~/.astrona/logs/linked-<cluster>-…); the screen shows one line per cluster as it becomes ready or fails, with the log path on failure.
  • The lab's own cluster is still created last, after all of them.

docs.title: Folder layout
docs.text:
Paths are relative to config.yaml, like everywhere else. By convention each linked cluster keeps its files in its own folder under clusters/, next to docs/ and solution/:

config.yaml
docs/                     # student docs
solution/                 # the lab's own reference solution
clusters/
  idp/
    bootstrap/            # sets up the idp cluster
    testing/              # the idp cluster's part of the reference solution
    teardown/             # its teardown scripts

docs.title: Renamed in v0.3
docs.text:
astrona v0.2.1 called these names differently. The old ones still work, so existing labs keep running — switch when convenient:

v0.2.1 Now runtime.kind.labs runtime.kind.clusters — labs is still read, with a deprecation warning from run and validate ASTRONA_LINK_<NAME>_* ASTRONA_CLUSTER_<NAME>_* — both are set ConfigMap astrona-links ConfigMap astrona-clusters — both are published, with the same data folders under labs/ clusters/ — only a convention; your paths keep working

docs.title: Reaching a linked cluster
docs.text:
All kind clusters share one container network, so a pod can reach a linked cluster's node. Publish what the lab should reach as a NodePort Service with a fixed nodePort:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: idp, namespace: auth}
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: {app: idp}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080}]

From any cluster of the lab: http://idp.astrona.internal:30080/. A ClusterIP Service name or a pod IP from the other cluster is not reachable — each cluster has its own service and pod network.

docs.title: Stable names: <name>.astrona.internal
docs.text:
Every linked cluster gets a fixed DNS name, <name>.astrona.internal, that resolves to its node in every cluster of the lab — the lab's own and the other linked clusters. It's the same name under astrona run and astrona test (where the container names differ), so manifests and configs can simply contain it: an OIDC issuer URL, a database host, a redirect URI.

  • Astrona looks up each node's IPv4 and writes it into each cluster's CoreDNS config (a marked block in the coredns ConfigMap), refreshing it after start and reset --cluster, when IPs can change.
  • .internal is reserved for private use. (*.localhost wouldn't work: curl and other clients resolve it to 127.0.0.1 without asking DNS.)
  • A lab that replaces CoreDNS's config with one lacking a .:53 server block keeps the container names ($ASTRONA_CLUSTER_<NAME>_HOST) instead.

The same URL on your machine: forward the service with hostPort equal to its nodePort (see below) and add the name to /etc/hosts once — then http://idp.astrona.internal:30080 works in your browser and in the cluster, which is what an identity provider's issuer URL needs:

127.0.0.1 idp.astrona.internal

(Astrona never edits your host /etc/hosts. Isolated Kind terminals get these addresses in their own container hosts file.)

docs.title: Everything astrona publishes
docs.text:
Astrona tells the lab where each linked cluster is:

Where What Every cluster's DNS <name>.astrona.internal The lab's bootstrap/testing/teardown scripts and command checks ASTRONA_CLUSTER_<NAME>_HOSTNAME (the stable name), _HOST (the node's container name), _CONTEXT, _KUBECONFIG (<NAME> upper-cased, - → _) In the lab's cluster ConfigMap astrona-clusters in namespace default: <name>.hostname, <name>.host, <name>.context astrona shell Every cluster's kubeconfig: kubectl --context "$ASTRONA_CLUSTER_IDP_CONTEXT" … works, plus the env vars. astrona shell <lab> --cluster idp makes the idp cluster the default context; astrona kubeconfig <lab> --cluster idp prints its kubeconfig

A linked cluster's own bootstrap/testing scripts run with KUBECONFIG pointing at that cluster.

Use the stable name, not the container name. Under astrona test every cluster has a different container name (astro-test-…) — <name>.astrona.internal doesn't change.

docs.title: Reaching a linked cluster from your machine
docs.text:
A port forward reaches a linked cluster with cluster: — the student's browser can open the identity provider's login page, a database client can connect to the db cluster:

runtime:
  portForwards:
    - name: idp
      cluster: idp              # forwarded from the idp cluster
      resource: svc/idp
      namespace: auth
      targetPort: 80
      hostPort: 30080           # = the NodePort, so one URL works everywhere
      scheme: http

It belongs to the lab like any forward: started after every cluster is up, paused and resumed by stop/start, removed by destroy, listed by astrona port-forward list. Like all forwards it binds 127.0.0.1 only.

docs.title: TLS between clusters: a shared CA
docs.text:
An identity provider is usually reached over HTTPS, and its clients must trust its certificate. runtime.kind.sharedCA: true gives the lab its own certificate authority, trusted by every cluster of the lab:

runtime:
  type: kind
  kind:
    sharedCA: true
    clusters:
      - name: idp
        addons: {certManager: true}
        bootstrap:
          manifests:
            - {name: idp, type: file, source: clusters/idp/bootstrap/idp.yaml}
          waitFor:
            - {resource: certificate/idp, namespace: auth, condition: Ready, timeout: 3m}

What every cluster (the lab's own and each linked one) gets:

ConfigMap astrona-ca in default ca.crt — mount it in a pod to trust the CA (curl --cacert /ca/ca.crt …, SSL_CERT_FILE, a Java truststore, …) Secret astrona-ca (kubernetes.io/tls) The CA's certificate and key — in cert-manager when the cluster has the certManager addon, in default otherwise ClusterIssuer astrona-ca Only with the certManager addon — issue certificates from the lab CA with issuerRef: {kind: ClusterIssuer, name: astrona-ca}

A certificate for the stable name then verifies from any cluster of the lab:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata: {name: idp, namespace: auth}
spec:
  secretName: idp-tls
  dnsNames: [idp.astrona.internal]
  issuerRef: {kind: ClusterIssuer, name: astrona-ca}
  • The CA is created per lab run (ECDSA P-256, can only sign leaf certificates) at ~/.astrona/kind/<lab>/ca.crt (key ca.key, mode 0600) and deleted with the lab; astrona test copies get their own.
  • Scripts, command checks and astrona shell get $ASTRONA_CA_CERT — the path of ca.crt — for curl --cacert "$ASTRONA_CA_CERT" … from your machine (with the /etc/hosts line and a port forward).
  • astrona never adds the CA to your system's trust store.
  • sharedCA is lab-wide: set it on runtime.kind, not on a linked cluster.

docs.title: Simulating a remote site
docs.text:
A linked cluster can behave like a site across a WAN — slow, lossy, bandwidth-limited:

    clusters:
      - name: idp
        wan:
          latency: 80ms      # added per round trip
          jitter: 10ms
          loss: 1%
          rate: 10mbit

astrona applies it with tc netem on every node of that cluster, after the cluster is set up (its bootstrap and readiness gates run at full speed), and re-applies it after astrona start — a restart drops it. It delays what the cluster sends, so the latency is added once per round trip; it affects all its traffic, including kubectl from your machine.

docs.title: Changing conditions live: astrona net
docs.text:
For exercises like "the identity provider got slow" or "the site is down — what breaks?":

astrona net my-lab --cluster idp --latency 400ms --jitter 50ms --loss 10%
astrona net my-lab --cluster idp --partition     # nothing it sends gets through
astrona net my-lab --cluster idp --heal          # back to the config's wan (or none)
astrona net my-lab --cluster idp --show          # what each node has now

Without --cluster it acts on the lab's own cluster. Changes last until --heal, astrona start (which re-applies the config) or destroy. While a cluster is partitioned astrona can't reach its API either — --heal still works, it runs inside the node containers. astrona status shows each linked cluster's configured conditions.

docs.title: Grading across clusters
docs.text:
A check grades the lab's own cluster unless it names a linked one with cluster::

validation:
  checks:
    - name: idp runs 2 replicas
      cluster: idp
      type: jsonpath
      resource: deploy/idp -n auth
      jsonpath: "{.status.readyReplicas}"
      expect: "2"

Works for every check type except http (which runs from your machine). A command check with cluster: gets that cluster's KUBECONFIG.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Linked clusters belong to the lab:

Command What happens astrona run Creates the linked clusters (bootstrap included), then the lab. Refused while the lab is running — astrona reset starts it over astrona list / status A linked cluster is listed as linked cluster of <lab>; status shows each one's state. Commands that pick "the only running lab" ignore linked clusters astrona stop / start Stops/starts them with the lab (start brings them up first) astrona reset --soft Keeps every cluster; puts each back to its just-bootstrapped state (lab namespaces deleted, bootstrap re-run, linked clusters first) — seconds instead of minutes. --soft --cluster idp does only that one astrona reset --cluster idp Rebuilds only that linked cluster of the running lab: its teardown, destroy, then create + bootstrap again (with the addresses of what it dependsOn). The lab and its other clusters are left alone; port forwards into it are restarted. Same name, so the lab's ASTRONA_CLUSTER_*/astrona-clusters stay valid astrona reset / destroy Runs the lab's teardown, then each linked cluster's teardown.init (reverse start order, KUBECONFIG pointing at it), then removes everything. On destroy of a lab from your own files, teardown.keepCluster keeps them all astrona test Creates test copies of every cluster, applies each linked cluster's testing, then the lab's, grades, and tears everything down — even on failure astrona check Counts their memory in the lab's estimate astrona diagnose / test --diagnostics Collects every linked cluster too, under clusters/<cluster>/ in the bundle

After rebuilding a linked cluster, open a new lab terminal to refresh its credentials. Your selected context, namespaces and other kubeconfig preferences are preserved.

Before bootstrap scripts run, astrona run and astrona test wait for the cluster's DNS (CoreDNS) — a script resolving a linked cluster's host in the first seconds after a cluster is created would otherwise fail with bad address.

astrona bundle packs linked clusters too — each must pin its node image (version or image); see Offline Bundles.

docs.title: Planning resources
docs.text: Each linked cluster is a full kind cluster: budget memory for all of them together (roughly 1–1.5 GiB per single-node cluster before workloads) — astrona check -c <lab> estimates it. A linked cluster's gateway addon gets no host ports, so it never clashes with the lab's own.

docs.title: Automatic cache limits
docs.text:
Disposable caches have a default retention of 30 days and a combined maximum size of 50 GB. Change them with:

astrona settings set cache-retention-days 30
astrona settings set cache-max-size-gb 50
astrona settings set cache-max-size-gb 0  # unlimited size; age limit still applies

Astrona checks the limits when astrona run or astrona test finishes, including when it fails after setup. These are the commands that download images, addons and Git checkouts; other commands never delete cache entries. It deletes expired entries first, then the oldest remaining entries until their combined size fits the budget. Age uses filesystem modification times; for a Git checkout, the newest entry within it determines its age. Reading a cache file alone does not reset its age. Images and their metadata are removed together. GB means 1,000,000,000 bytes, measured as logical file sizes.

The limits cover downloaded images/addons, cached Git checkouts, catalog metadata, update-check metadata and VM state left by older versions. They do not cover lab disks, student resources, results, logs, bundles, installed tools, credentials, or Docker/Podman storage.

This is cleanup after lab runs, not a background service or a download quota. Nothing expires while the CLI is not running. If any saved lab state exists, including a stopped VM, all cache eviction is deferred to protect dependencies. Cleanup never waits: if any other CLI command is running, it is skipped and tried again after a later run, so it never delays the command you started. Usage can therefore exceed the limits while downloads or labs need it. A notice on stderr explains deferrals and reports removed entries without changing JSON stdout or the original command's exit code. Help, completions, settings and data inspection skip release checks, so cleanup remains available without contacting GitHub.

Preview or explicitly apply just the configured policy:

astrona data clean --policy
astrona data clean --policy --yes
astrona data clean --policy --yes --dry-run  # preview only

Settings changes take effect after the next run or test, or on policy cleanup; changing a setting does not itself delete anything. Policy cleanup needs valid settings. Ordinary data clean and data reset remain usable for repair when settings are malformed. --policy cannot be combined with --temp-only.

docs.title: Inspect and clean manually
docs.text:
Inspect local files without connecting to Astrona or starting a container engine:

astrona data
astrona data -o json

The report lists file counts and logical byte sizes under ~/.astrona and the Astrona Git cache (~/Library/Caches/astrona/repos on macOS, normally ~/.cache/astrona/repos on Linux). It includes saved results, logs, VM state and installed CLI versions, but does not read their contents or follow symlinks. Logical sizes can exceed actual disk use for sparse VM disks. Docker/Podman storage and progress saved to your account are outside this report.

Preview cleanup before applying it:

astrona data clean
astrona data clean --yes
astrona data clean --temp-only
astrona data clean --temp-only --yes

Cleanup removes downloaded image/addon caches, cached Git checkouts, and the catalog/update-check metadata. Those files will need to be downloaded again; check that you no longer need them offline. --temp-only limits deletion to partial image/addon downloads older than 24 hours inside Astrona's cache. It does not scan the system temp directory or delete unrelated temporary files.

If any saved lab, VM, Kind, exam or port-forward state exists, caches are kept. Permanent mutation locks and helper logs are kept but do not block cleanup after the lab is gone. Stopped VMs can still depend on cached backing images. Use astrona list to inspect your labs and astrona destroy <lab> to remove those you no longer need. Do not delete state files to bypass this check. Symlinked cache locations are rejected, and symlinks at the top of a cache are kept for manual inspection.

docs.title: VM state from older versions
docs.text:
Older Astrona versions could leave a VM's state directory under ~/.astrona/qemu/<vm>/ without a handle.json. No command can reach such a VM, but its disks (large qcow2 files) would stay forever and keep caches from being cleaned. astrona data clean lists such a directory, with its size, as VM state from an older Astrona and removes it with --yes when all of these hold:

  • it is a real directory directly under ~/.astrona/qemu (symlinks are kept and never followed);
  • it has no handle.json;
  • nothing in it changed for 24 hours, so a lab that is still starting is left alone;
  • no qemu-system process started with -name astrona-<vm> is running. If one is, or processes cannot be listed, the directory is kept and the preview says so.

Once removed, it no longer counts as saved lab state, so caches can be cleaned in the same run. Automatic cleanup after run and test treats these directories like other disposable entries: they are removed once older than cache-retention-days or when the size limit is exceeded. astrona destroy <lab> removes the lab's own directory straight away, under the same process check. --temp-only never touches VM state.

Ordinary commands hold a shared maintenance lock, so they can run side by side; confirmed cleanup or reset requires an exclusive lock. A command that finds the lock taken prints Waiting for another Astrona command to finish with local data... on stderr and waits up to 5 seconds before it gives up with an error. Cleanup or reset therefore fails while a lab command such as astrona run is still in progress; finish it first. The background helpers that only report usage, send saved results or keep port forwards running do not take the lock; a playground's time-limit watcher takes it only while it destroys the playground. astrona connect releases its shared lock after setup, so an idle connection does not block cleanup or reset. Lab commands started by the connection take their own maintenance locks. The browser workspace server (astrona ui serve, started by astrona run) holds the shared lock while it runs and stops by itself only after 15 minutes idle, so confirmed cleanup or reset stops it first, the same way astrona ui stop does, and says so in one line on stderr. Its browser terminals close; labs keep running. If the server cannot be stopped, the command fails and asks you to run astrona ui stop. Older CLI releases do not take this lock. Finish those commands before applying maintenance. The .maintenance.lock and settings.json.lock files stay in place; their presence does not mean a process is running. Never delete them to unlock the CLI.

Reset saved CLI preferences and the selected lab:

astrona data reset
astrona data reset --yes

Reset deletes only settings.json, settings-review.json, current.json, update-check.json, and catalog.json. It works even if a settings file contains invalid JSON. This restores preference defaults and clears the astrona use selection; it does not restart or destroy a lab. Credentials, trust approvals, custom catalog sources, results, resources, bundles, logs and installed tools are preserved. Use astrona logout separately if you want to sign out.

Both commands accept -o json. Without --yes they only preview; --dry-run always prevents deletion, even when combined with --yes. The CLI cannot restore deleted files. To remove old logs or unused CLI releases, use the existing commands:

astrona logs clean --older-than 168h --keep 10
astrona versions list

docs.title: macOS Kind startup regression
docs.text:
The opt-in macOS Kind coexistence workflow (.github/workflows/macos-kind.yml) uses a self-hosted Apple Silicon Mac with Docker Desktop running under a standard account, outside the admin group. Install Go, Kind and kubectl for that user and label the runner astrona-kind-standard-user. Run it manually with workflow_dispatch on a reviewed branch; it does not execute pull-request code automatically. Do not use sudo to run the test.

The test creates two ordinary Kind clusters (one with a worker), then runs ATS013/section-010/module-01/playground signed out with explicit --headless setup. It verifies API-server health, node readiness, CoreDNS rollout and a service DNS lookup from a pod. After destroying the lab, it checks that its containers and lab state are gone, the prior kubectl context is restored, and both existing fixture clusters are still healthy with the same container IDs. Its exit trap removes the fixtures and preserves failure logs. It refuses existing clusters whose names would collide with the test.

To run locally:

go build -o /tmp/astrona ./cmd/astrona
ASTRONA_REQUIRE_MACOS_STANDARD_USER=1 bash .github/scripts/test-kind-coexistence.sh /tmp/astrona /tmp/macos-kind-diagnostics docker

The same script can run with podman on macOS or Linux without the standard-user assertion. That exercises coexistence, DNS and teardown, but does not validate Docker Desktop or prove that a non-admin macOS account works. Ubuntu coverage remains in the ordinary CI workflow.

Astrona state and kubeconfig are isolated. The test preserves the caller's Docker configuration and XDG configuration so per-user runtime connections still work. Allow room for four new nodes, plus your existing workloads. Failure diagnostics include only the test's clusters; existing user clusters are never selected for deletion. Raw logs can contain lab script output, so review them before sharing outside your team.

docs.title: Kernel keyring quota failures
docs.text:
When multiple clusters share a rootless engine, its Linux kernel keyring quota can prevent pod sandboxes from starting. The event contains unable to create session key: disk quota exceeded; this refers to kernel keys, not disk storage. A local macOS/Podman regression run reproduced this failure with the default 200-key quota. The automatic diagnostics preserved the events and all test clusters were removed.

astrona check and the startup checks read quota usage through an existing Kind control-plane node, including nodes created outside Astrona. They warn about small limits or nearly exhausted quotas. With no running Kind node the VM quota cannot be read this way; failure diagnostics still recognize the event and explain it. These checks never change kernel settings.

Ask the Linux VM/host administrator to review kernel.keys.maxkeys and kernel.keys.maxbytes, or reduce concurrent clusters. On macOS these settings belong to the engine's Linux VM, not macOS. Kind's upstream issue suggests maxkeys=20000 and maxbytes=500000 for rootless workloads: Kind issue #3806. A rootful engine connection has different quotas and can be tested separately; that does not establish non-admin Docker Desktop support. Increasing the DNS timeout cannot resolve an exhausted kernel quota.

docs.title: Offline Bundles
docs.text:
For classrooms and air-gapped machines: pack a kind lab with everything it would otherwise download, carry one file, run it without internet.

# on a machine with internet
astrona bundle create -c ./labs/k8s-web-01 -o k8s-web-01.tar.gz

# on the offline machine
astrona bundle inspect k8s-web-01.tar.gz    # what's inside (verifies, installs nothing)
astrona bundle load k8s-web-01.tar.gz       # verify, load images, unpack the lab
astrona run -c ~/.astrona/bundles/k8s-web-01-<hash>

docs.title: What's in a bundle
docs.text:
Content Why The lab directory (without .git) config, docs, scripts, manifests, reference solution Node image (runtime.kind.version / image, or --node-image) what kind boots the cluster from runtime.kind.preloadImages the lab's own workloads Addon manifests + every image they reference Calico, cert-manager, metrics-server install offline

Every image is a docker/podman save archive recorded with its SHA-256; astrona-bundle.json describes it all.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
astrona bundle load:

  1. Extracts safely — refuses absolute paths, .., symlinks and hard links, and anything over 30 GB / 100,000 entries.
  2. Verifies every image and addon manifest against its recorded SHA-256, and the CPU architecture (an arm64 bundle won't load on amd64).
  3. Asks before installing anything — a bundle is someone else's code, so you see what the lab will do, pinned to the bundle's SHA-256 (--trust to approve without asking; see Approving remote labs).
  4. Loads the images into Docker/Podman.
  5. Seeds the addon cache — only with manifests matching the exact versions astrona itself pins, so a bundle can't change what an addon installs.
  6. Unpacks the lab into ~/.astrona/bundles/<lab>-<hash>/.

After that it's an ordinary local lab — run, test, reset, submit work as usual, and addon images are loaded into the cluster nodes from the host (no registry).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• kind labs only — qemu labs already cache their base images.
  • The node image must be pinned — runtime.kind.version/image, or --node-image when creating; kind's built-in default can't be determined reliably.
  • No type: url scripts or manifests — they're fetched at run time; make them local files.
  • Not the gatewayAPI addon yet — Envoy Gateway starts its proxy image at runtime and it isn't listed in its manifest.
  • Linked clusters must pin their node image (version or image on each runtime.kind.clusters entry) — offline, an unpinned cluster would boot kind's default image, which may not be the one in the bundle. Their node images, preload images and addon manifests are bundled with the lab's (each once), and addon images are preloaded into every cluster that installs addons.
  • Bundles are per CPU architecture.

docs.title: Writing a Question Bank
docs.text:
A question bank is the knowledge check (quiz) at the end of a module: one YAML file with multiple-choice questions. It lives in the training repository next to the readings it asks about, and astrona.yaml lists it as a quiz item:

      - type: quiz
        title: "Knowledge Check: Shift Traffic With Weighted Routing"
        path: sections/section-020/module-01/quiz.yaml
        pass_score: 70          # percent to pass, above 0 and at most 100 (default 70)

The bank has a JSON Schema, so the bank doesn't need a copy of it in the training repository. Point your editor at it with the first line of the file:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://cli.astrona.io/schema/question-bank.schema.json

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://cli.astrona.io/schema/question-bank.schema.json
schema_version: 1
kind: question_bank
id: ats014-020-01
course_id: ATS014
status: draft
provenance: Original practice material written for this course; not official exam questions.
scope:
  type: module
  id: section-020/module-01
  title: Shift Traffic With Weighted Routing
questions:
  - id: ats014-020-01-q01
    type: single_choice
    difficulty: beginner
    learning_objective: >-
      Write a VirtualService route with several weighted destinations.
    source_readings:
      - sections/section-020/module-01/course-01-split-traffic-with-weighted-destinations.md
    prompt: >-
      Where does the `weight` field go in a weighted `VirtualService` route?
    options:
      - id: a
        text: Inside `destination`, next to `host` and `subset`
        explanation: Kubernetes rejects the object, because `destination` has no `weight` field.
      - id: b
        text: Next to `destination`, in the same item of the `route` list
        explanation: Correct. Each `route` item has a `destination` and a `weight`.
      - id: c
        text: In the `DestinationRule` subset
        explanation: A `DestinationRule` defines subsets. It never splits traffic.
    correct_option: b
    explanation: The `weight` field sits next to `destination`, not inside it.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Required Description schema_version yes 1 kind yes question_bank id yes Stable id of the bank course_id, exam_code no The training and the exam the questions practise for status no draft or reviewed. A draft bank works, but validation warns until someone has reviewed it provenance no Where the questions come from. Say so when they are original material and not official exam questions scope no What the bank covers: type (module, section or domain), id and title questions yes 1–30 questions. The site uses the first 30

Each question:

Field Required Description id yes Unique in the bank. Keep it stable once published, so results stay comparable type no single_choice, the only type (also the default) difficulty no beginner, intermediate or advanced learning_objective no What a student who answers right can do source_readings no Repository paths of readings to read again. Each must exist; one that astrona.yaml doesn't list as a reading gets no "read it again" link prompt yes The question. Markdown and code work options yes 2–6 options: id and text (required), explanation (why it's right or wrong, shown after answering) correct_option yes The id of one option explanation no Why the answer is right

A missing option or answer explanation is a warning, not an error — write them anyway: they're what teaches after a wrong answer.

docs.title: Checking it
docs.text:
astrona content validate ats ./ATS014

fails on what would keep a question off the site (a repeated id, a correct_option that isn't an option, a source_readings file that doesn't exist, fewer than 2 options) and warns about drafts and missing explanations. See Authoring a Lab for everything it checks.

docs.title: Remote Config Sources
docs.text: --config/-c (default .) and --file/-f (default config.yaml) are persistent flags shared by every command. Where they point isn't limited to a local directory.

docs.title: Local directory or file
docs.text:
astrona run -c path/to/lab           # looks for path/to/lab/config.yaml
astrona run -c path/to/lab/lab.yaml  # -f defaults to config.yaml, but an explicit file path is used as-is
astrona run -c path/to/lab -f lab.yaml

docs.title: Direct URL
docs.text:
astrona run -c https://example.com/labs/k8s-basics-01/config.yaml
astrona run -c https://example.com/labs/k8s-basics-01/          # -f appended: .../config.yaml

Only https:// is accepted for a lab config fetched over the network — astrona refuses a plain http:// config URL outright, and refuses to follow a redirect from an https:// URL to an http:// one. The download is size-capped (10 MiB) so a misbehaving or malicious server can't exhaust disk or memory.

docs.title: Git repository (--git)
docs.text:
astrona run --git https://github.com/org/labs-repo.git -c labs/k8s-basics-01
astrona run --git git@github.com:org/labs-repo.git --git-ref feature-branch -c .

With --git set, --config changes meaning: instead of a local path or URL, it becomes the subdirectory within the cloned repo to use (. for the repo root). --git accepts anything git clone does — https://, git@host:, or ssh:// — so authentication (SSH agent, credential helper) is entirely git's own, astrona doesn't handle credentials itself.

  • --git-ref checks out a specific branch, tag, or commit (default: the repo's own default branch).
  • The clone is cached under your user cache directory, keyed by a hash of the URL and ref as separate values. Repeat runs check the selected remote branch or tag's commit ID with git ls-remote. If that commit is already cached, no fetch is needed. Otherwise, Astrona fetches the selected ref and checks it out. No separate checksum file is required in the lab repository.
  • A full commit hash stays pinned and needs no network check once cached. Other revision expressions, such as main~1, use the normal fetch path.
  • If the metadata check or fetch fails, Astrona warns and uses the cached revision. A first-time clone still needs a connection. The selected commit is recorded in the cache's refs/astrona/cached Git ref; existing caches are supported without re-cloning.
  • Before reusing a checkout, Astrona checks that its saved Git origin matches the requested repository. A mismatch in a current cache stops the command and keeps its files. An older cache with a different origin is left alone; a fresh checkout uses the new cache key. Matching older caches remain usable offline and by running labs.
  • Astrona still restores tracked files and removes untracked and ignored files inside its managed cache on every run, even when no download is needed. Keep your own edits in a separate local checkout and use -c to run it.
  • Both the selected path and the final config file must stay within the clone. This includes --file and the default config.yaml: symlinks outside the repository are refused when starting or reopening a saved run. Symlinks to files inside the repository remain supported. Local -c paths without --git keep their usual behavior.
  • Progress says Cloning … for a new cache, then Checking … followed by Using cached … (no download needed) or Updating … on repeat runs. Progress goes to stderr so JSON output stays clean. Git's own checkout chatter is shown with --verbose, or on failure as part of the error.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text: --git is checked first: if set, it entirely determines how --config is interpreted (as a subdirectory, not a path/URL). Without --git, --config is checked in this order: a https:///http:// prefix (used as a direct URL), otherwise treated as a local filesystem path (file or directory).

docs.title: Path safety
docs.text: Every local path resolution — the lab's own base directory, script/manifest source: file/folder references — must be relative, is joined against the lab's base directory, and is rejected if it would escape it — lexically (../..) or through a symlink committed to the lab (JoinWithinBaseDir). Absolute paths are refused. A lab config can't reference files outside its own directory by accident or by a crafted source value.

docs.title: Approving remote labs
docs.text:
A lab from --git or a URL runs its scripts with bash on your machine (for kind labs), plus any command validation checks, and makes its http checks' requests from your machine. So before run, reset, test or submit executes anything from a remote lab for the first time, astrona shows what it will do and asks:

First time running this lab:
  https://github.com/org/labs@main (labs/lab-01) (01eed0bb08be)

It will:
  • runs on this machine (bash): setup (setup.sh)
  • runs on this machine (command check): kubectl get ns shop -o name
  • requests from this machine (http check): http://web.localtest.me:8080/
  • applies 2 manifest source(s) to the lab cluster
  • opens 127.0.0.1:8080 → svc/web
  • ⚠ fetched when it runs, NOT covered by this approval: https://example.com/extra.sh

Only continue if you trust its author. Run it? [y/N]
  • The approval is pinned: to the git commit for --git, to the SHA-256 of the config for a URL. Running the same version again doesn't ask; a new commit or a changed config asks again ("This lab changed since you approved it").
  • Scripts and manifests with type: url are downloaded when they run, so their content isn't covered by the pin — they're flagged in the prompt.
  • Local configs (-c ./my-lab) are your own files and never prompt.
  • Official catalog labs are pre-trusted, but only for the exact commit Astrona published — see Official labs.
  • Everything the lab supplies to the prompt (names, URLs, commands, resource descriptions) is shown on one line with control characters stripped, so a lab can't hide or fake lines of the prompt with terminal escape sequences or newlines. Resource listings (astrona run, astrona docs, astrona res) are cleaned the same way.
  • astrona destroy asks too, before running a remote lab's teardown scripts (only if it has any). Declining — or no terminal and no --trust — doesn't stop the destroy: the teardown scripts are skipped with a warning and the lab is removed anyway.
  • CI / no terminal: without a terminal, an unapproved remote lab is refused. Pass --trust to approve it — e.g. astrona test --git https://github.com/org/labs --config labs/lab-01 --trust. CI that tests its own checkout (-c .) needs nothing.
  • Approvals are stored in ~/.astrona/trust.json; delete an entry (or the file) to be asked again.
  • A lab whose astronaVersion sends it to another installed astrona is approved here first, before the hand-over — never by the version it asks for (see Astrona Versions).

docs.title: Official labs
docs.text:
A lab you run by its catalog name from an official training (a repository in the astrona-io GitHub organization, see Lab Catalog) runs without the prompt when its content is exactly what Astrona published. Trust is bound to the content, never to the name or URL alone. All of these must hold:

  • you named it from the catalog (astrona run astrona.io/ATS014/…), and it is fetched from https://github.com/astrona-io/<repository>;
  • the checked-out git commit equals the commit astrona.io publishes for that training — the commit Astrona synced the training's catalog entry from, read from https://astrona.io/api/labs over HTTPS when the lab is checked;
  • the checkout has no local changes.

astrona then prints one line on stderr and goes ahead:

Trusted as an official Astrona lab at 3f9c2e7a0d41b6c8e5f2a9d7b1c4e6f8a0b2d4c6 (published by https://astrona.io).

Anything else falls back to the normal prompt, with a line saying why: a different commit (a push astrona.io hasn't synced yet, another ref), a training with no published commit, astrona.io not reachable, local changes, a fork or another host, or a lab from a source you added. Only https://astrona.io vouches for official labs — a site set with ASTRONA_URL or a sign-in elsewhere never does (except in an unversioned development build, for testing a local stack). Nothing is written to ~/.astrona/trust.json: the next run checks again. --trust works as before; without a terminal (--headless, CI) an official lab at its published commit runs, and any other remote lab still needs --trust.

docs.title: Persistent CLI settings
docs.text:
astrona settings lists your preferences and shows whether each value is saved or comes from the default. Preferences live in ~/.astrona/settings.json, separate from credentials, lab state, and remote-code approvals.

astrona settings
astrona settings view
astrona settings view -o json
astrona settings review
astrona settings set keep-context yes
astrona settings set parallel 2
astrona settings set cache-retention-days 30
astrona settings set cache-max-size-gb 50
astrona settings get keep-context
astrona settings unset keep-context
astrona settings reset
astrona settings reset --yes
astrona settings path
astrona settings -o json
Setting Default Effect verbose no Stream full command output instead of the compact step view keep-context no Leave kubectl's current-context unchanged on commands with --keep-context parallel 1 Start up to 1–5 linked clusters at once on commands with --parallel login-reminder yes Offer guests login before each lab run; no hides reminders usage-samples yes While signed in, send a running lab's CPU and memory use to its lab session (every 15 seconds) and a usage summary with submit and playground deletion; no sends none of it — see Resource usage update-check yes Check for new CLI releases and show update notices cache-retention-days 30 Maximum disposable-cache age; whole days from 1 to 36500 cache-max-size-gb 50 Combined disposable-cache limit in decimal GB; 0 means unlimited size browser always After astrona run of a lab: open the browser workspace always, ask each time, or never

With ask, answering always or never to "Open this lab in your browser?" saves that answer here. On a machine with no browser (no display) the default keeps the run in the terminal; a saved always still prints the workspace link. --browser and --no-browser on astrona run override the setting for one run.

docs.title: Reset to the defaults
docs.text:
astrona settings unset <key> restores one setting. astrona settings reset restores all of them: it removes every saved value from settings.json. Without --yes it only lists what would change, with each saved value next to its default. Nothing is written until you pass --yes.

reset also repairs a settings file that astrona refuses to read (invalid JSON or an unknown key): the preview says so, and --yes replaces the file with the defaults. It leaves your lab, sign-in, trust decisions and catalog sources alone, and keeps settings-review.json, so the review questions are not asked again. To also forget the selected lab and the cached catalog, use astrona data reset.

settings, settings get and settings view display booleans as yes / no; set also accepts true / false and on / off. JSON output and saved files retain true / false.

Explicit flags override saved values, including --verbose=false, --keep-context=false, and --parallel=1. --update-check=false disables update checks for one command; save it with astrona settings set update-check no to keep that preference. The existing ASTRONA_NO_UPDATE_CHECK environment variable, CI detection, and non-terminal output still suppress update checks even when the setting is yes.

Only saved choices are written to the JSON file. Review saves each chosen value, including a default you choose to keep, so later releases cannot silently replace that choice. unset removes one override without changing the others; omitted keys use the built-in defaults. Listing or reading settings does not create a file. The JSON output contains configured values plus defaults, before flags or environment-based suppression are applied.

Writes are atomic, with file permissions 0600 and a 0700 directory when created. A lock prevents simultaneous CLI edits from overwriting each other; retry if another command is changing settings. Settings commands do not contact the network, fetch a lab, or change your sign-in.

You can also edit the JSON file directly. Values must be JSON booleans or whole numbers for parallel and the cache settings. parallel accepts 1 to 5; cache-max-size-gb accepts 0 to 9223372036 without overflowing the byte count. Unknown keys and invalid values are rejected before a normal command runs. A damaged file is never silently overwritten: use astrona settings path to find and repair it. Settings and lock files must not be symlinks. Remote-code trust and automatic confirmation cannot be enabled through settings. ui-task-width, which sized the task pane of the former terminal UI, is no longer a setting: a saved value is ignored and dropped the next time settings are saved.

docs.title: Review settings after an upgrade
docs.text:
astrona settings view gives each setting a readable block with its current value, source, built-in default and explanation. Booleans appear as yes/no; cache settings use days or GB when supported by your CLI version. It also lists pending changes and a review ID. -o json includes the same information; the existing astrona settings -o json remains a flat values object. Both are read-only and show preferences before flags or environment overrides.

Settings review is optional. Normal CLI commands, including headless and CI runs, use saved preferences and built-in defaults without asking for settings confirmation. Missing, outdated or damaged review receipts do not block commands. Starting a lab does not acknowledge settings on your behalf.

Run astrona settings review explicitly when you want to inspect and save choices. The first review covers every setting; later reviews cover only added, removed or changed definitions. A CLI version change alone does not trigger another review.

For each pending setting, the prompt shows its default and current choice. It explains why review is needed: a new setting, a changed default, explanation, behavior revision or explicit-choice requirement. A new default does not replace a saved value. Each chosen value is shown as current → proposed before the final approval prompt. Declining leaves both preferences and the review receipt unchanged; normal commands remain available without completing the review.
