docs.title: astrona resource
docs.text: Show, copy or run the files a lab ships for you (its resources)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
A lab can ship files you need — a setup script, a YAML file to fix, a small program — in its resources/ folder instead of asking you to paste them from the docs. astrona run copies them to ~/.astrona/resources/ and lists them; nothing runs until you ask.

Inside the lab terminal, ~/resources contains your editable copy and astrona res works there too. Full filenames such as count-versions.sh and existing short names both work. Opening more tabs preserves edits; full reset restores originals.

astrona res list the lab's resources astrona res show print one (a folder: its files) astrona res copy [dest] copy it here (or to dest) to edit astrona res path print its path, for $(…) in your own commands astrona res run [args…] run it

Which lab: --lab, else $ASTRONA_LAB if set in your host terminal, else the lab of -c/--git, else the one picked with astrona use, else the only lab with resources. With several labs open in several terminals, run astrona shell <lab> in each and every astrona res there works on that lab.

How run runs one: its run command from the lab (in its folder), .sh with bash, .yaml with kubectl apply -f, an executable with #! directly — in a kind lab always with execution inside the isolated terminal by default. --host explicitly runs on your machine using host tools. KUBECONFIG set to the lab's own kubeconfig, so nothing reaches your other clusters ($ASTRONA_LAB and $ASTRONA_RESOURCE_DIR are set). In a qemu lab it's copied into the VM (~/resources) and run there as the account astrona ssh uses; --vm picks the VM of a multi-VM lab. A plain file can only be shown or copied.

astrona resource [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
astrona res
  astrona res run setup-db
  astrona res copy broken-deployment
  kubectl diff -f $(astrona res path broken-deployment)
  astrona res run load-test --lab ats-014-lab-010-01 -- --rps 50

docs.title: astrona run
docs.text: Start a lab: create its cluster(s) or VM(s) and set it up

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Spin up a lab environment: create the kind cluster or qemu VM(s), run bootstrap init scripts, and apply bootstrap manifests.

Before creating Kind clusters, check the engine, resources and host ports. Memory estimates include running Kind clusters created outside Astrona. Estimates warn; definite environment failures block startup. On startup failure, collect diagnostics under ~/.astrona/diagnostics. Failed Kind creation exports retained node logs before cleaning up that new cluster; later failures leave the lab available for diagnosis. CoreDNS readiness defaults to 3m; runtime.kind.dnsTimeout can override it.

Ctrl+C (or SIGTERM) while the lab is being built stops at the current step, removes what this run created (its clusters or VMs, port forwards, the copy of its resources), closes the lab session it started and exits 1. A second Ctrl+C quits at once; astrona destroy removes whatever is left.

Once a kind lab is ready, kubectl points at it: its context (kind-) becomes the current-context of your kubeconfig ($KUBECONFIG is respected), and astrona destroy switches back to the context you had before — unless you've switched elsewhere meanwhile. --keep-context leaves your current-context alone. qemu labs are reached with astrona ssh.

For a kind lab with runtime.portForwards, the forwards are started last (bound to 127.0.0.1) and their URLs and status are printed when the lab is ready — see astrona port-forward.

A lab from the catalog (astrona run astrona.io/ATS014/section-010/module-01/lab-02, see astrona labs) offers login when you are not signed in: progress and results will not be tracked on Astrona as a guest. Answer yes to log in, no to continue as a guest, or never to continue as a guest and save login-reminder=no. Use --without-login to confirm in automation. If you sign in with astrona login, before anything is built astrona starts a lab session on Astrona; once the lab is ready it prints the lab page URL. Your matching course page connects to it without a redirect, and setup time never counts. Labs from your own files or repositories (-c / --git) run without signing in.

While a signed-in lab runs, a background helper sends its CPU and memory use to the lab session every 15 seconds, and submit and playground deletion send a usage summary; astrona settings set usage-samples no turns that off. --local-only keeps the whole run on this machine: astrona does not read your sign-in, starts no lab session and sends no progress, results or usage, and astrona submit records the result locally only. Starting a running lab over with --local-only detaches its session without closing it on Astrona.

If the lab is already running, run asks whether to destroy it and start over (or keep it as it is); --yes starts over without asking and is required when not in a terminal. If other labs are running, it also offers to destroy them first — only when asked in a terminal; --yes never touches other labs.

An interactive run with the browser setting at always (the default) or --browser opens the browser first: astrona starts the local browser workspace (or reuses a running one), prints its link and opens it. The tab shows the CLI terms when they still need accepting (declining stops the command), then the lab being set up, then the lab. Questions the terminal asks (start over?, log in?, trust?) are answered there. The link has a single-use code that expires after 2 minutes; astrona ui <lab> opens a fresh one and astrona ui stop stops the workspace (labs keep running). An exam's timer starts when you click Start in the browser, not when the lab is ready. With astrona settings set browser ask the lab is set up in the terminal first, which then asks "Open this lab in your browser?" (yes/no/always/never) each run, and never keeps runs in the terminal. --browser and --no-browser decide for one run. Without a terminal on stdin and stdout, or with no browser on the machine (no display), the workspace is not opened unless --browser or a saved always asks for it. --headless never opens the browser.

A QEMU (VM) lab opens the same way, with one terminal tab per VM, each the student's ssh login on that VM; run also prints the astrona ssh command for each VM, and astrona status shows them.

--headless keeps Kind and QEMU setup headless. It skips the browser workspace, login reminder and new account sessions, then returns after setup with the lab still running for external validation. Missing approvals fail instead of prompting, even in a terminal. Terms, settings review, remote-code trust and --yes for replacing an existing run still apply. This uses the normal lab name and setup; it does not grade or clean up automatically. Use astrona destroy when finished, or astrona test for the full setup, reference solution, grading and cleanup pipeline.

astrona run [lab] [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
astrona run astrona.io/ATS014/section-010/module-01/lab-02   # catalog lab: no login needed

docs.title: astrona run renew
docs.text: Give a running playground its full time limit again

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
A playground stops and is removed at its time limit (2 hours unless its config.yaml sets metadata.timeLimit). Still working in it? astrona run renew starts that timer again with the full time limit, without touching the playground. Its session goes on, and all of its time counts as playground time when it ends.

With no name, every running playground is renewed. A name is the lab as astrona list shows it (with or without the prefix shown in astrona list) or its catalog name:

astrona run renew astrona run renew astrona-io/ATS014/section-010/module-01/playground

A playground that already stopped can't be renewed — run it again.

astrona run renew [playground] [flags]

docs.title: astrona setup
docs.text: Install and start what this machine needs to run labs (asks first)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Get this machine ready for labs in one go. astrona setup looks at what astrona check would report, shows each step it would take, and asks before doing it:

• macOS: installs kind, kubectl and Podman with Homebrew, then creates and starts the Podman machine (or starts Docker Desktop if that is what you have). • Linux: installs kind and kubectl with Homebrew, or downloads the versions this astrona release pins into ~/.local/bin and verifies them against SHA-256 checksums pinned in astrona before anything is moved into place. A container engine belongs to your distribution, so setup tells you the command instead of running it with sudo. • Windows: use astrona.exe, whose setup prepares WSL 2 and installs astrona inside it.

It finishes with astrona check. Nothing is installed without a yes, unless you pass --yes.

docs.title: astrona shell
docs.text: Open an isolated terminal (or run one command) for a Kind lab

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Open an isolated container terminal with this Kind lab's credentials, so plain kubectl, helm, k9s, … talk to the lab — without changing your own kubectl current-context. Files are saved under ~/.astrona/runtime//work, mounted as /workspace. Your home directory and host tools are not mounted. Tools are downloaded on first use. Type exit to leave. $ASTRONA_LAB holds the lab name inside the shell (add it to your prompt if you like).

After --, runs that one command instead of a shell (no shell parsing).

A lab with linked clusters (runtime.kind.clusters) gets all of them: kubectl --context $ASTRONA_CLUSTER_<NAME>_CONTEXT reaches one. --cluster makes a linked cluster the default instead.

With no lab-name, uses the lab config from -c/--file/--git, or the only running kind lab. For qemu labs, use astrona ssh.

astrona shell [lab-name] [-- command [args...]] [flags]

docs.text:
astrona shell my-lab
  astrona shell -- kubectl get pods -A
  astrona shell my-lab -- k9s

docs.title: astrona submit
docs.text: Submit the lab to the Proctor for grading

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Submit the running lab to the Proctor for grading: every validation check and script runs, a failed one shows its hint (if the lab author wrote one), and you get a score. Every attempt is recorded — astrona submit --history lists them.

A submit is final: it ends the attempt, pass or fail, and then deletes the lab. To check your work without ending the attempt, use astrona submit --watch: it re-grades continuously while you work and records, sends and deletes nothing.

Saved runs use their local config and cached repository without checking GitHub or downloading again. Approval of the same source revision is reused.

Passing means every check passes, or — when the lab sets validation.passPercent — reaching that score.

With no lab named, none picked with astrona use and no lab config in the current directory, the only running lab is submitted; with several running, it lists them and how to name each.

A catalog lab started while signed in (astrona run ATS…) sends each result to its lab page on Astrona as well, with the time you spent. The result, PASS or FAIL, finishes the attempt and stops its timer, and once the server confirms it (or it is queued, below), submit automatically deletes the lab, exactly like astrona destroy, including in headless and JSON modes. The lab is never kept: teardown.keepCluster does not apply to a submit. A run with nothing to send (--local-only, a lab from your own files) is finished the same way once its result is saved here. Start a new attempt with astrona run <lab>.

Each submit carries its own key. When Astrona can't be reached (or answers with a server error), the result is kept in the outbox on this machine and sent in the background with the same key, so a retry never records it twice; submit says it is queued. A result Astrona refuses (the attempt has already ended, its time ran out, or it holds too many results) is not retried and the lab is left as it is: start a new tracked attempt with astrona reset.

Ctrl+C (or SIGTERM) while grading stops before the next check and exits 1 without recording or sending anything; the lab is left as it is. Once grading is done, the result is recorded and sent regardless. A second Ctrl+C quits at once.

Exit code: 0 passed, 2 graded but didn't pass, 1 something else went wrong. Sending the result to Astrona never changes the grade. A cleanup failure exits 1 and leaves the uploaded result intact.

astrona submit [lab] [flags]

docs.title: astrona test
docs.text: Run the full lab lifecycle for CI: bootstrap, testing, submit, teardown

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Run the full lab lifecycle for CI: bootstrap, apply the reference solution (testing), grade it, and always tear down — proving the lab's own solution passes its checks.

Ctrl-C or SIGTERM (a cancelled CI job) stops the run after the current step, then still collects diagnostics (per --diagnostics) and tears the environment down. Steps astrona is waiting on are not cut short by SIGTERM; send SIGKILL to quit without tearing down.

--repeat N runs the whole lifecycle N times on fresh environments and reports any check that doesn't pass every time (flaky), so race-prone checks are caught before students hit them.

Exit code: 0 passed, 2 graded but didn't pass, 1 something else went wrong (setup, tools, config) — see the CI guide.

docs.title: astrona ui
docs.text: Open a running lab, or every lab on this computer, in the browser

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Open a running lab (Kind or QEMU) in the browser workspace: astrona starts the local workspace server (or reuses a running one), prints a link with a fresh single-use code (valid for two minutes) and opens it in your browser. With no browser on this machine (no display), open the printed link yourself. Use it when a link has expired or the browser tab was closed; it never restarts the lab or its timer, and it uses the saved local files without checking GitHub.

Without a lab name it opens the only running lab. With none or several it opens "Labs on this computer", a page listing every lab and playground that still runs here (labs keep running after astrona run returns), where you open or end them. A lab named status, stop or serve is opened by its full name (astro-status), since the short name is a subcommand.

A QEMU lab opens with one terminal tab per VM, each the student's ssh login on that VM.

astrona ui status shows the workspace server and a fresh link; astrona ui stop stops it (labs keep running).

astrona ui [lab-name] [flags]

astrona ui
  astrona ui my-lab
  astrona ui astro-status   # a lab named status

docs.title: astrona versions
docs.text: Install and list older astrona versions, for labs that need one

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
A lab can say which astrona releases may run it (astronaVersion in its config, e.g. "<0.6.0"). Older releases install side by side as astrona- in ~/.astrona/bin — the newest stays astrona — and astrona hands a lab's commands to the newest installed version it allows. If none is installed, it offers to install the right one (at a terminal; --install-version installs without asking, e.g. in CI). Switching to a release older than the running one is always asked at a terminal, and refused without one — run that astrona- yourself instead. A remote lab must be trusted (--trust) before it's handed over, and never to a version older than 0.4.15 (the newest release with security fixes); only ~/.astrona/bin is searched, not PATH.

Downloads are verified against the SHA-256 digest GitHub records for each release binary. Add ~/.astrona/bin to your PATH to run e.g. astrona-0.2.1 directly.

Development builds do not install or hand commands to release binaries; use your installed release for version management.

astrona versions [flags]

docs.title: astrona whoami
docs.text: Show which Astrona account this computer is signed in to

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Show the Astrona account and site this computer is signed in to, renewing the sign-in if it has expired. Exits 1 when signed out, with how to sign in.

It also prints this computer's device key fingerprint: the same string the website shows for this computer under Settings → Devices, so you can tell which row is this one.

With -o json, stdout is one document {signedIn, username, site, keyId} — also when signed out (signedIn: false), which still exits 1.

astrona whoami [flags]
